Acting on the request of the Los An
geles- Pacific Railway company, the
elected city officials yesterday returned
the annual card passes they have held
over the lines operated by this COM
pany The railway has called in these
passes in conformity with the Wright
law, which prohibits interurban lines
from granting passes outside of the
city limits. The railway will issue
passes to the city officials good in the
city limits.


The Los Angeles-Pacific is the only
railway which has made this demand.
Passes issued by other railway compa-
MES to the city officials have the words
mot good outside the city limits"
printed on them in plain type.


But inside the city limits city Of
ficials have a right to free transporta-
ton on street railways. The franchises
under which the railways operate con-
tain a clause that makes it compulsory
to grant free transportation on these
lines. Elective officials have all been
given card passes. although not all of
them use the privilege. notably the city
attorney, who always pays his fare
even in the city limits and when travel
ing over the lines on official business.
But members of the commissions and
others connected with the city admin
istration who are entitled to free trans
portation have their passes in the form
of ticket books. These have not been
called in.

From the Dundee Advertiser.


The longevity OF olive trees is extraordi-
nary. In Syria recently have been found
some remarkably ancient olive trees.
whose ages are established beyond ques-
ton. A trust deed exists which relates
to an orchard covering 400 trees near
Tripoli. Syria, the trust deed having been
issued 400 years ago. Though the trees
look aged. they still bear fruit of fine
quality in abundance and are likely to
maintain their productiveness for many
hundreds Of years yet. An. olive grove
near Beirut is admitted to be the third
largest olive farm In the world. Syrian
fruit farmers are extending olive culture
with much zeal and effect. One planter
recently set out 100000 trees in block
for commercial purposes. Under Euro
pean systems Of culture the Syrians make
the olive tree bear each season. while In
the old days one crop in three years was
thought to be all that the trees could pro-
duce. This low cropping capacity OF the
trees was due to the native method Of
thrashing the fruits from the branches
with sticks. which seriously injured them.
The methods OF grinding the olives for
oil and picking the fruits are peculiar.
Neither the grinders nor pickers received
wages. but are paid on percentage. The
pickers receive 5 per cent Of the actual
fruit picked and the grinders get 10 per
cent of the fruit ground.

senate.

and Bougere opposed the treaty on the
ground that 1t was not sufficiently ad-

regard to silks and laces. They said also

not rigorous enough, and that the grant
ing Of the minimum rate on agricultural
machinery would be dangerous to home
industries


Minister of Commerce Cruppi and Min
lister of Agriculture Ruau defended the
measure with energy, pointing out that
the treaty was good business arrange

market for French goods.

rate on cattle fattened for slaughter,

From the Boston Transcript.


Unless active measures are soon
taken to save the Barnard Capen house
in Dorchester it will be razed. Already
plans have been made to sacrifice this
ancient landmark before February ID
in order to make way for an apartment
house. This old mansion, which stands
near Washington street, opposite Mel
Vile avenue, was erected some time be-
tween 1880 and 1858. 1t was one Of the
first houses built in the town after the
arrival of the colonists who emiSrated
from England under the guidance of
Rev John White, so often called
father of the colony"


This house is the second oldest in
New England With the exception Of
one wear it has always remained in the
possession Of the family. The west end
of the house was built first. One side
of the original building shows an ar
rangement whereby the inmates could
better protect themselves from the willy
the Massachusetts. whose hoStilities the
wise and judicious chief Chickatdbot,
often found it impossible to control
Several arrows, sent into this early
New England home. have been found
as reminder of those troublesome
days. Inside the living rooms the cell
ings are very low, the highest measur-
ing not more than seven feet. The
beams, projecting below the plaster,
were all hand hewn. as were also the
clapboards and lumber for the floors
Originally the house contained but two
rooms, the larger having an immense
fireplace, which carried the major por-
tion of heat up the chimney. The east
end of the house was erected one
hundred years after the main building,
and contains what was then called
many modern improvements" These
somewhat altered the primitive aspect
of the building, concealing the hugo
brick chimney. which in those days was
considered decided ornament.
Through all these years the estate has
been kept in excellent repair

The origin of dominoes has been at
tributed variously to the Greeks. the
Chinese and. Jews. but a Paris con-
temporary has. discovered that the
ever popular game owes it's invention
to the Benedictines of Mont Cassin.
Two of the order were sent into
lengthy retreat, and they hit upon a
method of Willing away the spare
time without infringing the rules of
silence by playing with square stones
upon which various dots were marked
While perfecting themselves theyaper-
fected. or rather evolved the game
and We're accustomed to frequently re-
peat when playing in the evening
psalms from yespers. especially the
first, that is psalm elk, which begins
"Dixit Dominus Domino meo.'' When
the retreat was over the game was
soon known in the convent. Then its
fame spread to the village and beyond.
The verse was reduced to one word
Domino hence the name as we have
received it.-London Globe.

Special Dispatch to The Star.


GREENVILLE, Tex, October 22.-Fol-
lowing the lynching of two negroes for
criminal assault here last night, this town
is in the hands of three military COM
panies, from one of which the mob had
wrested the two negroes. While the
town is still excited over the fight be-
tween the mob and the militia, it is
assault on the white woman has been
avenged and the mob has dispersed.


The trouble started late yesterday aft
ernoon, when a mob, headed by masked
men, went to the jail and demanded that
the sheriff turn over Frank Williams and
Louis" two negroes who had peen ar
rested. charged with criminal assault
on Mrs. VIII Lloyd. The sheriff refused
to grant the demand. William Carter,
Mrs. Lloyd's father, was in the jail, and
he spoke to the mob. asking that 1t dis
perse and let jury try the accused
blacks. The mob jeered at the re-
quest, and with battering rams and crow
bars attacked the Jail, tearing down the
outer doors and battering in the negroes
cell.


Governors Prompt Action.


Gov. Campbell telegraphed the sheriff
to call out the militia. Company NJ. 4th
Regiment, responded and reached the Jail
in time to take the two negroes from
the mob's leaders. A fight followed, the
members of the mob using their fists,
while the soldiers protected the blacks
with dubbed muskets.


The mob soon overwhelmed the SOL
diers and the negroes were retaken. They
were dragged to the outskirts of the city
and hanged. Further disorder was feared
because several members of the mob
threatened to move against other negroes
in the place, and two additional COM
panies of militia were dispatched.


Early this morning, however. the mob
dispersed and no more trouble is likely
to occur.

SEATTLE, Wash, July 3.-The fight

cussed on the floor of the National Wo-

noon, and the convention decided unan-
imously to unseat all the Washington
delegates.

ferred the contest to the national con-
Yention.


During the debate this afternoon a
Washington delegate declared the ma
tional convention should mind its own
business, and said that woman suffrage
had been lost in Oregon through it's in
reference.


National President Anna M. Shaw
broke into the debate to say that the
national body had jurisdiction. She
protested hotly against insults Of
fered by those who denied such juris-
diction."


The vote that unseated all the COM
batants was then taken. The state of
Washington now has no vote in the
convention, and the regulars are in
control of the state organization, but
under censure by the national body.

KANSAS CITY, July 1S,-Flood con-
ditions here and in this vicinity showed
much improvement today. The Kansas
and Missouri rivers had both been sta
tionary since last night and no further
rains were reported. The Atchison,
Topeka & Santa Fe railway opened its
main line to Chicago this morning, the
big break in the tracks at Dean, Lake,
Mo-, having been repaired. The Chi
cago. Milwaukee & st. Paul railway,
which had annulled it's nightly Chicago
train since Sunday, sent special to
Chicago over it's own line, and regular
service will be resumed tonight. Train
service south and southwest was still
demoralized. There was little delay
west. Union depot officials today esti-
mated that within the last six days
there have been fully 10000 travellers
held in Kansas City because of inef-
ficient train service. The depot matron
tells of great hardships experienced by
women travelling with barely enough
money to support them on their jour
ney. Hundreds have slept on benches
every night.

Herald: All political obligations now
possessed by men have been gradually
forced upon them unsolicited by their
mothers in prehistoric days men were
ever warlike and eager for the chase,
leaving their women and children days
and weeks. Staying and manning each
other in battle almost to defamation.
They fought for the best hunting
grounds and most pleasant districts
convenient to pure water, feed and fuel.
The women brought up the rear taking
quick possession and looking to all the
advantages of location in detail.


They had their judges and laws much
like some in force today. Many and
fierce were their disputes over land
lines land other property. The men re-
turning from afar, always tired and
overburdened with trophies of chase
and war, lay in camp resting, tending
their wounds, mending their bows,
preening themselves, Dragging. strut
ting about" here and there along the
running brooks in little knots of mutual
admiration clubs. They viewed the
petty turmoil of their women with
complacenoy out of the tail of their
eye from some nearby messy eminence,
with never a care. The yearly bearing
mother ruled, her word was law. Man
ever obeyed her, whether he would or
no. She knew the mysteries OF the
smelling pot and forge, was doctor,
lawyer, architect.


The forward. idling, gadabout, bab-
bling female was put in leash and
made to toe the mark. Those were the
days when man was lord. He pursued
the friendly shade around the cliffs
and rocks in summer and the sun like
wise in winter, consuming great guam
titles of mothers home brew, which
was as pure and free as tn eair. With
arched chest and double arched instep
he strobe along, eying the footprints
of his rival with critical gaze, thereby
noting any signs of waning courage.
Those were the days when man was
swift as the wind, leading the grey
hound in the chase; the days when the
present Marathon record was halved
and quartered, especially on the home
trip with broken bow.

CHICAGO. September 16.-Two women.
ssters-in-law and members of well-to-do-
families, are dead as the result OF
mysterious shooting in an apartment
house in the fashionable Hyde Park res
idence district yesterday afternoon.
One of the women. Mrs. Anna Silver,
had eleven bullet wounds in her body
and was found dead when the police
forced an entrance to the apartment after
being notified by neighbors.
Her sfster-in-aw Mrs. Judith Trip,
wife of Julius Trip. manager for the


manufacturing concern of Morrison &


Riley. in whose apartment the tragedy


took place, was found dying with a bull


let wound in the head and several knife
wounds on her arms and shoulders She


died shortly after being taken to Wash
ington Park Hospital


In the apartment was a revolver. the
property OF Mr.. Trip. with four empty


chambers and two loaded ones That it
had been fired recently was evident, but


the police found evidence that twenty


six shots had been fired in the room,
| eleven of which struck Mrs. Silver, one


Mrs. Trip and fourteen the walls OF
the room.


The first theory Of the police was that
1t was case Of murder and suicide


Further investigation makes this solution
impossible
A careful search OF the deliberately fur
hisned apartment failed to reveal a sin


gle empty revolver cartridge. The only
explanation Is that the person who did


The shooting carried away the discharged
shells.


Screams for Aid Are Heard.
Inc two women were thought to be
alone in the apartment when the shoot
| ing took place. and none of the neigh


bors saw any stranger enter or leave the
building.


The first intimation they had Of the
| tragedy was when Mrs. Trip ran to the
| rear door of the apartment and called to
| the janitor for help. Almost simulta-
| neously Mrs. Silver ran to the front en-


trance and screamed for aid, and then
| ran back into the apartment.


The janitor said he was afraid to enter
| the apartment. No one responded to Mrs.
| Silver's cries.


That there was a terrible struggle in


the room is evident. The furniture was
| broken and overturned and everything


was topsy turvy. Blood was everywhere.


Even the front curtain was blood-soaked,
and as the wind blew it looked like red
| flag.


Both women fought hard for their lives.


Mrs Silver had a vicious knife wound in
| her right arm, as though she had been
| stabbed while trying to ward off sti-
| letto thrust directed at her heart. There
| were other cuts and bruises on her body
| Knife wounds and bruises were also


found on the body Of Mrs. Trip.
Three Theories Of Tragedy.
| When the police arrived there were
only three explanations that seemed pos
| sible. These were that Mrs Tripp had
| murdered her sister-in-law and then
| killed herself; that tine two women had
| fought a duel and both had been killed,
and that a third person had entered the
apartment and murdered both.
The first two theories were diSsipated
| by the absence Of empty revolver shells


and bloody knives. leaving only the third


solution-that Of murder by third per-
| son.


After six hours Of investigation the


detectives believe that both women were


murdered either by an enemy or by a


sneak thief with whom they fought to


save their money and jewels. This theory


would explain the empty chambers in


Mrs. Trips revolver and the knife wound


and bruises on both of their bodies
The tragedy is one Of the greatest muir
der mysteries in the history of the Chi
cago police department.


Women Well Known Socially.
Both women were we'll known in the
| social set in which they moved, and Mr..
| Trip owns the apartment building in
| which the tragedy took place. They were
both well dressed when found and evil
IDENTIFY had been out of the apartment.
| They were the best Of friends. Neigh
bors scout the theory that they could
have quarreled and engaged in duel

legislature authorizing such action. The
announcement that Miss Harriet Eddy
county library organizer, would be here
within a day or two for the purpose of in
yestgating conditions, brought the matter
before the people who are interested along
that line, with the result that more or
less determ ined stand will be taken against
the proposition. The trustees of the Santa
Ana public library have had meetings at
which the subject discussed, and the
opinion was expressed that the law throws
the library into politics.

There are many little ostriches Matched
this time of the year near Phoenix, Ariz.
The old birds sit on eight to ten eggs,
which are very large. weighing from three
to four pounds each. 1t takes about six
weeks for the eggs to hatch.


Sometimes when it rains the eggs are
taken from the nest and put in large in
cubators, as the ostrich will not 81. on a
wet nest. The ostriches are very different
from chickens. The mother bird. being
gray cannot be seen in the daytime, and
the father. being black, cannot be seen
very well at night. SO the mother sits on
the nest during the day and the father at
night, which helps to hide the nest.


The little ostriches are about the size
OF bantam hen when Matched and are
very delicate. If they get wet they die.
When first Matched they are not fed very
much for week. Later they get all the
alfalfa grass and broken bones they want.


They grow very fast, and when six
months old they are six feet high, and
their pretty feathers are then cut from
their wings. They are full grown when
one year old, but do not lay eggs until
three or four years old.

NASHVILLE. Tenn, January 10
With the stage set for the Cooper muir
der trial. the witnesses present ana the
prospective jurors summoned. it became
known today that the state had prepared
surprise for the defense by having
had the body of Senator Carmack ex-
humed and an autopsy held.


Following the murder in the excitement
attendant upon the crime. the state neg
lected to order a post-mortem. 1t Is
essential in the trial that the direction
from which the bullets came be deter
mined. The defense asserts that Car
mack fired first. The states theory Is
that Carmack, with his hat raised To
greet lady, was shot from behind. and
it appears that. some time between the
date of the killing and the present time,
the state, secretly at night. exhumed the
body of the slain editor and caused
careful post-morteIn to be performed.


The course of the bullets thus was de-
termined and the state claims to have
proof that the bullet which killed Car
mack entered his neck from behind.


Does Not Upset Defense.


This, however. does not entirely dis
prove the theory of the defense. Even
the defense does not claim that Col.
Cooper fired the shots. 1t maintains that
Robin Cooper, believing his fathers life
was in danger, fired upon Carmack to
protect his parent and it is not commended
that young Cooper stood elsewhere than
behind Senator Carmack.


The work of completing the new court
room for the opening OF the trial was
rushed far into last night. Carpenters,
electricians and other workmen labored
under orders of the officials, and as a
result the big new temple OF justice was
ready for the opening of court at Daylight
today The sheriff reported to Judge
Hart that the summons for both Jurors
and witnesses had been served, and that
nothing except objections of counsel stood
in the way of the opening of what prom
Used to be the most famous criminal triai
in the history of Tennessee.


Defendants Enter Court.


Both sides announced a readiness to
proceed and Judge Hart ordered the panel
sworn. The courtroom was crowded
within ten minutes after the doors
were thrown open. Many women. were
present and for these Judge Hart ordered
places made inside the bar.


Col Duncan B. Cooper and his son
Robin entered the courtroom arm in arm.
John d. Sharpe. the other defendant. fol-
lowed them and was greeted affectionate-
ly by his wife and his father. Mrs. Lu-
cius Burch, daughter of Col. Cooper. met
her father and brother with a cheerful
smile, and seating herself between them
conversed animatedly with them. Young
Cooper was fashionably attired and SEEM
ed in splendid spirits His father was
very quiet and showed the effects of
prison confinement.


Ask Time to Confer.


Before the panel was called both sides
asked time to confer, which was grant
The defense has seventy-two peremptOry
challenges, twenty-four for each de-
PENDANT, and the state eighteen challenges.
or six for each defendant. Judge Hart
ordered 500 men summoned for jury serv-
ice and says he will order the next panel
to consist of 1000. There are 400 quail
fed names on the jury wheel Should
these be exhausted without the selection
of a jury, the case will not go to trial at
all.


At IL O'clock the attorneys for the
defense returned to the courtroom, their
conference having lasted an hour and
twenty-five minutes.


The defense reported ready, but the
state asked for more time, and the court
adjourned until 1:30 O'Clock pm.

censored dispatches from Madrid agree
that Gen. Brandos, the military com

crushed the revolution there. executing
many ringleaders, and that the gov
ernment is now in control of the sit
uation, reports filtering out at Car
bere on the French frontier none of
which, however, was later than noon

until then had the upper hand and that
nothing in history with the exception
of the commune approached the fero-
cious drama being enacted. All the re-
ports agree that the movement was
slxillfully organized and broke like
bolt from a clear sky. Three facts
stand out prominently.


First, the troops in the earliest stages
refused to fire on the mob either be-
cause they We're numerically inferior
or because they were ia sympathy with
the mob; second, the movement was
distinctly revolutionary and anti-cler-
ical, and therefore the fury of the mob
was vented almost entirely against the
church and its representatives, private
property being generally spared.


Curse the Police

where acclaimed the troops, while
cursing and fighting The police and the
civil guard, and the cries were Down
with the government! Down with the
king! Long live the rcrublie!"


Stories of the ferocity of the mob
toward church property and the
priests, monks and nuns are incredi-
BILE. The monks who could not escape
through the subterranean passages in
the monasteries were beaten and
killed. The nuns, fleeing from the
burning converts, were driven half
naked through the streets, and the
priests, 1t is reported, were shot at
the steps of the altar. 1t is even stated
the mangled bodies of monks were
carried on poles through the streets
by 10000 people and that the captain
general was powerless to interfere.

everything. Notwithstanding this anti
clerical ferocity, other reports intimate
that the Carlists, who stand for

Before the day was over hundreds

PHOENIX, Ariz., Nov. 12.-One OF
the most thrilling experiences of the
Los Angeles-Phoenix race terminated
today when the baby Ford came limp
ing into Phoenix in apparently renewed
and fresh condition.


The story of the baby car of the feet
OF cars that left Los Angeles amidst
such cheers as were then heard sounds
more like a romantic tale of the frontier
than the actual truth.


The long delay and continued absence
of the little car had begun to cause
many forebodings of disaster, and a
searching party was organized to go on
q hunting expedition for the car and It's
gallant crew, that had refused to turn
its back to Phoenix but pluckily pro-
ceeded on Its way to the finish, regard
less of record or time. Accordingly
Roger Stearns, the Los Angeles agent
for the Ford cars, who had come into
this city for new steering knuckle,
accompanied by two friends, secured
Pope Hartford and set out In search of
the lost car yesterday at noon.


The search car found the lost baby
Ford on the desert between Salome and
Buckeye. about ninety miles from Phoe-
nix. she was travelling on the right
road to Phoenix, after two days OF
wandering over desert roads.


Charles Harris, one of the drivers of
the baby Ford in the Los Angeles
Phoenix race, lost on thedesert with
William T, Pratt, the other driver,
reached here this evening on the stage
from Buckeye, in very bad condition,
but will pull through all right in day
or so. There was no injury except ex-
haustion.


pratt came in early this morning with
Roger Stearns in the lost Ford car.
Creech, who drove the Pope Hartford
for Stearns on the relief expedition, is
not back yet.


Harris and Pratt sent word Monday
that they had brokeH a knuckle joint of
the car near Quartzite. Stearns, who
was in Pheenix, wired them and sent
repaired joint to Vicksburg, but they
never got either message or joint,


In the meantime they made tempo
rary repairs at q prospector's camp,
passed Vicksburg and Salome and
started toward Winters Wells, between
Salome and Buckeye, across the longest
desert and worst road east of the Col
orado.


Thursday morning Stearns felt sure
they had met trouble, getting no an
swer from his wires, and ample time
having elapsed for repairs and finishing
the trip. Taking Creech Thursday
morning he went after them, and found
them in the desert twenty-eight miles
from Salome, eleven miles from Win
ters Wells and forty-five miles from
their car


They had been wandering around for
twenty-four hours, entirely lost and off
the road. suffering for food and water.
Harris with one shoe practically gone,
both in bad shape, but Pratt the strong
er and better.


Stearns and Pratt with the new joint
repaired the machine and brought her
in, arriving this morning. Harris was
too i'll to travel further than Buckeye
last night and finished the trip by
stage today. Harris and Pratt, espe-
cially the former, were rapidly losing
their minds from exhaustion when
found about noon Thursday


They spent two hungry nights with
coyotes and rattlers, Harris stepping on
snake, but fortunately avoiding a
bite.

mouths of the cannon after hand to
hand fighting.

when the Moors finally retired. The

2000 men.

Spanish force in Morocco, directed the
struggle. encouraging his men forward
heroically.

Dear Aunt Laurie:


This is a true story about who
Did It?'' and 1 will say right now that
my grandmother did it when she was
young.


In western Kansas there was an old
schoolhouse which was separated from
the cemetery by high, thorny hedge,
near where grandmother lived.


The schoolboys had cut a hole
through the hedge to go through to
get the ball when it went over, but
new sprouts had hidden the hole from
view.


One evening there was to be q magic
lantern show at the schoolhouse, and
as the first wagonload of happy young
people came toward the building they
were Mortified to see a white ghost
move quickly along the hedge row and
disappear through the impenetrable Gas
they thought) fence into the cemetery.
Several of the more timid ones faint
ed, the show was abandoned and the
party went home.


This ghost story was prevalent
around the neighborhood for quite a
while, but grandma always smiled
when she heard it. She had been for
a walk and was taking a short cut
home across the school yard, and when
she heard the people coming she went
through the old hole in the edge and
went home across the fields.


MARIE DUNLAP.

AMERICAN FORK, Utah, July "a
Four bolts of lightning struck the resi-
dence of John H. Singleton last night,
killing his wife, rendering himself and
his 4-year-old son unconscious and
knocking down his brother and a
neighbor who came to their assistance.


While Singleton and ]. E. Farrell, his
neighbor, are still unconscious, their
recovery is hoped for.


Singleton's son was sitting on the
front porch when the first bolt struck
the house. He screamed and Single
ton rushed out, finding him lying on
the porch unconscious. He carried
him into the house and placed him in
tub of water to resuscitate him.


While he was holding the boy the
second bolt struck the house and
Singleton was hurled across the room.
The boy received a second shock when
his father was hit, and was again pros
trated.


When the second bolt struck, the
house was enVeloped in a blue flame,
which attracted the attention of neigh
bors. Mrs. Singleton rushed into the
kitchen, where she found her husband
lying unconscious on the floor and her
son in the tub She rushed to the
front door to call for help, but when
she reached the door the third bolt
struck her, killing her instantly.


Singleton recovered sufficiently to
stagger into the front room. He saw
his wife lying on the floor and ran
out on to the street to call for help.
He met his brother Dell and Farrell
out at the front gate. Everything was
in darkness and Dell Singleton carried
a lantern.


Before they reached the front porch
the fourth bolt struck the house. Dell
Singleton was ahead and he was hurled
several feet. Farrell, who was close
behind him, was knocked unconscious
on the sidewalk.

SAN BERNARDINO. April s.-Frank
Avery was brought to this city late
last night froms Little Bear valley suf-
fering from injuries received while
blasting boulders from the new road
being constructed to that point.


Eight charges had been placed by
Avery and the intention was to dis
charge them all at the same time. One
of the charges failed to explode, and
after waiting a reasonable time Avery
approached the spot where the explo-
sive had been located and was bend
ing over when it went off, driving the
burning poyder and dirt into his face
and eyes. The cap was defective and
did not ignite the powder. but the fuse,
after smoldering for some time, finally
burned through the thin layer of dirt
on top of the charge, resulting in the
unexpected explosion.


The injured man was hurried to this
city for medical attention, and al
though his face is badly burned and
his eyes filled with the powder and
dirt, it is not thought that the eyesight
will be totally lost.

VICTORIA, B. c., Sept. 22.-Details
which arrived tonight from Australia,
of the capsizing of the American mis-
sionary yacht Hiram Bingham Jaluit
in the Marshall group, the death of
Rev. T. Walkup from exposure and the
terrible experiences of the castaways,
without food. The survivors were res
cued by the steamer Germania and
landed at Sydney August 2S.


The Hiram Bingham, motor schoon-
taitari with Rev. T. Walkup, eight
Caroline Islanders and a native child
on board. The schooner was lost the
morning of May 4, 20 miles north of
the Gilbert islands.


Vessel Capsizes


The wind had died away and Walkup
went below to start the oil auxiliary
engine when a tropical squall came
suddenly and heeled the vessel over on
its beam. Walkup rushed up and with
the crew made frantic but unavailing
efforts to right the vessel, which, with
a heavy list, refused to answer her
helm and capsized. A moment after
ward a dead calm prevailed:


The ships company. precipitated into
the ocean, clung to the rigging of the
vessel which was lying on its side and
was full of water.


Release Small Boat


Several natives tried to dive under
the wreck and release the boat lashed
in the davits. and after a while sue
ceeded. Ultimately a couple of oars
were recovered and all hands clambered
into the boat, abandoning the Hiram
Bingham.


For 81 days the castaways drifted at
the mercy of wind and wave. Be-
fore leaving the wreck, Is cocosnuts
were picked up, this being all the food
for nine adults and a child for three
weeks.


Rain squalls prevailed and the mis-
sionary caught rain in his oil skins
and served rations in cocoanut shells.
Became Raving Mad


All hands became exhausted after
rowing for four days and a sail was
improvised with sheeting. The priva-
tions soon bore effect. The castaways
became i'll and some were raving mad.
Sharks were seen in number following
the boat


May 26 land was sighted and island
ers assisted the exhausted castaways
to land on Edon island in the Mar
shall group. Rev. Walkup died soon
after landing and was buried on the
beach. His wife and family returned
to America. just before the fatal voy-
age began.

months, were ordered to leave the
county before s O'Clock tomorrow after
noon under pain of jail sentences by

men of the party were arrested sew

and their families in fear of thefts,
and that the gypsy women were nuis-
ances in their desire to tell fortunes.


Judge Smith suspended sentence and
ordered the nomads to leave the county.
Adams said he and his tent dwellers
would obey the order of banishment at
once.

cordance with the Indian custom, so

happy hunting grounds, but relatives
placed in his grave his riding whip and
his blankets.


Geronimo died in the old faith. the
religion OF his forefathers, which knew
no white mans God. The sun was his
conception Of deity. -Four years ago.
the injuries received from a fall from
his horse would prove fatal, he joined
the Reformed church. He was sus-
pended from the church two years
later because of excessive drinking
gambling and otherwise breaking the
rules of the church.


Asa Dukluge, who has been acting
chief of the Apaches in all their deal
ings with the government, will likely
succeed Geronimo.

NEW YORK. May 22.-The dealings
in the stock market this morning were
in somewhat reduced volume in COM
parison with the average scale of ac-
tivity which has been maintained dur
ing the week. but the trading preserved
a firm undertone and fair distribution
of interest was exhibited.


The London stock market was some
what heavy. but American shares were
steady there. and the rather small op-
erations in the local market for for
eign account showed an excess of pur-
chase.


There was little in the mornings
situation calculated to invite specu-
lative ventures I'm either direction. The
usual weekly reports Of the mercan-
tile agencies upon the state of the
country's trade We're, broadly speaking,
encouraging. although irreguarity in
business condition was reported and
was blamed upon the slow progress of
the revision of the tariff.


Little interest appeared to be taken
In the outlook for the weekly bank
statement. and the preliminary fore
casts of that document suggested that
rather negative exhibit could be reck-
oned upon.


Some of the Firm Features.


In the stock market the United States
Steel shares, and notably the common
stock. were again conspicuous and firm
tone was fairly common in that general
department of the market. Western
Union enjoyed a substantial rise, and
firm features were Distillers' Securities,
Amalgamated Copper, American Smelling
and American Locomotive.


Further pressure upon Third Avenue
was about the only feature of the days
local traction issues.


The railway shares list ruled firm dur.
ing the greater part of the business with
pronounced strength displayed by Great
Northern preferred, Northern Pacific,
Reading, Union and Southern Pacific and
the 500 stocks. Rumors of an increased
dividend on Chicago. Burlington and
Quincy accompanied the strength Of the
so-called Hill stocks.


Long Island Advances.


The stock market showed increased
strength of activity with the progress of
the morning. The Southern railway shares
were notably strong, as were the stocks
of other lines in the southern states.


sharp advance in the Long Island
stock was q feature OF the dealings in

MESSINA May 3.-Three hundred per-
sons of the poorer classes who have been
living among the ruins of Messina a few
days ago invaded in body a village of
huts built by the relief authorities, at
Giostra. in the outskirts of the city.


The huts. which number about fifty,
were still unfinished. but the invaders
took summary possession. installing their
belongings and barricading the doorless
doorways and unglazed window frames


The authorities promptly ordered i'm
mediate evacuation. declaring that the
shelters would not be allotted till they
were finished. and only then to applicants
who had observed proper formalities.


The refugees refused to leave. where
upon about fifty carbineers were sent to
enforce the edict. The occupants, how
ever. loudly protesting that they had
urgent need of shelter. resisted stub
bornly.


Finally they gained the day, and are
now the victorious possessors of the roof
less, windowless. doorless huts

LEAVENWURTH, Kan, April lit
took 1900 United States soldiers to
maintain order and prevent prisoners
from escaping during fire which de-
molished four buildings of the federal
military prison here early today.


All the 500 prisoners were marched
out of their cell houses, when 1t seemed
the whole prison certainly would De
consumed, and were held under heavy
under control. Then, after some of the
cell houses had cooled sufficiently, they
were marched back again.


The fire was detected by sentry,
who hastily gave the alarm, and the
fire department of Fort Leavenworth
turned out.


The Thirteenth infantry. armed with
rifles, surrounded the prison. The tlre
gained rapid Roadway, against the
prison guard working with buckets and
small hose. The fire department OF
Leavenworth answered an emergency
call and joined forces with the soldiers
in a battle against the flames.


The fire was confined to the central
row of buildings and consumed the IN
dustrial departments of the prison, in
Guiding the paint shop, the tailor shop,
carpenter shop and laundry. The cell
houses rapidly became filled with
smoke, and became suffocatingly hot.


When the fire started there was glee
among the prisoners.


LET 1t burn" they yelled.


The water pressure was very poor
and as the water sputtered uselessly
from the hose, the prisoners laughed
and cheered. The flames leaped higher
and gust of wind whipped smoke into
the nearest of the three cell houses.
The tone of the prisoners changed then.


Prisoners Terrified


For Gods sake, take us out!' they
screamed, battering against the steel
bars in great terror. Colonel Laugh
borough saw the danger of the situa-
ton, when the leaping flames got near
the cell houses, and ordered the prison
provost guard to unlock the doors. The
prisoners fell in line, each convict with
his hands on the shoulder of the man
in front of him. At double quick they
marched to the farthest corner of the
prison enclosure, where they huddle1
while 100 prison guards guarded them
with leveled rifles. Two of the terror
stricken crowd of convicts tainted. Half
an hour after the fire broke out, the
Leavenworth city fire department
reached the fort. Nothing could be
done to save the burning buildings.
however, and the firemen devoted their
attention to saving the main structure.


A new military prison is under pro-
cess of construction and it is not prob
able the burned buildings will be re-
built.


A few men were overcome by the
heat during the fire.


Major Thomas H. Slavons, command
ant of the prison, said the fire prob
ably was caused by defective wiring.
He placed the damage at $65000.


The buildings burned were among
the oldest at Fort Leavenworth. They
were erected in 1857 and 1858, under
the supervision of General L. C. Eas-
ton, and We're first used for an army
commissarys house. 1t was many
years later that they became a part of
the United States penitentiary and la
ter converted into a military prison,
following the erection of a new federal
prison here.


The prisoners now confined there
number about 800 men and all are
practically short term army offenders
convicted in court-martials.

wooden two story lodging house at
4Os Terrace street, in which scores were
sleeping. and an aged woman. Mrs.

by the fall Of the ruins while they
were searching for bodies, it being
feared at the time OF the fire that
many dodgers had perished-

police headquarters, and the people
driven out by the flames were sheltered
in the police station. Most of them
escaped with only their sleeping
clothes. The property loss is small.

PASADENA Aug. 26.-For the first
time in the history Of the church, the
portals Of Saint James Episcopal chap
ell in South Pasadena opened at eight
o'clock tonight to admit wedding
party.


The ceremony solemnized was that
of Miss Mabel EthelWyn Tanner of
1910 Fletcher street, in the exclusive
Huntington Drive district, and lionel
Vane Redpath, editor and owner of
the Masonic Chronicle, fraternal
paper published in Chicago.


To the strains of the Mendelssohn
march, Miss Tanner, accompanied by
her sister, Miss Maud b. Tanner, went
up to the alter where she was met by
the bridegroom and his brother, Ken
meth Vane Redpath who came on from
Chicago for the ceremony. The Rev.
Frederick ]. Henstridge, priest in
charge at st. James read the beauti-
full Episcopal service which made the
couple man and wife.


The wedding was followed by a brief
reception to the friends of the bride
and her husband, who filled the church
to overhowlng. Mrs. Redpath has been
popular here, both for herself and for
her remarkable talent as an amateur
actress and dramatic reader. The
church was prettily decorated with
palms, ferns, amarylis and asters.


The bride was very attractive in a
white lingerie gown of simple style.
She wore a white picture hat and car
ried Cecil Bruner roses. Her sister as
bridesmaid wore a pink lingerie gown.
pink flower hat and carried sweet peas.
After the reception the newly mar
ried couple left for Coronado, from
which place they viii visit the Grand
Canyon and then journey to Chicago
where they will make their home.

NEW YORK, Oct. 25.-Miss Augusta
V. Park, an attractive young woman
of Oakland, Cal, is the heroine of a
storm-fraught voyage which her
fathers big American sailing ship the
Acme has just completed.


1t Tired 12S days for the Acme to
round the Horn from San Francisco
to this port and during that time the
vessel experienced many adversities.


Miss Park shipped as a companion
for her father, but before the voyage
was finished she had become skilled
as a surgeon. nurse, cook, seamstress
sailor and fisherWoman.


After rounding the Horn the Acme
ran into a terrific storm, during which
the first mate was hurled from the
wheel, his arm being broken in two
places and his right hand split open.


While the storm ragged Miss Park
set the broken bones, mended the hand
and put the arm in splints, and since
then she has served as trained nurse
to the mate.


In other storms many of the sails
were carried away and the decks were
under water, but at no time did the
young woman display the least symp-
tom of fright.

WILMA, Russia, July 24.-Terrible de-
tails of a desperate conflict between a
number of convicts and the guards of the
prison yesterday were made public today.


Yesterday one of the guards entered the
cell in which four convicts were confined.
He had scarcely opened the door when
they made rush at him and one of them
cut his throat with knife. They took
his keys and revolvers and released other
prisoners from an adjoining cell. The
eight then dashed along the corridor and
attacked and killed two guards who at
tempted to stop them, cutting their
threats and taking their revolvers.


Killed Right and Left.


On reaching the courtyard they shot
down a guard who was stationed there
and started climbing the prison wall. The
sentinel at the gate opened fire on them
with his carbine, killing one of them on
the spot and severely wounding another.


The survivors got clear Of the prison
and ran out into the streets. Two OF
them, with daggers, attacked the first
policeman they met, inflicting fatal
wounds.


\ short distance further they met an
other policeman with drawn sword. A
furious fight ensued. The convicts We're
no match for the policeman, who, With a
single slash for each, decapitated the two
men.


The three remaining convicts stole some
Workmen's clothing and thus disguised
continued their flight. They were closely
pursued and took refuge in clump OF
bushes. A fusilade of shots riddled one,
and another, being severely wounded,
placed his revolver in his mouth and blew
off the top of his head. The third man
aged to escape and is still at large. The
authorities endeavored to keep the mat
ter quiet, but too many people had been
witnesses of the incident.


Other Prisoners Frenzied.


The 200 prisoners remaining in their
cells became frenzied and had they OBJ
tanned their liberty a general massacre Of
officials would have followed.

LIVERPOOL. December 2s.-Fire was
discovered in the hold of the White
Star liner Celtic last Wednesday when
the vessel was four days out from New
York The liner arrived here early
yesterday The fire was still burning,
but its presence was known to none
of tie 400 passengers. Immediately upon
arrival the work Of discharging the car
60 in an effort to reach promptly the
origin OF the blaze was begun. The work
was continued today. The fire started
amid the bales of cotton in hold No 6.


Capt. Hambelton ordered that the
matches be closed and sealed Efforts
to locate the fire were then begun, but
the matter was carefully guarded from
the passengers. whose passage was not
made less pleasant by the anxiety OF
tee crew. Above decks there was no
evidence Of anything unusual, but for
the next five days the fire was burning
steadily below.


The hold has been flooded. The extent
of the damage could not be determined
today.

MONTEvIDEO, Aug. 24.-Between
$50 and 200 persons were drowned or
otherwise killed when, in driving
rainstorm early today. the Argentine
excursion steamer Colombia and the
North German Lloyd steamer Schlesien
collided at the entrance of Montevideo
harbor.


The Colombia was entering port and
the Schlesien was outward bound for
Bremen. The Colombia's bow was
crushed in, and it sank almost imme-
diately.


The Colombia carried about 200 pas
sengers and a crew of 4S men. Most of
the passengers were asleep and a panic
followed the crash. Small boats Were
hurried to the sinking steamer, but
rescue was rendered difficult by the
high sea. About 20 persons were
brought ashore.


Most of the dead were women and
children. A majority of the survivors
are men.


The Colombia was carrying excur-
sionists from Buenos Aires to the fes-
tival at Montevideo.


The disaster has caused the keenest
emotion. The Uruguayan government,
In consequence, has postponed the fetes
arranged for the celebration of the
inauguration of the port.


The Schlesien was only slightly
damaged and has been detained here
by the port authorities. Her COM
mander attributed the collision to the
wind and the high seas, which made
both steamers practically unman-
ageable.

The channel is partially INSTRUCTED
by the wreck of the Colombia Most Of
the survivors of that vessel were taken
from the masts and many of them
were injured. While great numbers
of women and children were drowned,
almost every one of the ships crew
was saved.

graphic and telephone communication
between Buenos Aires and Montevideo.

NEW YORK, January OH the heavy

ferryboat Pierpont crashed into an empty

partly ripped away. The 200 passengers
and teams on board were thrown into
panic. No one was badly hurt.


The Pierpont had left her slip in Brook
lyn and was proceeding to the Manhattan
side. She was opposite Governors Is
land when the huge car float in tow of
tug loomed up out of the mist.


1t was too late to prevent collision The
pilot of the ferryboat threw the wheel
hard over with the result that the Pier
pont struck the float glancing blow


The impact was terrific. Passengers
were dumped from their seats in the cab
in. Horses standing in the runway were
knocked Off their feet.


The smash put the starboard paddle of
the Pierpont out Of business. She drifted
helpless with the tide.


The skipper finally managed to effect
landing alongside a dock at the foot Of
Main street, in Brooklyn, where the PAS
sengers disembarked.

the complete success of the manoeuvres in Mo-

Zeluan have been occupied At the latter town

Moors the details of which have not yet been
published. The ring around Mount Guruga is
now considered almost closed. and the position
of the Moors is desperate. Caid Amas appeared
before General Marina, the commander of the
Spanish forces, yesterday and asked terms of
surrender for the tribes intrenched Mount
Guruga The results of this conference are not
known. but ii is believed the Moors are ready to
submit without conditions.

successes in Morocco the Cabinet has decided to
restore the constitutional guarantees, except in
the provinces of Barcelona and Corona, and to
summon the COrtes on October 10.

ing Of the town accomplished by General
Tovar's brigade General OrozcO effecting the
enveloping movement. Only a few of the Span
iards were wounded. but the casualties among
the MOors were very great.

against the Moors. which has been going on
since July. would be of inestimable advantage
TO the government of Premier Maura against

section of the UPPER classes. however. CIV

ketchum and MS wife returned from

Part OF the island upon which the

the overlooking sea water reaching a

Sweeping westward the tropical

raised. The water backed Up into the

however. was confined TO the beach

A hurricane for East Texas was
foreeasted early in the day. When the
storm broke Galveston was prepared.
The inhabitants of the few scattered
houses sought safety and the vessels
were riding at anchor in the bay.


The fury of the storm was soon
abated. and the anxiety of those who
entertained fears OF another tidal wave
was thus early relieved.


So short was its duration that the
Mallory line steamer. booked to start
for New York shortly after noon. left
on time


TELEGRAPH CABLES PARTED


A heavy dredge had been blown
against the single bridge. which con
meets Galveston island with the main
land, and the telegraph cables had been
parted. AS result all manner Of
rumors were soon rife that Galveston
had again suffered such a storm as that
which practically destroyed the CITY
nine years ago.


Few buildings were blown down. but
it is believed that many warehouses
were flooded and that goods on the
bottom floors of these buildings were
ruined. Consequently it will require
several days to ascertain the amount
of the damage. The storm covered a.
wide area along the gulf coast.


Many Lives i'm Danger

forty people were rescued by the pilot
boat Texas and brought 10 Galveston.

ter of Henry t. Burnley, a prominent
raneher and well known sportsman of
Marin county. saved a~littIe child from
serious injury at her home here today
through her clever craftsmanship
with a % caliber. rifle


Miss Burnley is entertaining as her
guest her sister. Mrs. Arthur Minor of
Richmond, Va This morning Mrs.
Minors daughter Alice, aged s. was
playing with some young chickens in
the rear of the Burnley residence. The
little girl had been feeding the chicks
with bread crumbs. and thinking that
she was safely occupied her mother left
her


Shortly afterward Mrs Minor and
Miss Burnley were startled by the cries
of StFie child. Uncertain of what dan
ger the little one might be in. Miss
Burnley seized her rifle from its place
in the rear hall and hurried to the
back of the house At first she was
uhdbAC ~ hlu IHc Ciiius but lJS cries
finally directed her to a high fence
which inclosed the chicken yard. The
little girl had crawled through a small
hole in the fence, and. as the door was
locked, Miss Burnley could not enter.


Just as she was about to climb the
paling the plucky girl observed a large
hawk circling over the yard. She took

ward she fired. Meanwhile Mrs. Minor

WASHINGTON, July 2.-After MAX

mishap, which will delay further tests
until next week.


The machine, with Orville Wright at

Fort Myer drill grounds for the ninth
time in its second flight when the motor
stopped so feet above the earth. The
great, birdlike machine came to stand
still, then glided TO the earth without
injury to its occupants at the place the
propeller blade broke last September,
which resulted in fatal accident


In gliding today the machine struck a
tree and was swerved around with such
force that the skids were broken and
the right wing badly ripped


Despite the mishap. the two flights
today were the most successful that Or
Vile Wright has made at Fort Myer
since his return to complete the gov
eminent trials. On the first attempt he
flew about the field IL times in IL min
utes and so seconds. and on the second
trial he had gone around eight and a
half times when the flight was termi-
mated

higher and faster than in the trials of
the two previous days. It was esti-
mated that his speed was about 81 miles
an hour on an average although the
machine probably exceeded 40 miles
when flying with the breeze

back room on the second story. The

closed window, inf1icting painful cuts.

Leavenworth, Kans.-The military
prison at Fort Leavenworth was par
TALLY destroyed by fire late Wednes-
day night. The 500 prisoners were re-
moved from the cell houses under
heavy guard of United States troops
and confined in stockades. None of the
prisoners escaped, so far as known.


Owing to the low water pressure the
fire department Of the fort was almost
useless. The fire was fought by the
soldiers of the fort, who were all or
dered out of their quarters, and those
who were on leave in the city were at
once called back to the post.


Two soldiers were injured while
fighting the flames, but none of the
prisoners was hurt in any way.


Much excitement attended the re-
moval of the prisoners, many of whom
are desperate characters. 1t was feared
that they would make an organized
break for safety.


The fire broke out about 10 o'clock
in the carpenter shop and soon it was
seen that the main building was
doomed. A great outcry at once
broke out in the prison, the convicts
fearing they would oe burned to death.
They battered on the doors of their
cellhouses as the light of the fire
streamed in through the windows.
Many screamed in terror as the author
tiles for the moment refused to remove
them.


Soon, however, several companies of
soldiers, including cavalrymen, were
under arms. A strong Gordon of troops
was thrown about the prison, and
every precaution taken to prevent es-
capes. All the soldiers that could be
spared from the ranks of fire fighters
were detailed as guards, and then the
delivery of the prisoners began.


When the bolts of the dollhouse
doors were shot back, the flames had
reached the main building. Soldiers
with leveled weapons greeted the con-
victs as they were marched out. They
had been previously warned that the
slightest belligerent move would
mean death.


Shoot them down in their tracks"
commanded the officers, ''if they don't
keep in line. The first man that tries
to escape dies"


The rifle barrels of the soldiers and
swords of the officers glinting in the
freight, with the knowledge that it
was United States soldiers they were
dealing with, effectually awed the pris-
oners and they meekly followed their
heavily armed guards to the stockade.


Not only did the strict military rule
prevent any escapes, but it effectually
stopped the panic that had broken out
among the convicts.


The Leavenworth fire department
was rushed to the fort and combined
forces with the forts fire fighters. The
lack of water pressure, however, rem
dered their efforts almost useless.


The blacksmith shop, tailor shop,
machine shops and other buildings
went first All this while the whole
prison had been surrounded BY troops.
Then when the main building actually
had begun to burn, the stern military
rescue was carried out with precision.


The sick were removed first, placed
in ambulances, and taken to the Fort
Leavenworth hospital under guard of
cavalry The records were removed
from the administration building. Then
the general order was given for TAX
ing out all in the building.

DOVER, July 27.-Hubert Latham,
the French aviator, made another dar-
ing attempt to cross the English chan
mel at o'clock this evening. He sue
ceeded in covering nearly nineteen
miles of the twenty-one miles of the
channel when he fell into the water
two miles off Dover.


Five French torpedo boats accom-
panied him from the French side of the
channel, but were left behind by the
fast-flying monoplane. Latham had
given out earlier in the day he hoped
to hyffrom Calais across the channel,
thence continuing his journey overland
to London, eighty-five miles inland,
thus eclipsing the record of Louis
Bleriot.


This accident prevented the accom-
plishment of either of theee feats, but
his record of flight is next Do that made
by Bleriot.


The weather conditions, with the ex-
ception of slight rain, were favorable
when the aviator left the Sangatte
cliffs. The monoplane made a splendid
flight, but when victory was almost
within Latham's grasp the motor gave
out and the machine fell into the sea,
two miles off the admiralty pier.


Makes Daring Exploits


Hubert Latham is a comparatively
recent participant for flying honors, but
several daring exploits already had
gained him much attention. He was
the first to attempt fight of the Eng
fish channel, but his effort failed. After
waiting many days. for favorable
weather conditions he set out from
Calais July 10 last headed for Dover.
He cleared the cliffs beautifully and his
flight appeared propitious until mid
way in the channel, when his motor
failed and his monoplane settled gently
on the waters. He was picked up by a
torpedo boat.


Before his attempt to cross the chan
mel Latham had made several success
full flights at Mourmelon- Leagrand.
plane record by remaining in the air
one hour, seven minutes and forty
seven seconds.


NJ. Latham was slightly injured when
the monoplane struck the water. His
head was bandaged and blood was
flowing from his nose when he entered
the harbor on board the torpedo boat,
where he is now attended by the fleet
surgeon. The aeroplane was damaged.


A large number OF tugs and other
vessels that were being held in readi-
ness started to assist the aviator, but
he was rescued by the French torpedo
boat which brought him into port.


The Frenchman lost no time at the
start, and after making a short circle
overland launched out over the sea, dis
appearing five minutes later from the
view of thousands who gathered along
the cliffs above Calais.


On nearing the English coast Latham
encountered a heavy rainfall and a
thick mist hung over the water.

NEW YORK, May 1.-THE British
steamer Veraston arrived today from
Kingston, Jamaica, with practically a
new crew on board, having left fifteen
men in a hospital at Kingston suffering
with pernicious malarial fever. The dis
ease was contracted while the steamer
lay in the Madeira river about 1900
miles from Para, where the crew. al
though screened at night with mosquito
nets, could not altogether escape the at
tacks Of mosquitoes.


When the steamer got to sea after leav-
ing Para the cvrew was stricken until at
one time only three deck officers were fit
for duty, while the engine room force
worked as it was able. On eman died
at sea and another died after arrival at
Kingston. Fifteen men were sent ashore
for treatment and their places filled with
new men. The vessel was disinfected by
the port physician and permitted to pro-
coed. No further illness occurred.

The two-masted schooner Bill Nye. one
Of the best known Of the lumber-carrying
fleet, which was employed in the pine
apple trade between the Bahamas and
the Chesapeake, has completed her serv-

mock river point, loading lumber for At
lantic City. On her last trip from the
Bahamas to Baltimore the schooner had
a good trip until almost at the capes of
the Chesapeake. when a heavy gale
struck her. Capt. Gaskell hove the YES
sci to. and for over thirty hours she rode
out the gale, with seas constantly break
ing over her from end to end. The
weather moderating, she resumed her
voyage, and again a storm struck her.
This time it was from the northwest, and
when the gale was over Capt. Gaskell
found that his ship had been blown over
200 miles off her course. The speedy
little vessel was able to make her way
back to the capes in short time. and
this time she made Chesapeake bay with
out further mishap.

MADRID, July 29.-Oficial dispatches
received here today admit the battle
between Moorish tribesmen and the
Spanish forces outside of Melilla was
a disastrous defeat. The Moors cut
off communications with the Spanish
outposts, and the main force of the
Spaniards was driven back under the
walls of the city where fighting con-
tinued desperately.


The Spanish killed and wounded
number almost 5000, which takes no
account of the men at the advance
posts, who evidently have been aban-
doned to their fate.


Melilla is full of wounded.


The extent of the disaster is plainly
apparent from General Marina's dis
patch as given out at the war office
today. He says:


July 27, the Moors cut the railroads,
severing communication with out
posts. Our batteries shelled the Moors
but the advance posts were endan-
gered and they had to be abandoned.
The situation at Melilla is grave, des-
pite the desperate bravery of the
troops who are now fighting under
the walls of the city.


"Our losses in the engagement were
General Pintos, a colonel, two lieu
tenant colonels, five captains and
many officers and subalterns and
about 1000 men. The wounded
number at least 1900, including
MANY officers. The hippodrome Is
full of wounded soldiers. Two gen.
erals were mortally wounded"

of the anglers who spent the day fish

water today did not have very good
luck some of those who went out in
launches for bass made good catches.


The best catch reported was made
by a party from Los Angeles who
passed the entire day with Captain
Lynch in his launch Pearl, trolling be-
tween Point Firmin and Point Vincent.
The party included Frank Coons, Lew
Smith and some friends, and sixty-four
fine bass were landed.


The same party brought in sixty bass
and barracuda last Sunday, which was
the record for several months. The
outlook for fish in the channel is very
good for the coming weeks.

ger and cold until rowboat from Cross

visions aboard the Violet. The tug car
rieS mail from the Beaver Islands and

voix. For several days the three men
aboard were unable to attract attention
from the shore.

visions. and one of them. Ed. Martin was
taken ashore and arranged for the tug
Blazer of Manistique to come to the Vio-
lets rescue. 1t is believed that unless

WABASH, Ind, April IA tornado
passed over this city last night, injur-

sands of dollars worth of damage. The
storm struck the city at o'clock.
passing through the northeast section
of the town.

Mrs James Hayes and four children
were pinned beneath the wreckage OF
their home, which caught fire. The
mother was fatally burned and the
children were seriously hurt. William
Sheppard, wife and two children We're
held beneath fallen ruins and the
neighbors extricated them.


Wires went down and the city was
in darkness throughout the night. The
entire second story of the dwelling oc-
cupied by William Hams was carried
away, leaving the family in their beds
exposed to a drenching rain.


The wind was followed by a cloud
burst and the river rose, flooding low
lands.


Many bridges are washed away and
the streets are impossible owing to
fallen trees.

night, when 5000 of the popular mis-
sives were run through the stamping g

o'clock. All of these cards were dis
tributed today, along with thousands
of parcels of other mail matter.

through the postoffice this month has
far exceeded that handled during the
corresponding month of any year since
the postoffice was esta blished.

this year has been greatly expedited
because of the change made in sending
the registered mail direct from the
trains to the local postoffice. Hereto
fore the registered mail first went to
San Francisco and was then sent back
to Alameda.

NORFOLK. Va. September 3.-With
wind of only four miles an hour from the
southwest and a light haze covering the
water, the battleships and cruisers of the
Atlantic fleet continued their battle target
practice, maneuvers and general evolu-
tions on the southern drill grounds today
under less advantageous conditions than
yesterday The day dawned with clear
skies, but these grew into cloudiness with
an early haze formation over the ocean.
The fleet continued intact during the day,
however, with one exception, the absent
ship being the armored cruiser Montana.
which had put into Ham, ton roads for
coal and stores, as well as for the ad-
justment of gun sights. The scout cruis-
ers Birmingham and Salem from Boston
appeared on the drill grounds during the
day, their arrival being announced by
salute of thirteen guns to Rear Admiral
Schroeder, fleet commander. The battle
ship Missouri from Provincetown is the
next vessel expected.


The torpedo fiotilla of eleven boats, un-
der Lieut. Commander F. n. Freeman.
which is now coaling and taking on stores
at the Norfolk navy yard, Will proceed TO
Hampton roads late Saturday. and from
there to the drill grounds early Monday.
The torpedo boat Porter, which broke
down en- route from Newport. r. l., to
these waters, must receive repairs to her
machinery before she can join her sister
boats in fleet maneuvers. These, how
ever, will be completed early next week.

Covington, KY. March 22.-Judge Harbeson, in the
Kenton County Circuit Court, to-day held uncon-
stitutional the law establishing the State Racing
Commission The effect of the decision is to place
Iatonia racing on it's former basis, the commission
having adopted restrictive measures, which now
become void


The Court before passing the question or
the constitutionalty Of the racing commission act
decided in favor of the racing commission on sew
eral points notably the contention that the state
had the right 70 control the racing business by
police power and pass rules regulating race bet
ting that would even go the extent Of conhscat-
ing the racetracks by rendering their business
wholly unprofitable He said that the contention
of the Latonia Club that its track could not be
operated proftably without hookmaking made no
difference to the law in the case


Judge Harbeson held that the law creating the
Kentucky Racing Commission gave that body
power TO regulate running races; that trottrg races
and running races came under the same legal cate
CORY and that therefore the law was class legis-
Iation and was unconstitutional The Court IN
other words held that the law, TO be valid must
give the racing commission specific authority over
both trotting and running races


The commission will take the case TO the Court
of Appeals.

NEW YORK, June because of
the traditional right of a woman to
change her mind the steamship Kaiser
Wilhelm II was delayed many minutes
yesterday in sailing for Europe.


The Misses Julia and Georgia Car
son of Pittsburg had booked passage
and early yesterday Miss Julia de-
clared she was indisposed and would
not sail. Their trunks had then been
sent aboard and Miss Georgia went to
the pier a few minutes before sailing
time and ordered the trunks taken
from the ship.


After four of them had been taken
off it was discovered that the fifth
was in the hold and this trunk con-
tanned about $4,000 worth of jewelry.
The captain ordered the hold opened,
and the sailing time of the vessel had
passed when Miss Julia Carson arrived
in a taxicab and announced that she
had again changed her mind and would
sail on the ship.


The sisters went aboard and several
minutes more were lost in putting the
trunks back on the vessel.

activity doubles the duties of the kid
neys, and in time-the strain tells.

affiict old age with great discomforts,

too frequent or involuntary passages

CAMBRIDGE, Mass, April 17.--With
a powerful and finished stroke the
Harvard varsity crew defeated
weaker and less expert crew from Co
lumbia on the Charles river today by
six full lengths in race or mile
and -eighths.


After tho first few strokes there was
never any Question regarding the out
come. AS IL impelled by powerful
motor the Harvard crew swept proud
ly down the Charles river basin, before
5000 people on the river bank, and
shot like an arrow across the finish
line.


Behind them trailed the Columbia
shell with the oarsmen plunging their
blue and white blades into the water
in vain effort even to keep up with
the flying crimson shell.


Despite the almost perfect river
conditions the Columbian boat rolled
like a knockabout in heavy sea, and
1t was with difficulty that Coxswain
lockwood kept the nose of his boat
heading down the course.


Harvard's veteran crew showed all
the dash and force which wore out
Yale at New London last year, while
the exhibition of Columbia. even to
Coach Rice, was disappointing.


The start came almost exactly at p.
m. With the firing of the pistol the
Shell WdS lL0 lilSb " BOT away
Both crews hit up the stroke above
40, and for a hundred yards more
rowed side by side. Then Harvard be-
gan to draw away. Columbia continued
the high strooke for a couple minutes
longer, but presently Capt Cerussi
dropped back to SO. At the quarter
mile Harvard was half length to the
good, and at the half mile flag there
was open water between the boats.
The Harvard boat gained steadily the
Crimson stroke decreasing to 80, and at
one time as low as 28.


Under Harvard bridge dashed the
Crimson crew with 5000 people watch
ing. Ten seconds later the Columbia
she'll swept underneath and the two
crews started down the last mile of the
course. The water was now rougher
than in the upper reaches of the river.
The motion had no effect whatever on
the Harvard shell, but the unsteadiness
of the blue and white boat was the
feature of the race from this point on.
Stroke Sargent of the Harvard crew
again dropped the stroke below 80, but
when the mile and half flag was
reached there were Ave lengths Of water
between the boats.


Coming down to the finish, Columbia
was the first to squirt but there was no
gain on Harvard. AS the finish line
was neared Sargent called upon his
men for the last effort.


Up went Harvard stroke, while astern
the Columbia shell wobbled uncertainty.
The red flag fell and Harvard had won

SAN PEDRO, Dec. 25.-"With over
weathered ribs and ragged sails the
schooner r. G. Slade limped into port
this afternoon after experiencing the
worst storm along the northern coast
that had ever been encountered in the
long experience of her skipper, Capt.
Sonerud.


The schooner sailed from Aberdeen
twenty-five days ago, Capt Sonerud
bringing with him his wife and two
daughters. Soon after leaving Gray's
Harbor the schooner ran into. a heavy
southeaster and before Cape Blanco
was reached four more heavy storms
struck the vessel. The. wind attained
a velocity of 70 miles an hour and
grave fear was felt that the schooner
and all on board would be lost.


When off Cape Blanco calmer
weather was found and Capt Sonerud
had chance to ascertain just what
his damage was. The staysail and
two of the mainsails had been carried
away. The jbboom was cracked and
practically useless and $4,000 feet of
lumber, a part of the deckload, had
been washed into the sea.


With his jibs and the two mainsails,
that had stood the storm set, the cap
tain then encountered strong, fair
wind that carried him to Point
Arena, a distance of $50 miles, in one
day and the balance. of the trip south
was made without incident.


AIt was the worst storm 1 ever ex-
perienced," said the captain tonight
land [ trust l will not have to go
through another one like it, especially
if my family is with me. They stood
the trip bravely, but are very glad to
reach port again, can assure you"

LONG BEACH, Dec 25.-Snowbound
eastern friends of jovial party of
visitors to this city will be surprised
beyond measure next week, when they
receive photographs taken here today
depicting Christmas scenes, which win
impress the shivering easterners as the
oldest of which they ever heard.


The pictures show a Christmas tree,
not stuck up on parlor table or rear
ing its head In some warm living room
corner, but in Gods out-of- doors, set
firmly in the sand of the seashore
The members of the party enjoying
the outdoor tree were not clad in com
plete and heavy attire, but in bathing
suits, and the Santa Claus who Off
ciated was swathed In long robes of
kelp, upon which, to give a little Of the
snow effect, patches of cotton had been
placed. With his long sash of kelp,
and his hair and whiskers of like ma
terial, he looked more like the Old Man
Of the Sea than a reindeer pilot from
the land Of the frozen north.


Hung from the branches Of the little
Christmas tree were shells holding
candy. Other gifts also We're suspended
among the limbs. Santa Claus passed
out the gifts and shells of candy
Sacks of popcorn which were passed
aronud through the crowd were shared
with the seagulls, which swooped down
and snatched the kernels from the
sand. After the presents were passed
around the members of the party sang
a song ior two all raced out into the
surf and took a Christmas swim; the
official photographer doing his duty
also, for the sake Of the folks back
home.


Christmas at Hotel Virginia


Last night a tree was arranged in
the Hotel Virginia for the employees
1t was profusely decorated and lighted,
and after music and chimes, II. E.
Alger, the head waiter passed out
gifts for all. Popcorn balls, taffy
more music and dancing whiled away
some happy hours. This morning the
guests enjoyed a tree, too, this one
being in the salon.


The chimes rang out and the orches-
ira played few selections. and then
+. S. Cook, n visitor from Salt Lake
City, enacted the role of the good
Saint Nick and passed out among the
guests a great number of gifts.


A grab-bag had been kept in the
office all week. and the guests placed
therein such gifts as they had pre-
pared for their friends in the house.


A large crowd visited Long Beach
today. enjoying the surf and ocean
rides. The luncheon hour was a gay
scene at the Virginia, and tonight there
were nearly 200 extra guests for din
ner, including the University of Cali
fornia Glee club, which sang several
numbers during the dinner hour. The
club gave a concert in the auditorium
here tonight


The Elks, the Salvation Army and
the Parent-Teachers' associations re-
membered hundreds of families today
with timely gifts of food, clothing and
toys

KALISPELL, Mont, May 15.-The
contest which, for the past few weeks
has strenuously engaged the surveying
crews of both the Puget Sound and the
Great Northern railroads, has drawn
to a close with the filing this morning
of final maps of definite location of
both companies covering remaining
distance to the international boundary.


The Milwaukee people filed their
map fifty minutes ahead of the Great
Northern.


Throughout the contest they have
maintained the lead and now claim to
have the route secured from Coram
along the North Fork river, to the
Canadian boundary distance of over
forty-five miles.


At places the maps show lines as
following the same course, and many
points mark where they cross or con-
tinue side by side.


The contest will now shift to the
courts, where a number of condemna-
ton suits instituted by both sides will
be threshed out.


The first great Northern summons is
returnable May 20, and the first Mil
waukee suit will probably open on
May 81.

at Naples. The affair originated many
years ago in feud between the families
of two chiefs of the Camorra in the
Monte Calvario quarter. One chief, Va
lerio, seduced the sister of another called
Marino. and afterward abandoned her.
Marino went to shoot Valerie, but by mis-
take killed that chiefs wife instead.


Marino. who had just reutnred home
after serving ten years In the convict set
tlement. called together his partisans to
wreak vengeance on his hated enemy,
Valerie. who is the managing director of
gambling houses under the control of the
Camorra in that part of Naples. A fear
full affray began toward midday, each
rival being supported by small army of
kinsfolk and comrades.


Valerie was shot through the heart and
then pierced with daggers. His wife had
her throat cut and her fingers chopped off

MOULINS, France, Sept. Is
The dirigible army balloon Repub-
lique exploded near here today,
while 500 feet in the air.


-Four aeronautS were instantly
killed, and the balloon completely
destroyed.


CRUSHED TO DEATH.


The aeronauts who lost their
lives were Captain MarchaI and
Lieutenants Chaure, Vincenot, and
Reux. They were crushed to death
when the ballon car struck the
ground after a frightful plunge.


The cause of the explosion has
not yet been determined, as all of
the occupants were killed and the
balloon so badly smashed that there
is little chance Of learning the
cause from this source.


UNDER CONTROL.


When the Repub!ique passed over
Molins, from La Palisse, she was
apparently under perfect control.
The explosion occurred within
quarter Of an hour, when the bal
loon was FIVE miles from Moulins.
The explosion was plainly heard
in Moulins.


The Republique had been in COM
mission but little more than a
year. and was the pride of the
war department A great crowd
rushed to the scene of the wreck,
and It was necessary for soldiers
TO hold the excited throng in check.


Died Instantly.


All four Of the occupants OF the bal
loon were dead when the first Of the
crowd reached the scene. Captain Mar
chal and Lieutenant Beux we're terribly
mangled.


Eye witnesses Of the accident say that
the balloon fell to the ground within a
minute after the explosion. For a sec
ond. II seemed 70 pause IN the air, then
It shot 10 earth with frightfuI rapdity.


The Republloue is the second first
class army dirigible that has been lost,
the other being the Patrie, which broke
away from 200 men who were trying to
hold II during a storm and was car
ried out TO sea. The destruction OF the
RepubIique leaves the French army
without dirigible balloon worth the
name and places, the country at a de-
cided disadvantage with Germany in
aeronautic experimentation the latter
country having war dirigIbIes Of the
Zeppelin. Gross. and Parseval types.

OF the Rspublique. acting In the name

accident we're brought to the city. and

The city of Tampa, Fla, has adopted
a mode of warfare against the mosquito
that is proving highly successful. There
are many rain water tanks and cisterns
throughout the city for supplying wa
ter for lavatory and various other pur-
poses, and these are favorite breeding
places for mosquitoes. The warfare
against the annoying pests consists in
stocking these reservoirs with small
fish to feed on mosquito larvae. This
method has been tried in one place and
another in Florida and has proved sue
cessful in every case. The fish eat the
larvae greedily, keeping the tank water
clear at all times. They live for years,
even in tanks that are covered and
their living place one of darkness.

text:
COVINGTON, KY, March 22.-Judge
Harbeson today rendered his decision
in the noted case of the Latonia Jockey
club against the Kentucky racing
commission, holding that the law es-
tablishing the commission is uncon-
stitutional. The effect of the decision
is to place Latonia racing back to It's
former basis.


Judge Harbeson held that the law
creating the Kentucky racing commits
sion gave that body power to regulate
running races; that ,trotting races and
running races came under the same
legal category and that, therefore, the
law is class legislation and unconst1tu-
tional. The court, in other words, held
that the law to be valid must give the
racing commission specific authority
over both trotting and running races.


The decision is a complete victory for
the Lsatonia Jockey club. The racing
commission had insisted that Latonia
use mutuel machines. Latonia put in
these machines, but said they were
run at a financial loss and then all
lowed bookmakers to operate. The
club secured court injunction pre-
venting the racing commission from
interfering with the races while book
makers were operating last season.
The commission will appeal.
