IMPERIAL, Aug. 16.-Heavy showers
that have been threatened for several
days fell last night and today all over
the Imperial valley, causing some dam
age and much inconvenience and wash
ing out the Southern Pacific main line
near the Salton sea in several places.


The principal loss IN the valley was
that of hay. Throughout the whole dis
trict ranchers are just now cutting
large quantities of alfalfa for feed and
much of this was badly soaked. The
sun came out bright and hot this aft
ernoon and If cloudy weather does not
follow the losses will be comparatively
light


Two or three ranchers report the loss
of young live stock by drowning. The
floods in some of the deepe" roads broke
into bitches at points, but no serious
damage to mains or laterals on which
the ranchers depend for irrigating is
reported.


The greatest benefit accrued to the
corn growers. Cotton planters report
some shoots beaten down, but in the
main all crops were in good shape to
receive the shower.


At this time of the year everyone
in the valley lives most of the time out
Of doors, and some cOmical and few
unfortunate experiences were had.


AS a result of the rainfall very little
irrigating will be done for several days,
and the water companies have seized on
this breathing spell to clean bitches
and do necessary ditch structure work
while the ranchers can get along with
out running water

AUBURN, Cal, Nov. Palma Bell
was acquitted today of the murder Of
Joe Armes, her sweetheart, on June 5
of this year.


The jury was out only short time.


The verdict was rendered on the
ground that Alma Bell was insane at
the moment of the shooting, but was
sane Immediately before and immedt-
ately after the homicide. The instruc-
tions Of Judge Arnot were to this eff
feet.


After the verdict Alma Bell was re-
leased from custody and received the
congratulations of her attorneys,
friends and members of the family.


Her brothers declared this morning
that they would send her to relatives
in the east where her history is not
known.


The Jury took three ballots, the first
being eight for acquittal, one for man
slaughter, one for murder in the sec
ond degree and two blank. The second
ballot was two for conviction, ten for
acquittal, and the third ballot being
unanimous for acquittal.


History of Case


Alma Bell was accused of shooting
her sweetheart, Joe Armes, on the
night of June 5 last. The girl called
Armes from the cabin, where he was
sleeping with his brothers, and shortly
afterward a pistol shot was heard from
the direction in which the couple had
gone.


Frank and Manuel Armes, brothers
of Joe, and Tony Grinko, friend Of
Joe, rushed out of the cabin and found
Armes dead body lying in the road.


The sheriff was notified, and the next
morning he found Alma Bell crouching
in the brush near the scene of the
shooting.


After the shooting Miss Bell went to
a nearby ranch house and told the IN
mates that she had killed her sweet
heart. She left, but returned later and
said she knew he was not dead because
she could hear him crying.


She left for the second time, and was
not seen again until she was found the
next morning by Sheriff McAuley..


on the night of the shooting Anna
Bell came to the cabin occupied by
Joe Armes and his brother and de-
manded admittance that she might ex-
plain some stories which she asserted
had been told about her.


Stayed In Cabin


After some parley she was admitted,
and remained in the cabin two hours.


On leaving she persuaded her sweet
heart to accompany her and, according
to the testimony of the brother and
Grinko, a shot was heard moment
later.


Immediately following the shot the
two men asserted that Joe cried out
"Oh, boys; oh, boys" and that Alma
Bell exclaimed, GOOD by, Joe."


According to the story OF the sheriff,
the girl admitted the killing and as
serted that she fired the shot because
her sweetheart had Tilted her. She ad-
mitted to the sheriff that she had been
intimate with Joe Armes.


During the trial the defense sought
to prove that Alma Bell was betrayed
under the promise of marriage. Ex-
perts testified that under the circum-
stances the girl had no sense OF right
or wrong when she did the shooting.


Alma Bells own story or the shoot
ing was not brought out during the
trial.


The trial began the first week in No
yember and ended at 8 o'clock today.

Before midnight Sheriff William Tay
lor, Constable George Agpew and Dep
uty Sheriff George Martin arrived and

the dark.


Westcott was hard pressed and finally
he gave up in despair and. leaving his
horse, ammunition and provisions be-
hind in the chaparral, he slipped back
toward the cabin and blew out his
brains.


Among the man hunters the news
OF the murderer's suicide was heard
with general tones of relief, for West
cott had long borne the reputation of
bad man and one who was quick
with the gun.


From what can be gathered the
murderer slew his wife in a quarrel
brought on by himself in fear that she
would tell the authorities what she
knew of number of mysterious fires
in the camps along Tomales bay Six
months go the desperate was lodged

derporf, went to the switchboard on

returned a few minutes later and was
bending over the stove arranging some
pans when the flames in some manner
communicated to the reservoir and an
explosion resulted.


She ran screaming from the room
and neighbors who heard her cries
rushed to her assistance and smoth-
cred out the fire in her clothing.

woman was taken to the receiving hos
pital, where she was treated by Po-
lice Surgeon Garrett. Later she was
removed to the Clara Barton and at
tendants there say she is resting COM
fortably and will recover.

alarm which had been turned in and
succeeded in extinguishing the flames
before they had gained much headway.

considered that the city had mar
row escape from destruction.

ports from Toxic and other points show

lost, had Yokohama been so severely
shaken. There was considerable ex-

ing houses.

LEAN EN- WORIH, Nam. April lit
took 100 United States soldiers to main
tain order and to prevent prisoners from
escaping during a fire which destroyed
four buildings of the federal military pri-
son here early today.


When the fire was started there was
glee among the prisoners. LET it burn.'
they yelled. The water pressure was
poor and as the water sputtered uselessly
from the hose the prisoners laughed and
cheered


The flames leaped higher and a gust
of wind whipped smoke into the nearest
of the three cellhouses. The tone of
the prisoners changed then. For Gods
sake take us OUT they screamed. batter
ing against the steel bars in great terror.
They thought they would be burned to
death.


Col Loughborough saw the danger of
the situation when the leaping flames got
near the cellhouses and ordered the
prison provost guard to unlock the doors.
The 800 prisoners fells in, each convict
with his hands on the shoulders of the
man in front of him. At double quick
they marched to the farthest corner of
the prison enclosure. They huddled there
while 100 prison guards guarded them
with leveled rifles. Two of the terror
stricken crowd of convicts tainted.


After some of the cellhouses had cooled
sufficiently the prisoners were marched
back again.


Fire Gains Rapidly.


The fire was discovered before midnight
by sentry. who fired his pistol; the fire
call was sounded and the entire garrison
Fort p =, <,,rn
Infantry. armed with rifles, was thrown
around the entire prison.


The fire, which prabably started in the
prison tailor shop. gained rapid headway
against the prison guard working with
buckets and small hose. The fire depart
ment Of Leavenworth answered an emer-
gency call and Joined forces with the SOL
diers in a battle against the flames. The
fire was confined to the central row of
buildings, and consumed the Industrial de-
partments of the prison. including the
paint shop. the tailor shop, the carpenter
shop and laundry. The buildings con-
tanned many combustibles, and the flames
threatened the buildings. The cellhouses
rapidly became filled with smoke and got
suffocatingly hot.


After bugle calls were sounded the first
guard line was placed about $50 feet from
the prison wall. and the men in 1t were





was 200 feet farther back. The companies
were extended In open order Through
this line no one except an officer or
soldier on duty was allowed to pass.


Unable to Save Buildings.


Half an hour after the fire broke out
the Leavenworth city fire department
reached the fort. Nothing could be done
to save the burning buildings. however,
and the firemen devoted their attention
to saving the main structure and keep
ing the fire from the military prisoners.


There was a scene of great confusion
until the infantry was called out. All
the men at the garrison ran to the prison.
but they were kept back from the cells
by a double guard line.


The sick prisoners were removed from
the prison hospital when the fire was first
seen. The records were taken from the
administration building also, and prepa-
rations made to blow 1t up II necessary.
A new military prison is under construc-
tion. and it is not probable the burned
buildings will be rebuilt.


few men were overcome by the heat
during the fire. Lieut. w. c. Jones, 18th
Infantry. was painfully scalded by a gust
of steam and hot water from a burning
roof. He was taken to his quarters.
where IL was said his injuries would not
prove serious.


Defective Wiring Responsible.


Mai. Thomas Ii. Slavens. commandant
of the prison, said the fire probably was
caused by defective wiring. He placed
the damage at $4,000


The buildings burned were among the
oldest at Fort Leavenworth. They were
erected in 1851 and 1858, and were first
used for an army commissary storehouse.
Many years later they became a part of
the United States penitentiary and later
were converted into a military prison, fol-
lowing the erection of a new federal
prison here. The prisoners now con-
fined there. about 500 men, are practi-
cally all short-term army offenders con-
victed in courts-martial.


Prisoners Taken to Leavenworth.


MOCNDSvILL.E. W. Va, April LIN
charge Of United States Marshal Eliot
and ten deputies. seventy-eight federal
convicts were taken from the penitentiary
here today en- route to the government
prison at Leavenworth. Kan. Before
leaving here Marshal Eliot received a
telegram from Leavenworth assuring him
that the fire at the military prison last
night would not interfere with his bring
Ing the Moundsville prisoners to that
place.


The men. handcuffed in twos and threes.

filled with confetti to mark cross roads

journey. Dai H. 2ewis, pathfinder for the

taken.


Swathed in canvas and rubber cover
ing. thirty automobiles were then parked
in an inclosure in Cadillac square. wait

pathfinder on the 2,636-mile journey
which is to take them through Chicago.
Minneapolis and Denver to Kansas City.
They had passed from the control of
their owners until the tour is over. and
were in charge of the contest commit
tee and the observers who represent it
In each machine.


Big Crowd Saw the Start.
Cadillac square, where the cars have
stood since they checked in to Chair

country. They made the air ring with
cheers when Pathfinder Lewis drove
away from the starting line in front of
the Hotel Pontchartrain.
In the hotel everything was hustle and
hustle among the officials in charge of
the tour, the drivers and observers and
passengers who are to make the long
drive in the machines. The twenty nom
contesting cars which will carry news
paper men and officials on the trip stood
| about the square waiting for their own
ers and passengers to see the start Of
the competitors at 10 o'clock.

Inside the hotel Chairman Hover gave
the final Instructions to the corps of OBJ
servers, and handed to each one the
sealed bag of extra parts which Is car
ried in every car, under the supervision
Of the observer who will see that the
machine is penalized il 1t becomes neces-

Side by side In the park across the

cars and little runabouts, whose small
ness was accentuated by their big neigh
bors. Under the rigid rules governing the
contest not one OF them could be touched
by its driver or owner until one-half hour
before the start Of the tour at 10 o'clock.

went to their respective cars, and under
their watchful eyes the drivers and me-
chanics took off the covers of the ma
chimes and made them ready for the
starting signal. Luggage was placed in
the tonneaus, and the passengers took
their seats.

Twenty minutes before the first car was
sent off, Chairman F. B. Hover and
Charles j. Glidden, donor of the trophy
from which the tour has taken Its popular
name. entered the pacemaking auto
mobile, which none of the contestants
can pass, and followed Pathfinder Lewis
out Michigan avenue toward Kalamazoo,
the first stop.


Starter Ferguson then took his place at
the starting line armed with his green
flag. and the drivers seated themselves
ready for the start. A Premier car had
the distinction of being the tirst contest
ant sent of on the long journey. Then
at intervals of one minute the names
and numbers of the other twenty nine
drivers were called by the starter. Each
driver was handed his time card as he
went over the line, and great cloud of
dust along Michigan avenue signitied that
the run had begun.

CHERRY, ILL.,, Nov. 19,-Science and
desperation have greatly checked the
fire that snuffed out 300 lives last Sat-
urday in the st. Paul coal mine. Men
braved today the fire-swept tunnels to
bring the dead to the surface.


Charity has poured aid into homes of
suffering survivors But all of this
could not subdue the grief of Cherry s
inhabitants when the sight of the dead,
lifted from the tomb blasted their
hopes that the men might be rescued
alive.


1t has been just six days since fire
started in a bale of hay and swept
the bread winners of this community to
their doom, and in all that time of
anxiety only five bodies have been re-
covered, four today and one last night.


1t is expected that many bodies Will
be recovered tomorrow. More were
found today, and explorers working
deep into the second gallery were
forced to flee, as they were about to
bring them out, when falling earth and
rock endangered the rescuers.


Miners Put to Work

the galleries replacing burned timbers
and clearing obstructions which i'm
pede access to the coal veins for more
than 250 feet from the main shaft. Be-
yond this point fires still burn, and 1t
will be some time before they can be
extinguished.


The second and saddest act of the
st. Paul mine tragedy-the recovery
and attempted identification of the
dead-began early today.


Four bodies, those of three men and
boy, were brought to the surface to-
day. Four others were dragged from
the debris of the second gallery and
taken in reach of the cage, but We're
not brought to the surface.


Fifty or seventy-five bodies beyond
reach, for the time because of the fire,
were seen in the wreckage of smoul-
dering timbers and mud.


The sad prospects for the day be-
came apparent when firemen spread
canvass on the prairie beyond the main
shaft. Here the three bodies which
were the first to be brought out were
laid

children formed a great circle about
them, but many turned away, unable
to endure the sobs and cries of those
who mourned seeking their dead. TWO
of the bodies were quickly identified
but not until scores of women had
gazed on the blackened features and
turned away to await the next dread
load from the ueplnS Oh the iililS was
the third body recognized.


Body Is Identified


"Why, 1 know the lad; it's poor lit

Eyes, it's Dickle, the stable boy. an
other said, looking at the lads face.


"Old Man" Stearns, an invalid,
whose only boy is among the missing,
limped to the outer fringe of the crowd.
He has haunted the mine since Sat
urday.


81 can't; Oh, I can't look" he fall
tered. with his hands covering his
face.


Finally word was brought him that
the body was not that of his boy.


The body of Louis Gibbs was next
identified. Gibbs widow was i'll at

nized by comrades.


There were many women. but there
were more children. With their heavy
shawls about their heads, the women
pushed their way to where the bodies
Law, and one after another turned

Many scattered about the yards and

CONVICTION. Ky, March 23-Judge
Harbeson In the kenton county circuit
court. yesterday held unconstitutional the
law establishing the state racing commits
sion. The effect of the decision is to
place Latonia racing on its former basis.
the commission having adopted restrictive
measures. which now become void


The court before passing on the ques-
ton of the constitutionality of the racing
commission act, decided in favor of the
racing commission on several points.
notably the contention that the state had
the right to control the racing business by
police power and to pass rules regulating
race betting that would even go to the
extent of confiscating the racetracks by
rendering their business wholly unprofit-
able. He said that the contention of the
Latonia club that It's track could not be
operated protitably without bookmaking
made no difference to the law in the case


Judge Harbeson held that the law Great
ing the Kentucky racing commission gave
that body power to regulate running
races: that trotting races and running
races came under the same legal cate
CORY. and that therefore the law was class
legislation and was unconstitutional The
court, in other words, held that the law
to be valid must give the racing COM
mission specific authority over both trot-
ting and running races.


The commission viii take the case to the
court of appeals.

The Arabs, even though barbarians and half
savage, are the most humane people Every
one knows the fame of Arabian horses The
Arab loves his horse as much as he does any
member of his family. And in return the
faithful horse loves him. Each would offer
his life for the other. The Arab never touches
his horse with whip or spur, but wins his ODE
dience and affection with kind words There
is story told of the freeing of Hassan, the
Arab. Hewas captured by some enemies and
put in prison. He was bound hand and foot
and laid outside of the tent-prison. When
night came Hassan could not sleep. Soon he
heard the whinny of his faithful horse. He
rolled to where the horse stood, and the dumb
animal shifted about him and recognized his
master. He picked up his master by his gir-
die and ran all the way home with him be-
tween his teeth. When they reached home
the poor animal died. The Arab never forgot
his friends last act. Thus we see there are
humane people all over the world. Brooklyn

band played, cannons were fired at inter-
walls, and each Of the Wright boys made

tors. and their sister Katherine were

proudest fathers in the world. Bishop
Milton Wright Katherine was the first

"Oh. there's daddy" shouted Miss
Wright as she ran ahead of her brothers

him again and again. Then Orville and
Wilbur drew up and each embraced and
kissed his father. The aged mans heart
was too full of happiness for speech and
he pulled his broad felt hat down over his
eyes to hide the tears that were starting.


Wilbur, holding his overcoat and suit
case in one hand. picked up his little
niece, Ivanette. In the other and smoth-
cred her with kisses. The crowd cheered.


The throng then pushed forward to get
look at the famous aviators, and 1t was
with difficulty that the party reached
their carriages. Close personal friends of
the brothers and lifelong neighbors stop
ped the procession to grasp their hands
Beautiful bouquets were thrust upon
them, and their path leading to the car
riages was strewn with carnations.

with flags and bunting, and the streets
were lined with thousands Of people. AS
the carriages drew near the Wright
home, modest frame dwelling, a band
fell in line.


At home a gay sight met their eyes.

were bobbing back and forth in the trees

MADRID. December 24.-Heavy rains
floods, the destruction of which has as
sumed the proportions of catastrophe.
At Ciudad Rodrigo at least eleven per-
sons have been drowned and hundreds
are homeless. Some fifty houses have
collapsed and many others are sub
merged.


The havoc of the water continues to-
day. The valley of the Tonnes is pos
sessed by raging torrent. Bridges have
been swept away, roadbeds washed out,
cattle killed and crops ruined. The viii
lage of Tiguellino is under water. The
Douro river is out of its banks and the
adjoining district has been badly flooded


The beds of the railroad lines leading
toward Portugal have been washed out
and the service is tied up. Communica-
ton by telegraph throughout the range Of
the floods has been interrupted.


Worst in Fifty Years.


Rain storms in the provinces of Sala-
manca and Leon have caused the most
disastrous floods experienced in fifty
years. The towns of Burgos. Zamora
valladolid and Bilbao suffered most.
Many houses have been swept away.
Several towns are without light owing to
the inundation Of the gas and electric
plants.


The governor of Salamanca telegrap..s
that fourteen persons were saved miracu-
lously from the roof of a house. where
they had taken refuge from the engulfing
waters during the night.


Damage From Overflow.


The Tonnes river to the north of Sala-
manca has also overlooked it's banks
causing great damage. Troops were dis
patched to Salamanca today to aid in
the work of rescue.


The railroad lines into Portugal have
been washed out.


LISBON, December 2.-The rivers of
Portugal are raging torrents today, fol-
lowing an unprecedented rainfall. The
material damage is considerable.

CHICAGO. June 2s.-The thirty-first
bomb in the explosive warfare on Chicago
gambling houses was set of shortly be-
fore midnight In Calhoun place in the
heart Of the theatre and all night restau-
rant district.


These bomb explosions in and under
gambling houses have been going on for
months. but to-night's explosion was
more violent and destructive than any Of
its predecessors.


The theatres had Just poured their
Sunday night crowds into the streets
and the sidewalks in the loop district.
where all the transp9el ltion lines centre.
were jammed with people.


One man was fatally wounded, two
women were seriously hurt and several
other persons were cut by falling glass.


Tho bomb was exploded in the rear OF
Stoll 4 Bowen's saloon. l20 Dearborn
street, in the very heart Of the Loop
district. The entire rear walls OF several
buildings in the vicinity were demolished
and plate glass windows In stores as far
as three blocks away were cracked.


Every building for several blocks was
rocked and occupants rushed to the street
to learn the cause OF the disturbance.
Within five minutes from the time OF
the report Madison. Dearborn and Clark
streets were jammed with people, and
II was with difficulty that the police
cleared the way for the fire apparatus.
Powers 4 Gilbert's saloon. at llo Clark
street, and Mosh Tenne's place, 121 Clark
street, are within 100 feet Of the. scene OF
the explosion. These were quickly
deserted the patrons fearing that
another explosion might folloY.


Tho explosion broke the telephone
service in the whole Loop district and
the police were unable to work oon-
certedly. The reserves were called from
all stations within two miles and the
work OF seeking the bomb thrower and
taking care Of the injured began. but
no quick reports could be made for lack
Of wire connections.


In Calhoun place is one Of the big gest
and most prominent gam bling houses in
Chicago. and 1t Is certain that this is the
place the bomb was meant for.


Glass in nearby buildings was shat
tered. and this fell on passersby in the
streets. Glass from the Tribune Build
ing. the Hartford Building and several
other tall structures fell in shower and
q large number of people were cut and
moro or less seriously injured.


There was q panic In the Edelweiss
restaurant, almost across the street from
tbs explosions Gussts ran frofn the place;
fearing repetition OF the catastrophe
that occurred there several years ago.


Two restaurants in Madison street just
In front Of the gambling houee in CAL
houn place where the explosion occurred
were wrecked. In Thompson's several
were thrown to the floor by
the force Of the explosion and the cashier
was seriously injured when the big plate
glass window was shattered and the
fragments fell about her.


In Weightman's, next door. almost the
same conditions prevailed. The cashier
there also was seriously injured when
the heavy plate glass window fell.


In the Hotel Morrison. just half q
block west Of the explosion, there was
panic among the guests. No one was in
jured. however. although all the glass in
the upper windows was shattered.


In the Hartford and Tribune buildings
every pane Of glass above the fourth story
was broken by the force Of the explosion.

ecutive boards instructions. the report adds that

SALT LAKE CITY, July A wind
storm swept over Great Salt Lake this
evening, dashed the heavy water In
huge broadsides against the Saltair
pavilion and threatened the existence
of two small pleasure boats that were
cruising off shore.


After a struggle with wind and
waves. in which the voyagers were
drenched with salt water, the launches
regained the pavilion. In making a
landing one OF the boats was hurled
against the pier and seriously dam

The gale, although of brief duration,
was one of the most violent in the his
tory of the lake. Rumors that one of
the boats had gone down with sixty
passengers reached here and there
was great anxiety until the outcome
was known.

ROANOKE, Va, March N.-The lives of
c. A. Robinson. colored, and his two chill
dren. aged five and seven years, respect
lively, were sacrificed last night In fire
that destroyed the stable on the Robinson
premises in Northwest Roanoke. TWO
horses and three cows were cremated with
the bodies Of the three negroes.


Robinson, who for fifteen years had been
a letter carrier in the Roanoke post office.
had accumulated considerable real estate
and lived in comfortable home. Last
night he went to the stable to see about his
stock, and the two children accompanied
him. They went into the loft with hand
lantern and turned it over. The flames
soon enveloped the barn. Robinson tried
to rescue his children, and all three were
killed. Robinson was one Of the Oldest
employees of the post office, and was we'll
known to the people of the city.

RICHMOND, Va, March 6.-Railroad,
telegraph and telephone companies report
today they have all about recovered from
the effects of the storm Of the last sew
eral days in and around Washington,
Baltimore, Wilmington and Alexandria.
when wires and poles were blown down
and all kinds of business tied up tight.


The Western Union Telegraph Company
was the heaviest sufferer from the bliz-
zard. This company reports that the
ninety wires between here and Washing
ton have been repaired and that the ticker
service was opened UP again this morn
ing after a two day silence.


Service north of Washington over the
Western Union lines is still in bad shape,
but will be in good working order by
Monday morning. Ten miles of cable is
being put in between Washington and
Baltimore.


The Postal Company has gotten six OF
seven wires through to Washington. and
hopes to have this service restored by
tomorrow North Of Washington and
between that city and Baltimore the
wires are in such condition that it will
be Monday or Tuesday before normal
business can be resumed.


Trains between Richmond and Wash
ington, which have been seriously inter-
rupted on account of the wires being
down. have resumed operations. The
morning mail train arrived two hours
late today. Nearly all trains are run
ming within an hour of schedule time.

Mogg, it's owner, to heed the warnings

Mogg beached his vessel for the winter.


He was warned by those in the vi
cinity that his vessel would be in

the southeast.

aboard her at the time.

complete wreck. Three small boats of
the mosquito fleet were also carried
ashore but were not damaged. The
storm was one of the worst experienced
here in years.

OXNARD, Cal, Sept. 16.-An area
more than fifty miles square, contain
ing oil wells, grain crops and rich
pasturage, was burned over by the fires
in this vicinity, which finally were sub
dued tonight after burning continu-
ously for four days. The amount Of
damage cannot be estimated accurate
ly yet, but it is considerably more than
$150,0O0,


Scores of men who have been fighting
the flames returned to their homes
here and in Ventura tonight, COM
pletely exhausted. They were on the
lines of fire almost continuously since
Sunday, and many had to be put to
bed, where they will remain several
days recuperating their strength and
recovering from the numerous burns
and injuries. In several cases the fire
fighters had all their hair singed off,
and came home baldheaded. Many
who went forth bearded returned with
only fire-scarred stubble on their lips
and chins

met long line of hills, north of the
Las Posas valley this n corning at 1
o'clock at Balcoms Grade. They had
been coming together for four days.
Fifty men at that point worked dog
gedly all night trying to back fire and
stop the flames.


The home of Miles Balcom and Il
large barn, the contents belonging to
L. Schifferley, were destroyed. Ike
Stockton's home I also is reported
burned.


Thirty men from Somis made the
last stand against the flames, which
are still burning along Balcom's can
yon, but it is expected will be extin-
guished today.


Two men, S. L. Garner and John
Braley, were lost in the hills and n
searching party was sent into the can
yon after them. The message located
them at Santa Paula, twelve miles
across the hills, this morning.

ening of prices seemed to encourage pur-
chases, either for the long or short ac-

"Will tomorrow ever Gomez" has
been the plaintive cry of the former
employees of the Humane Animal
league, who are now out of Jobs and
who have not received their salaries
for more than three and a half
months.


The question they have been asking
will be answered this morning, for
tomorrow" will come today and they
will be able to get the back pay which
so many of them sorely need. Yester-
day Joint resolution was prepared
and will be filed this morning asking
the court to dismiss the injunction
suit against the city auditor, which
has prevented him from issuing pay
warrants to the former employees OF
the Humane Animal league.


Although the persons interested in
bringing the suit got everything they
asked when the Humane Animal
league gave up it's contract with the
city for taking care of the dog pound
and when the new animal commission
that succeeded the league discharged
every employe, including Tommie
Vacher, yet it was not until yester-
day that action was taken to dismiss
the injunction suit SO that these en-
ployes could get their wages.


This apparently unnecessary delay
which the interested employees blame
on Mrs L. E. Giese and her attorney,
Grant Jackson, has been the cause or
real hardship Although each or the
employees has nearly $500 coming to
him in back wages, some of them
have been thrown out of their homes
with their wives and children, be-
cause they could not pay the rent
One man, whose grocer refused MIN
further credit, had to sell his house
hold goods, and his wife returned to
the home of her parents, stating that
she would live with her husband again
when he was able to feed her.


Yesterday a grocer refused further
credit to one of these employees who
has several children and whose wife
is sick. There was little food in his
house and he was much worried to
know how he would feed his family
His landlord also notified him that,
unless the rent was paid this week,
he and his sick wife and children
would have to get out of the little
house they call home.


When Mayor Alexander heard these
hard luck stories he called up Attor-
ney Grant Jackson on the telephone
and suggested he take action as soon
as possible.

NEW YORK, Sept. 2.-Three new
ocean records fell to the Cunard liner
Lusitania on her latest trip from
Queenstown, which ended tonight.


The Lusitania made the passage in
four days, eleven hours and forty-two
minutes, thereby clipping three hours
and eighteen minutes from her fastest
previous time.


She maintained an average speed of
1855 knots for the entire voyage, beat
ing the Mauretania's record of 1854,
and finally, by landing her passengers
at the Cunard pier shortly before 8
o'clock tonight, she became the first
liner to dock on the fourth day out of
Queenstown.


The Lusitania left Daunt's Rock last
Sunday morning at 10 o'clock. Her
days runs follow: Sunday 81, Monday
$50, Tuesday 652. Wednesday 651,
Thursday CAT, and from noon today 1913.
Total PISA.


The Lusitania and Mauretania here
tofore have left Queenstown Sunday
and reached the Ambrose channel light
ship too late Thursday evening to al
low them to dock before Friday. Today,
for the first time one of them proved
herself a Thursday ship" in the YER
nacular of the sailormen on board, and
thereby became a real four-day boat.

Fifty-two bodies have been recovered
from the wrecked steamer Penguin OF

went on the rocks Friday night off Cape
Terawhiti

bered 100 The ship struck about IL

manned on the bridge and after his
vessel slid into deep water was able to
steer her closer into shore

small boats and rafts which were
hastily launched could not withstand
the waves.


The boats and RATS were overturned
but while the boats practically sank,
the RATS righted themselves a number
of times.


Many acts of heroism were per-
formed, some of the stronger of those
struggling in the water helping the
weaker to regain the frail crafts.


After several hours of buffeting, the
majority of the survivors on the RATS
reached the shore, demonstrating that
rafts are more serviceable than boats
in heavy sea close to a rocky shore.


One raft with ten men aboard thrice
capsized when but a short distance
from the land, but all scrambled back
and were ultimately cast upon the
cliff and were saved.


-Four boats came ashore some hours
later and all were badly crushed.

SAN PEDRO, May 31.-In the tail OF
half of gale-and when it blew up TO
a velocity of twenty-three knots 1t
seemed a full gale-twenty-four fleet
sailing yachts and half a score launches
came across the channel today.


The return of the South Coast Yacht
club flotilla from It's annual cruise to
Santa Catalina was an event filed with
adventure and misadventure.


All kinds of weather, and a variety of
winds that ran the gamut from zephyrs
to gales that called for reefs and more
reefs, wind that was good for backyard
topsails, and a screaming, whistling
blow that sang through standing rig
cling made the amateur sailing men
show their seamanship.


At the beginning of the days cruise
only little catspaws ruffled the calm
waters of the channel just outside of
Avalon bay. 1t was all the canvas
from baby jib topsail to spinnaker.
The heavy groundswells lifted the
white winged boats as they smoothly
slid out into the channel.


Shortly after the start, when the
yachts were well spread out, Venus,
which had run farther to north ard,
struck a doldrum that was peculiarly
her own, and lay becalmed. The wise
mariners on the Wasp noted this and
stood about on a starboard tack that
carried them away from the quiet spot
where the Venus lay, and later they
took full advantage of refreshening
winds and only shortened sail at the
last moment, when they saw that they
were SO far in the lead that their old
rival could not overtake them.


Predict Successful Season


Mah-Pe', Joe Pughs new racer, with
her rigging tuned up on her three days
run, her sails drawing beautifully,
filed out and hardened from huff to
1eech with never a wrinkle, showed
herself to be keen boat. To say that
she beat Mischief II by eighteen min
utes shows that she has latent speed,
which Captain Pugh will develop to it's
fullest later in the season.


The other sailing craft all made ex-
cellent weather of the heavy blow and
strong cross seas on this side of the
channel


There was plenty of spray in the salt
sea just outside the breakwater, and
the boys came in with sparkling eyes
and rudy cheeks, which showed how
they enjoyed the little mixup with
Neptune out on the blue briny.


Joe Fellows was the recipient of
hearty congratulations on the showing
made by his fast boat Campbell. The
launch attracted much attention at
Avalon, and the boatmen at the island
fell in love with her. Despite the ham
dicap Of the heavy cargo, and the tug
ging tender towed at the end of long
painter, Joe made the trip from Avalon
to the club house in two hours and
twenty minutes.


Scores of tired but happy yachtsmen,
with their wives and friends, went into
Los Angeles tonight, declaring the
cruise had been the most successful
since it became an annual event.


The yachtsmen are enthusiastic that
the present season will be the most
successful and enjoyable ever expert
enoed in Southern California waters.

Dear Aunt Laurie:


" HE place where was born was an


old farm house about twenty miles


from Nashville, Tenn. The house
belonged to my grandpa, who was a
dealer in cotton. The large sycamore
trees almost hid the house from the
view of passersby.


Beyond these trees was the spring
and fertile meadows stretching away
to the north. Back of the house was
the farm yard, with its horses, cows,
chickens and pigs. There was the pig
sty, the barn and hen house where the
chickens scratched and cackled all day
long.


To the east spread the vast cotton
fields, here and there dotted with negro
cabins. Most of the darkeys that picked
cotton for grandpa lived on the planta-
ton. Over in that cabin Aunt Chloe
lives with her five children. 1 remem-
ber their names as Robert Lee, Eman-
cipation, Ulysses Grant, Mirandy and
Hunch, so called because of her hump
shoulders. In that cabin by the rail
fence dwells Uncle Tom, all alone Uncle
Tom made the best of whistles. Aunt
Nancy knows every herb in the woods,
and her tumble-down shanty is filled
with them. Uncle Jake, in this cabin is
a great story teller.


This is the place where I was born.


JENNIE EDMONDSON.

STOCKHOLM. August 4.-The labor
conflict in Sweden shows signs this morn
ing of becoming more acute. While the
ranks OF the strikers are considerably
sweled, the general strike called for to-
day has not yet become entirely effective.
Many organizations, although sympa thlZ-
ing with the strikers. hesitate to join
them actively. The employees OF the
street car lines and the cab drivers stop
ped work this morning. and neither cabs
nor street cars are availa BILE. The fact
that the troops are protecting the gas
works and the electric lighting plant has
incensed the wo.kmen, whose leaders
threaten to call out all the men unless
the soldiers are withdrawn.


The printers union held a meeting this
morning but resolved to postpone for the
present any decision in the matter OF go'
ing on strike.


CORPS of Workmen, some thousand
strong is being organized, with the OBJ
ject of maintaining order, and the people
generally bankers. merchants, etc, are
arming themselves for self-protectlon.
The gun shops of the city are practically
,ienuded of revolvers and small arms
All tourists have left Stockholm, and
the number of visitors now in the city
is smaller than at this season for many
years past.


Troops Guard Railroads.


Although the railroad men have de-
cided not to strike, the government Is
taking the precaution to guard the tracks
with troops, fearing attempts to blow
mp bridges or injure the permanent way.
Quantities of dynamite are reported TO
have mysteriously disappeared recently
from the government stores.


The leaders Of the strikers claim that
the end of the week will see notable
spread of the movement; that the rail-
road, postal, telegraph and telephone en-
ployes and the printers will by that
time have joined the strike.


This afternoon guards were posted in
the market places and the railroad sta
iions. All milk supplies have been cut
off and the thousands of babies are suf-
fering from lack of nourishment and the
change from cows milk TO canned milk.
Streets Filled With Idlers.


The streets of Stockholm flled
with idlers who promenade back and
forth chatting the volunteer street clean
ers. many of whom belong to the better
classes. All the saloons are closed today
aud only the best restaurants are per-
mitted to remain open. and even here
il is possible to get wine only with solid
meal.


The ferries have stopped running and
there is little communication between
Stockholm and the suburbs reached by
water routes. This fact will result in
a further diminution of food supplies.
For the present all is quiet in the city.
but trouble is expected when the stocks
of food begin to run low.

position between the North Canadian
river and Deep Fork creek, about seven
teen miles east of Henryetta.

troops, considered it unwise to push the
pursuit and engage the Indians in the
darkness. Accordingly he bivouacked his
troops for the night.

KAMPALA, Uganda, Dec. 22.-Colonel
Roosevelt and Kermit were out early
today hunting the sitatunga, rare
species of antelope.


This was only the start for busy
day Later in the forenoon Colonel
Roosevelt called on Mother Paul, the
American mother superior of the con-
vent here; visited the Catholic mission:
helped to dedicate wing recently
added to the Church Mission society's
hospital and lunched with Bishop
Hanlon.


This afternoon the colonel received
King Daudi Chwa of Uganda, and with
the latter attended a dinner given by
f. A Knowles, the subcommissioner.
Tonlght the expedition pitched camp
at site provided for it near the
Church Mission society's headquarters.


Already the scientists of the party
nave obtained many new specimens of
birds and mammals in this vicinity.

thirty to forty-five minutes late. The
Buffalo express on the Pennsylvania left
here tonight one hour late.

New York division Of the Pennsylvania
railroad. A snow-clogged switch caused
one Of the cars Of the Congressional
limited. northbound. to jump the track at
Mill Stone Junction, blocking three Of the
four tracks. The passengers were trans
ferred to the cars ahead Of the derailed
car and the train proceeded after losing

OAKLAND, Aug 1.-THE monster
balloon City of Oakland, with two pas

morning.

than twelve hours and thus establish
a record for the Pacific coast.

ceremony of christening the airship,
which was performed by Miss Jeanne
Won der Naillen, daughter of the pres
ident of the club


The balloon took a south southeast
erly course.


The balloon, however, came to grief
in Livermore valley this afternoon at
PAS O'Clock.


After leaving Oakland the big air
craft struck a fifty -mile-an-h hour gale
and the balloon sank and drifted
across barbed wire fences and through
trees until it collapsed.


Captain Van Tassell, the pilot, was
slightly injured.


Prof. Won der Naillen, the passenger
escaped without injury.


The balloon was only partially de-
molished.

MONTREAL. Quebec. May 25.-There
was great excitement along the water
front here to-day when the United States
ship Nashville. an obsolete cruiser Of the
United States Navy, steamed into port
on her way to the Great Lakes. where she
will be used as training ship for the
Illinois Naval Reserve.


When the Nashv lille attempted to poke
her nose into the fret lock of the Lachine
Canal Major H. R. Lordly. chief engineer
oi the canal. and the dockmaster refused
to open the gates on the ground that the
presence of the Nashville on the upper
boundary waters between the United
States and Canada would directly con-
travene the treaty between the two
countries. They based their action on
the ground that they had not been
notified from Ottawa that permission had
been obtained from the Canadian Govern
ment for the vessel to pass through.
Capt. Purdy Of the Nashville had all the
papers and credentials necessary from
Washington and said Washington had
already obtained the necessary permits
sion from the Dominion. He also pointed
out that his vessel was unarmed, but il
was said later that he intended to take
on his guns, which are being sent over
land, at Buffalo.


Finally. through the intervention Of Mr..
Bradley. the United States Consul here,
and an exchange of kilograms with Ottawa,
the misunderstanding was Strengthened
out and the Nashville proceeded on her
way this afternoon.


The arrangement between the United
States and Great Britain as to armed
vessels on the Great Lakes dates back
TO 1917 1t provides that no armed ves-
sells Of more than 100 tons burden and
armed with no weapon more powerful
than an Is pound gun shall be main
tanned on the Lakes.


The Canadians so far have nothing but
small fishery protection cruisers on the
Great Lakes. Since the close of the
Spanish h-American war the United States
has sent four comparatively modern and
powerful war vessels to the Great Lakes
the Nashville being the fifth.

topsy turvey. When the sophomores

market. The exchanges in all the mar

deal with the Independent commission
concern. The suit charging that the deal
ers were in a pool was brought in the

tripIed, according to the antitrust law,

VANCOUVER, B. c., June 19.-The
locomotive of the Great Northern-Se-
attic express, due in Vancouver at 3:46
%. M, jumped the track at 3:10 this aft
ernoon while crossing the Frazer river
over Westminster bridge. The engine
and tender went into the river and En-
gineer George Zeigwid was drowned,
also the fireman. No passengers were
hurt.


The wreck was caused by an open
switch. Four cars filled with passen-
gers were left standing on the brink
of the trestle over which the engine
and tender had plunged. The escape of
the passengers from death was miracu-
lous, as little more than the length OF
one car separated the switch point
from the edge of the trestle.


That the entire train did not run into
the river was undoubtedly due to the
fact that as soon as the air connection
was broken when the tender went over
the brakes on all cars were set auto
matically.


The accident occurred while the train
was running slowly. When the engine
and tender went over into the river the
combination baggage and mail car was
left standing on the brink, its front
end hanging over the river.


1t is declared by eye witnesses of the
accident that when the locomotive
struck the water the boiler exploded.


1t is said an immense cloud OF steam
and water was thrown high in the air.
Neither the engineer nor the fireman
was seen after he went into the river.
The cab of the engine was torn off and
foated away on the swift current. the
river where the engine went down is
forty feet deep.

God comfort those who try, but fail;
who falter. fall. and rise again;
who struggle on from day to day
With hope OF only scant reward;

To reach what seems some nearby goal,
But which, delusive to their sight.
Is ever just beyond their grasp.
No laurel wreaths e'er crown their brows,
Or loud huzzas proclaim them great.
They play the smaller. humber parts
on life's vast stage, where fellowmen
Achieve renown, and mount to heights
TO which they never can attain.

Meath sombre sorrows darkest skies,
Through all the trials OF i'll success

BUENOS AIRES, February 2O.-The
Argentine steamer Presidente Roca. from

Puerto de San Antonio and Puerto Ma
drin, on the east coast. The steamer
caught fire. and it is believed the crew
and 200 passengers have persisted. 1t is
reported also that the steamer sank.


Press dispatches received here this
afternoon state that the flames spread
with great rapidity. and that the steamer
was headed In to shore as rapidly as
possible. A panic prevailed and many
lives were lost, some Of the estimates
reaching as high as 200. The Presidente
Roca was on her way north from Puerto
Madrn to San Antonio.


Twenty Lives Lost.


Later official messages. however, report
that the vessel sank, but that only twenty
lives were lost. Three hundred and fifty
passengers and members of the crew were
saved, according to these advices.


The Presidente Roca belonged to the
Hamburg South American line. She was
the largest steamer trading regularly be-
tween Buenos Aires and the southern
ports of the republic.


The steamer Presidente Roca was
mailboat, 300 feet long, fl feet BEAM
and was 1907 tons gross. She was built
In Middlesborough in 1896.

vaded and the home of the resident gen.
eral has not been immune. The schools

For year the sanitary authorities ap-
pointed by the Japanese resident general
have been cleaning up the city, but only
those who have gone into the alleys and
byways of Seoul can know the uncleanli-
ness OF the place. Two years ago cholera
would have swept Seoul. as the city then
was without drainage of any kind. The
rain was the only scavenger. Now there
is a reasonably good water supply and
some kind of operating drains have been
made.


With the use of disinfectants there Is

NEW YORK. July 2O.--Sitting tight in
his locomotive cab and using every
method he knew to stop the wild rush OF
his six-car freight train toward the East
river on North Main street, Williams
burg, last night. Joseph Zachgo. the en-
CINE driver, stuck to his post until the
last OF the six coal cars had plunged into
the water and his locomotive was fol-
lowing them from the pier of the East
ern District Terminal Company.


Zachgo sprang through the cab window
while the locomotive was in the air and
they struck the river together He had
his collarbone broken. but swan 70 a
pier. where he was helped ashore.


His loaded train had been drawn up
an incline running above the pockets OF
the Paterson Coal Company. and the cars
had been emptied. The train was then
started back toward the pier, but the
brakes failed to work.


The cars gained speed with every foot
and the three men in charge of them
jumped as they shot across the pier, re-
ceiving only slight hurts. The first car
to strike the heavy bumpers cut through
them and shot over the end of the pier.
followed by the other cars and the loco
motive.

daughter of Billy Roche. the fight ref

ened away when the girls screams

street to her rescue.

attacked, although she had been with
her mother and brothers until a few
minutes before

lowing. and ran for a little way When
she stopped she saw a negro close
behind her and two others keeping her
pace across the street. In fear she
ran onto lawn. The pursuer followed
and grabbed her, trying TO drag her
from the lawn.

ment Davis appeared, and the three

big class yachts will be held Friday,

every respect. Her only competitors

and Alison Armour's Utowana, due to
arrive here Thursday or Friday.

and his wife and Baron Won Dem
bussche of the foreign office arrived
today. The emperor is due on Wednes-
day.

the Sonderklasse races, the first of
which will take place Thursday. Three
boats making the most points in four
races will represent the German yacht

September, under the auspices of the
Eastern Yacht club.

SAN JOSE March 7.-Former Sen
ator Eli Wright, who was expelled from
the senate in 1905, together with Sen
ators Bunker, Emmons and French.
and was with them indicted by the
grand jury of Sacramento county for
bribery and who jumped his bail here
October 10, 1905, returned to this city
yesterday a free man after four years
of wandering about Central and South
America.


Wright was a member of the house
for six years and was elected to the
senate in 1904 The crime for which
Emmons and Bunker have served time
in San Quentin was holding up the
Continental Building and Loan asso-
citation by threatening them with ad-
verse legislation and accepting brides
from their agents.


During his absence Wright has Wis
tied nearly every Central and South
American country and was engaged as
general agent for the International
Harvester company at Buenos Ayres
when he received word that he might
return.


The indictment against him was dis
missed on November 25, 1908, through
the efforts of friends here, the motion
being backed by District Attorney
Wachhorst of Sacramento.


Wright intends to return to South
America with his family.

BETHU-NE, Pas de Calais France.
January 1.-THE first infections of cap
ital punishment in France for a num-
Der of years past We're witnessed in this
town today. when four murderers were
decapitated by the guillotine. The exc
cUtions We're public and took place in the
presence of a large crowd.


The record of crime against the four
men was a long one. Working together,
they formed band which had terror
lied northern France and southern Bel
gium for several years. robbing. assault
ing and numbering at will. The muir
derers were Abel Pollet and his brother
and two other men. named respectively
Canut and PERU.


The condemned were ignorant up to a
short time before their execution that
they were to die. They had slept un-
disturbed and have had the serene con-
viction that their sentences would be
commuted They attended mass and
were then led out in front of the prison,
where the guillotine was erected.


Made Degrading Spectacle.


The executions were carried out rather
quickly. yet the multitude from the town
and the surrounding country. which
gathered early last night. was impatient,
and upon the appearance of the con-
demned began yelling for instant death.


The effect upon the crowd was the
most horrible feature of the executions.
AS Abel Pollet marched detiantly to-
ward the steps of the platform cries of
rage broke from the crowd. which en-
deaVored to break through the lines of
soldiers closely formed around the gull
lotine Old Pollet brutally repulsed a
priest who sought to console him. Shouts
of joy burst from the crowd as the knife
dropped.


cutions dispersed the crowd and ended
what was regarded by foreign observers
as a degrading spectacle and as suggest
ing terrible scenes of mobs athirst for
blood during the revolution.


Spent the Night Carousing.


The night was passed by >the crowd in
drinking and caroloing in the cafes of
Bethune which were kept open all night
for the occasion. Rain fell steadily. and
morning broke dark and gloomy. With
daylight the people swarmed from the
cafes and headed for the square in front
of the prison. They were hooting. sing
ing and laughing and exchanging coarse
witticiSms at the expense of the men who
were To be executed. The clamor against
the murderers was renewed as dawn
showed the Scaffold dimy lighted with
lanterns.


The French parliament recently passed
a resolution in favor of the retention of
the death penalty in France. and the
cabinet fortnight ago decided to carry
out parliament'S ruling.


The law permitting the infliction of
capital punishment had ben practically a
dead letter, for it has been the custom of
the president of the republic to commute
all death sentences to life Imprisonment.
There remain today eighteen persons in
France under sentence of DEATH

parties had worked all the previous night

OAKLAND. July 22.-Yong You, the
reverent Chinese who disturbed the
serenity OF Police Judge Mortimer
Smiths court yesterday by stalking
into the chamber and salaaming before
the magistrate. broke into jail again
early this morning and will be held
for an examination as to his mental
balance.


Judge Smith got rid of his celestial
worshiper yesterday by writing Q h
on paper which set forth that Yong
You had passed three days in Jail. The
oriental took the paper to Sam Toy,
who runs a Chinese eating house, and
tried to collect $1,000 by virtue of the
magistrates handwriting.


Failing to get the money, Yong You
broke all the windows and Sam Toy
promptly had him arrested for various
things. including disturbing the peace
and defrauding an inn keeper.


Yong You appeared before Police
Judge Samuels today, who continued
the cases in order that the police might
get complaints of insanity against the
prisoner.

completely wrecked, It's owner and
driver injured, and his uncle severely
shaken up today. The fact that Motor
man B. c. Chandler had his car under
close control probably accounts for the
fact that both men were not killed.


The work train was coasting down
the hill in South Ramona avenue, when
the men and the machine started In
the same direction a few rods ahead.
A short distance below Mr.. Toilette,
not hearing the motor and fiat cars
coming up from behind, started to cross
the tracks. The Thomas was struck
broadside, showed some seven or eight
feet along the road and half overturned.
The older man, who refused to give his
name, was thrown back into the ton
neau and escaped injury, save for a
few bruises.


His nephew, however, was caught
Beneath the car when It turned over,
and the left foot badly crushed, sew
eral of the bones being mangled and his
flesh torn and bruised. He will be con-
fined to his home for some time to come.
The uncle admitted he had not heard
the train coming and did not think Mr..
Toilette had, either. The Thomas was
completely wrecked. the wheels being
telescoped, the chassis bent and
twisted, the body crushed and the diff
ferent parts Of the engine wrenched.

One day through the primeval wood
A calf walked home, as good calves should,
But made a trail all bent askew,
crooked trail as all calves do.
Since then three hundred years have fled,
And l infer that calf is dead.
But stil he left behind his trail,
And thereby hangs my moral tale.
The trail was taken up next day
By a lone dog that passed that way;
And then a wise bell wether sheep
Pursued the trail Ger vale and steep,
And drew the flock behind him, too.
As good bell wethers always do
And from that day, DER hill and glade,
Through those old woods a path was made.
And many men wound in and out
And lodged and turned and bent about,
And uttered words of righteous wrath
Because twas such crooked path.
But still they followed-do not laugh
The first migrations Of that calf.
And through this winding woodway stalked,
Because he wabbled when he walked.
This forest path became lane
That bent and turned and turned again;
This crooked lane became road,
Where many a poor horse with his load
Toiled on beneath the burning sun,
And Travelled some three miles in one,
And thus a century and half
They trod the footsteps Of that calf.
The years passed on in swiftness feet,
The road became a village street,
And this, before men were aware
citys crowded thoroughfare.
And soon the central street was this
OF a renowned metropolis;
And men. two centuries and half,
Trod in the footsteps of that calf.
Each day a hundred thousand rout
Followed this zigzag calf about,
And DER his crooked journey went
The traffic Of a continent.
A hundred thousand men were led
BY one calf near three centuries dead.
They followed still his crooked way,
And lost one hundred years a day.
Tor thus such reverence is lent
To well-established precedent
A moral lesson this might teach
Were l ordained and called to preach;
For men are prone to go it blind
Along the calf paths Of the mind.
And work away from sun to sun
To do what other men have done.
They follow in the beaten track
And out and in and forth and oack'
And still their devious course pursue
To keep the path a sacred groove
Along which all their lives they move;
And how the wise old gods laugh
Who saw the first primeval calf
All, many things this tale Nigh teach-
But I am not ordained to preach


Sam Walter Foss.

napolis avenue, Mount Winans, was
drowned last night shortly after clock
by falling into the wafer Of Gwynns falls
at Westport. Miss Polenck. who, with
her sister, Miss Annie Polenck was en-

Westport. and upon reaching the "three-
cent bridge" at that place found it al
most impossible to find their way through

walk along the car tracks. When the
trestle was reached the ladies walked
across the concrete conduit Of the Con-
solidated Cas- Electric Light and Power

that Miss Polenck fell into the water
This conduit is about three feet wide
and is located between the road bridge
and the United Railways and Electric
Company's trestle. 1t spans GWynns falls
a distance Of about 600 feet


The body was found over an hour later,
some distance below the bridge, having
been washed there by the current. The
body was rolled and every effort was
made to resuscitate the young woman,
but life was extinct. The body was
viewed by Justice Miller Of Mount Win
ans. who deemed an inquest unnecessary
and gave a certificate of accidental death
due to drowning.

SAULT STE. MARIE. Mich. November
1o.-The steamer Isaac L. Elwood ram
med the upper gate of the Poe lock In
the Sault canal today. demolishing the
south leaf of the gate and probably plac-
ing the big lock out of commission for
the rest of this season. Navigation will
not be interrupted, however. as both the
Canadian and weitzel locks are available
for ships.


A repetition of the accident to the Ca
madam lock which occurred earlier I'm the
season was prevented by the fortunate
circumstance that the lower gates were
closed when the Elwood crashed into the
upper one. Consequently there was no
damage to the lock except to the upper
gate.


There were four vessels i'm the lock-
the steamers Hecker and Lyncoming and
the barges Sweetheart and Mary y.
Burke-when the accident happened. None
of them was DANA ged. The Isaac L.
Ellwood. down bound. was approaching
the upper gates was closed. Capt. Cum
mings of the EllwoOd declares that as he
approached the lock entrance he signaled
his engineer to back the engines, but that
instead he started them full speed ahead.
Capt. Dolsen of the government tug
Noble. which was near the Ellwood, cor
roborates Capt. Cummings statement.
The big steel steamer AS feet long,
crashed into the gate, which injured the
mechanism so seriously that the canal
engineers believe. from their preliminary
survey, that IL will be impossible to use
the lock again during this season.


Had the lower gate been open the ELL
wood and the four vessels in the lock

REDDING, Conn, Dec. 24.-Mark
Twains invalid daughter, Jean, met
death tragically this morning while
bathing. bringing reignant grief at
Christmas time to Stormfeld, the
country home of the great American
author.


She was his youngest daughter en-
deared to him not only by. long COM
partnership but by her frail health,
caused by recurrent attacks of epi-
lepsy. Her death leaves Clemens with
out kin in this county to share his sor-
row, for his surviving daughter, Clara,
was recently married to Ossip Gabrilo-
witsch, Russian pianist, and is on
her way to Europe


Jean Clemens died not directly from
drowning, as was first supposed but
more probably of strangulation due to
an attack of epilepsy or from heart
failure. The body was found in the
bathtub with the head only partly sub
merged, and medical examination to-
night showed that the lungs contained
little water.


Miss Clemens has shown physical
WEAKNESS Of late, probably induced by
the excitement incident to her sisters
departure and the recent return of her
father from Bermuda But yesterday
afternoon she rode her favorite horse
to the postoffice to get the early Christ
mas mail and last night she cheer
fully prepared Christmas tree, from
which she had planned to distribute
gifts tomorrow morning.


On retiring she asked her maid to
call her early and when she arose this
morning she went to the bathroom,
where her lifeless body was found
later Her failure to respond to the
maids knocking on the door revealed
her death. With characteristic phil
osophy Mark Twain is bearing up
bravely.


Jean Clemens was 80 years old and
was her fathers close companion.

20 the murdered. They are baffied by
the mystery which surrounds the case.


The woman and child were found on

Of mile south of the Horse Shoe Lake
car line. They apparently had been
murdered while they slept. as there
were no signs of a struggle.


The police found the woman. about
thirty years old, with bullet hole
through her right ear The child was
behind her on a pillow. She also had

behavior of Patrick, known as the irish
monkey, when three sacred monkeys,
imported from India, were introduced

his conduct was due to nothing less
than his unfortunate intellectual con-
victions.


In the happy land of India the simple
natives protect a certain kind of ring
tailed monkey, which they keep in their
temples and bow down to. These are
the sacred monkeys. The crew of a
tramp steamship trapped three of these
sacred monkeys several months ago
while along the shores of india This
they did for the sake of the money they
knew they could get from the Bronx
Geological gardens.


DR.. w. Reed Blair kept the sacred
three under quarantine observation for
a time to see that they hadn't imported
anything but their religious convictions,
and yesterday they were placed in tne
cage where Patrick and several sacred
monkeys, who have taken up with his
ways of thinking. were disportins
themselves and eating peanuts. When
the strangers entered the backsliders
remembered the days of their youth
and innocence and stood aside respect
fIllly. Not so with Patrick There was
an instant's lull before the storm, and
in another moment Patrick was using
the three new arrivals as a triple mop
on the floor of the cage and digging at
them with his teeth and hands between
times for the sake of variety. John
Reilly and Frank Engleholm interfered
with the argument, and now Patrick
views the sacred three from afar, long
ing 10 continue the discussion.

Would you like to make some new
friends and meet some pleasant merry
folks this spring?


Hunt up some bits of cotton batting,
pieces of horsehair, string and tow and
little strips of cloth. Fasten these to
bushes and limbs of trees, fence posts
and any other handy place. Then wait
and see what will appear.


AS soon as the snow melts away, on
the very first warm days of spring,
YOU will see some little feathered folks
come hurrying back from the south.
And the very first thing these wise
little creatures think about is a home
for themselves and a nest for the new
babies that always come to them in
spring time. Their sharp eyes can
peer into every nook and corner, and
you may be sure that your little or
ferings will be seen.


You will be surprised to find how
early they begin their building, what
merry time they seem to have and
how many kinds of nests they make.


Such strange taste some of them
have! The kingbird and the golden
robin, for example, will want all your
cotton batting and will fight off all the
other birds that have the same fancy.
The chipping sparrows will carry off
every horse hair and never seem to
have enough. The other birds have,
one and ALL, their own choice of build
ing material and know just where
their nest must be and all they ask
is be let alone.


Do not fail to provide bird house
also, for some of the more helpless
ones Take a starch box, cut hole
in one end for door and nail the
cover on firmly. Set 1t in a well pro-
teeted crotch of some old, knotted APP
pie tree, and you will see how the birds
fight for it, They know what you
mean--they understand that you are
offering them home. Mr.. and Mrs.
House Wren will hurry into 1t and the
bluebirds or tree swallows will run a
race for it's shelter.


In a few weeks your building ma
terial will have vanished, but all sum-
mer long the birds will sing pretty
songs, will wake you in the morning,
orserenade you at sunset and thank
you for your kindness.

In Elmwood cemetery. Memphis, are
two notable monuments to women.
Both were erected by public subscrip-
ton and mark the resting places of an
gels OF mercy. who were regarded as
unclean until the yellow fever epidemic
OF 1873. When that terrible scourge
fell upon the city the Magdalens sent
the inmates OF their houses to the
north, opened their doors to homeless
people who fell i'll. and nursed them
with devoted heroism until they them
selves succumbed to the disease.


One OF the monuments. which repre-
sents an angel bestowing a crown,
bears this epitaph:


Matte Stephenson.


The Martyr:


She died for us October Is. 1873.


The epitaph upon the other monu-
ment reads:


Emily sutton.


A victim Of the epidemic.


Died October T. 1873.
Let sweet faced memory plead for her
who calmly sleens beneath this sod
Nor erring man in pride usurp


The province OF her judge-her God.
No one knows who these two women
were or where they originally came
from. They were human derelicts-
drifting about LIES ocean. Both were
supposed 10 be from the north, and
lived In Louisville before coming to
Memphis. At the time OF their death
which was toward the close Of the most
appalling period in the history of the
city when half the population fed in
fNFht and not enough were left to
nurse the sick and bury the dead, their
bodies were hastily deposited in the
common burial ground. But after nor
nal conditions were restored, and the
physicians. sisters OF charity and others
who had remained through the sum-
ner. told the story Of their heroism and
devotion, a fund was raised by sub
scription. lots were purchased in the
best part OF the best cemetery their
remains were transferred and these
monuments were erected.-Washingto
Star.

NEW YORK, Dec. 25.-It requires a
big two-horse wagon each day to carry
the holiday mail that arrives in New
York for the officers and bluejackets
of the Atlantic fleet.


In the consignment that awaited
them upon their arrival here were one
or more presents for practically every
man in the fleet while the fancy postal
cards conveying Christmas greetings
from relatives and friends were more
than 10000 in number.


Today the ships of the feet were full
of Christmas cheer liquid as we'll as
solid. Throughout the morning the
generous Christmas dinner that the
government provides was in prepara-
tion on each ship. There was big.
fat turkey for every six men and about
5000 plum puddings and mince pies,
topped off with cigars and cigarettes
i'm unlimited number, and all the ice
cream and fruits that the men could
possibly eat.


The football game for the champion
ship of the fleet will be played on New
Years day. A series of championship
basketball games will also take place
during the coming week.

killed, more than 20 severely injured
and a dozen others slightly injured as
the result of the explosion of motor
cycle, and fire which followed it.,

gardens today.

tofcycle burst and the rider lost con-
troll. The benzine exploded in a burst

barrier which broke down.


The rider was thrown off and fell

pitched to the track, several being Sc
verely injured. So terrific was the

ers. who, with clothing ablaze, rushed

BUTLER, Pa. July 1S.-In a riot
following the unexpected arrival here
of detachment of state constabulary
late this afternoon a striking empIoye
of the Standard steel car company of
Lyndora was probably fatally injured
and two bystanders were seriously
wounded. Thirty supposed strike lead
ers were arrested.


The strikers gathered around the
plant, angered at the arrival of the
troops. This caused the clash.


The entrance today of 500 employees
of the Standard wheel company, a con-
Germ manufacturing pressed steel
wheels, into the ranks of the $500
striking men of the Standard steel car
company. has caused the situation here
TO be regarded as serious.


The approach of the constabulary
became known through strike pickets
An alarm was sounded throughout the
little suburb of Lyndora, where the
plant of the Standard steel car COM
pany is located, and within a few mo-
ments thousands of strikers and their
sympathizers lined the streets.


Slowly the troopers cleared the
streets and alleys until the way appar-
emily was clear as far as the car COM
panys plant.


Marching order was again formed,
but the troopers had not ridden 20
yards before they were pelted with
bottles, Stag, pieces of board and Jumps
of coal thrown from the tops of houses
along the narrow street.


The troopers were ordered to draw
and load their guns. As>the column
of 40 men advanced the crowds again
surged into the streets. Putting their
horses to a trot the constabulary rode
into the crowd. firing their weapons
into the ground. 1t was during this
clash that three persons were shot
The strikers used revolvers freely. it
is said.

The bursting of an ammonia pipe
early Monday morning in the China's
refrigerating apparatus filled the liners $
staterooms with the pungent gas and
caused a panic among the passengers,
some OF whom were rendered uncon-
scious and were saved from fatal
asphyxiation only by the promptness
with which they were dragged into
the fresh air. The liner arrived here
yesterday and. among the women pas
sengers, pulses were still fiuttering at
the recollection of the choking of the
day before To make matters worse, a
high sea was running, and it was i'm
possible TO open the outside ports
either in staterooms or saloon, and for
nearly an hour the pungent vapor had
full charge of the China's first class
passenger quarters on the main deck.


The accident occurred about o'clock.
The China had so many passengers on
board that breakfast was served in two
sections. The first section was wrest-
ling with its mush and milk when the
pipe broke, and the second section was
dressing or still slumbering. Ammonia
gas is exceedingly volatile, and almost
simultaneously with the bursting of
the pipe came the screams of women
and children, who suddenly found
themselves in the grip of an unseen
enemy that clutched with relentless
fury at windpipes. From one room a
woman. unconscious, and three scream
ing children were dragged, and by the
time they reached the saloon entrance
pandemonium had turned loose there.
The rush of vapor filled the big dining
hall and, table manners were forgotten
in the wild scramble for the companion
way leading to the upper deck.


While the breakfast party was climb
ing 10 the fresh air, the ships officers
were dragging women and children
from the staterooms and helping them
on deck, where, in record time, the
whole company of passengers was soon
mustered.


Meanwhile, the engineers had shut
OF the flow of ammonia, and by 9
o'clock the air in the saloon was suf-
hciently cleared for those who felt like
it to resume the suddenly abandoned
breakfast.


Among the women passengers were
two who did not lose their heads, and
who rendered valuable service in allay-
ing the panic. particularly among the
children, of whom there were 33 on
board. These heroines of the China s
ammonia panic were Mrs. John Brooks.
sister in law of the governor of
Wyoming. and Miss c. Disbrow, a Mon
tana girl, who has been in Japan teach
ing the children of American resi-
dents how to speak French.

The technical committee which took
over the Maxwell co. after its remark
able 10,000-mile nonstop run few
weeks ago has made an exhaustive re-
port on the condition of the car which
speaks eloquently of its stand-up quail
tiles. The report in part follows:


The Maxwell BriscOe Motor COM
pany, Boston, Mass.


Gentlemen: The committee appointed
on your 10,000mile nonstop touring
car has examined the condition of the
machine and submits the report of
findings as follows:


The car was turned over to the COM
mittee at Copley square, Boston, April
u at about 4:25 p. m.


A ride of about ten miles was taken
to observe the general running of the
machine. The route selected was Com
monwealth avenue to Summit avenue
to Beacon street and return. This
route included the climb over the noted
Corey hill in both directions. The live
load in the car consisted of the four
members of the committee and the
driver. The performance of the ma
chine on this run was satisfactory, al
though at no time was the car speeded.


The last portion of the Common
wealth avenue grade was taken on the
intermediate gear In this gear the
car was turned into Summit avenue
and run about tWo-t thirds of the dis
tance up the rear side of Corey hill,
when the gear was shifted to the low,
on which gear the climb was finished.
Proceeding down the grade on the
front side of the hill the car was
stopped to test the brakes At the foot
of this grade the car was turned about
on Beacon street, and the climb over
the hill from the front side was made
on the low gear. At the top of the hill
the cap was removed from the radiator
and the water was found to be not
boiling. About half way up this ascent
the car was brought to a standStill and
again started. Going down the rear
side of the hill the car was stopped on
the steepest grade and reversed. After
backing for some distance the gear was
shifted and the return run made to
the Massachusetts Institute of Tech
nology, where the committee made the
examination of the power plant.


For all of the stops that were made
the brakes held the car and the clutch
did not slip in making the starts. One
set of brakes only were used, the ex-
ternal contracting, the internal eX-
panding set emergency having been
disconnected.


The engine ran smoothly and
knocked only when hard worked. The
exhaust was regular and there was no
skipping.


The committee pronounced the car
in apparently good general running
condition.


All the parts were found in proper
position and properly connected with
the exception of the emergency in
ternal expanding brakes. The shoes
for these brakes had been removed
from the wheel drums and the rods
connecting with the operating lever
and clutch were disengaged.


There We're no split washers under
the cap screws for the guide of No. l
exhaust valve push-rod, and one of
the bolt flanges on the casing of the
first universal Joint was broken off
and the bolts gone.


No cotter-pins were missing and all
bolts and nuts were set up hard with
the exception of one cap-screw on the
water manifold, which was loose; the
four lower cap-screws of the exhaust
manifold which were slack, and one
slack nut on the inlet manifold. All
other fastenings were properly hold
ing.


The radiator was tight, as were also
all water connections.


The whole car was extremely dirty.
Sand. mud, oil and grease We're liter
ally plastered to some of the parts
and a mixture of these ingredients was
spread over the engine and all of the
machinery. The megneto had no pro-
tecting covering.


General Condition


The car when delivered to the COM
mittee was in practically good gem
eral running condition.


The amount of water in the engine
was very slight or inappreciable except
in the exhaust valve gear.


The main journals and connecting
rod bearings were in exceptionally
good condition.


The piston, piston-rings and cylin-
ders We're smooth and apparently
tight.


The exhaust valves were not prop
erly timing.


The inlet valves were operating sat
isfactorialy.


Bolts and fastenings were properly
holding.


The amount of carbon in the cylin-
ders was not excessive.


The machine was extremely dirty.


Respectfully submitted,


CHARLES F. PARK.


CHARLES j. BAILEY,


WRIGHT, A. CHART

~ our ancestors regarding this lnys-

BERLIN, Sept 18.--Curious official
statistics are published indicating the
favorite seasons for committing suicide
in Prussia. May, June and July are
the popular" months. Men prefer July,
while women favor May. The fewest
suicides take place in February. Thirty
per cent of the male and % per cent
of the female suicides occur in the
spring time, and the next most in the
summer, autumn and winter, in the
order named.


Berlin registers an average of twenty
suicides weekly in June. Youthful per-
sons prefer the night time for suicide,
while adults oftener choose the morn
ing or afternoon. The fewest suicides
occur Immediately after sunset. Mon
day, Tuesday and Thursday are the
"favorite" days The fact that most
suicides occur on Monday and Tuesday
is attributed to the reaction after too
joyful Sundays.


Friday shows the fewest suicides, be-
cause persons on the brink of despair
often recover their courage in anticipa-
tion of the payment of weekly wages
next day. The smallest number of sui
cides take place on Saturday (pay day.
and Sunday, although the number Of
women who take their own lives on
the Sabbath is relatively high. This is
attributed to the fact that women who
live alone feel their loneliness espe-
cially on Sundays.
