Mrs. Elizabeth Doyle, 81 years old,
living at 942 Wall street, was fatally
injured when she was struck by a
street car at Eighth and Spring streets
shortly before o'clock last night. She
was knocked to the pavement and sus-
tained a basal fracture of the skull,
dying Immediately after her removal
to the Crocker street hospital.


The woman alighted from a street car
at Eighth and Spring streets and was
attempting to cross the street. She
failed to notice a car on the other
track, and was directly between the
rails when struck. The car had just
started and was going slowly. The
motorman saw the woman would not
be able to get across the track in time
and applied the brakes, bringing the
car almost to a standstill before strik-
ing her.


The body was taken to the undertake
ing establishment of Pierce Bros,
where Coroner Hartwell will hold an
inquest.


The persons at the house where the
unfortunate woman made her home
stated they knew little about her, and
that she had lived mostly on the char
ity of other roomers.

SEATTLE, Dec. 2.-Improved condi-
tions marked the second day of the
switchmens strike in Western Wash
ington. The railroads have moved
some freight and expressed confidence
that they would be able to increase the
volume rapidly until normal conditions
were restored. Both Great Northern
and Northern Pacific railroads sent out
their passenger trains on time, and the
Great Northern had no difficulty in
making up and sending out it's special
silk train that carried the steamer
Minnesotas cargo to New York.


Between Seattle and Tacoma local
freight service was maintained today
At Tacoma three switch engines were
at work during the morning and five in
the afternoon. The officials declared
they would send out one train of mer-
chandise and one train of coal from
Tacoma tonight, and that local freight
service on branch lines would be in
operation tomorrow.


Both here and in Tacoma several
men were put to work. Most of these
were new men, but in some instances
men who had walked out were among
those who applied for work. The rail-
roads are putting to work any men who
have had railroad experience. Along
the Columbia river freight traffic is
moving considerably better than yes
terday. Two freight trains were dis
PATCHED to Tacoma from Vancouver
Wash, while three have come in from
points on Puget sound and towns south
since midnight Wednesday, Local
freight service and the Spokane, Port
land & Seattle railroad is uninter-
rupted.

VIENNA, Feb. 5.-The present ses-
sion of the Austrian parliament came to
an end this morning after a scene OF
turbulence extraordinary even for an
assembly where violent outbreaks are
comparatively common.


The trouble, which arose from the old
racial feeling between the Germans and
the Czechs, broke out during the debate
on a government bill, the object of
which was to reconsider these difficult
ties.


The radical Czech constructionists
who have been hindering the debate on
this measure for several days, with
continuous din from drums and tin
whistles, so exasperated the Germans
this morning that the opposing deputies
came to close quarters and a fierce
scrimmage enSued.


One of the radical Czech deputies, a
man named Speczek, who has been par
ticularly violent, was captured and
lashed until he howled for mercy.


Another Czech was bitten by a Ger
man on the cheek and sustained an
ugly wound, and black eyes and sore
heads were numerous.


The premier, Baron Won Bienerth,
seeing the uselessness of attempting to
pass legislation, closed the session and
sent the deputies home.


The departure of the ministers was
followed by another free fight in which
the opposing factions rushed upon one
another to the strains Of revolutionary
songs, and wild confusion reigned for
half an hour.


The deputies finally became exhausted
and the battlefield was gradually de-
serted.


The sudden closing of the session and
the political import of the disorder have
had an adverse effect on the bourse.

SAN QUENTIN, Jan. 8.-"Sacred
heart of Jesus have mercy on my SOUL"
With these words ringing clear from
his ,colorless lips, Thomas Fallon, con-
victed of shooting his wife to death,
dropped through the gallows trap this
morning and expiated his crime with
his life. Twelve minutes later the
attending physicians took their stetho-
scopes from the stilled breast and de-
clared Fallon dead.


The death march commenced prompt
ly at 10 o'clock with Father Walsh in
the lead. As Fallon staggered up the
13 steps of the gallows he was praying
audibly. He stepped upon the trap and
then deliberately faced the hangman.
With utmost calmness he raised his
head and looked at the moose. An in
slant later the rope was around his
neck and the black capped figure shot
through the aperture.


Until last evening Fallon held to the
hope that the governor would commute
his sentence to life imprisonment. That
hope was lost last night, however, when
Warden Hoyle received a communica- :
tion from the governor giving his rea-
sons for not interceding with the court
judgment. In the letter the governor
said that according to the testimony
Fallon knew what he was about. and
his intentions were deliberate when he
killed his wife in San Francisco in
1904.

BERLIN, Nov. 30.-Emperor Will
liam opened the reichstag today by per-
sonally reading his speech from the
throne. The speech dealt largely with
domestic legislation, and contained the
important announcement that the gov
ernment has prepared measure eX-
tending the sick benefit insurance to
the working classes not heretofore pro-
tected, and creating a system of IN
surance for the dependent relatives OF
deceased workers.


The imperial insurance Organization
will be modified in important particu-
lars.


Says Fortlfy Finances


One of the principal tasks of the
government, the emperor said, was to
fortify the financial position of the en-
pire with the means provided by the
finance hill of the last session, and
this task would be accomplished
through the appropriation bill for
1910. which would be laid before tho
house.


"Our possessions over seas, in Africa
and in the south seas" said the em
peror, "are developing well. The
growth of their own incomes will re-
lieve the empire considerably of colo
nial expenses"


Reference was made also in the
speech to the proposed extension for
two years of the trade agreement with
Great Britain, which expires December
81, the trade treaty with Portugal, the
French German agreement over Moroc-
co, and the triple alliance which had
preserved the peace for a generation.


Triple Alliance to Stand


81 nourlsh the confidence" said his
majesty, that the three allied en-
pires will continue to act together.
using their strength for the welfare
of their peoples and the maintenance
of peace"


The opening of the reichstag TODAY
was as brilliant as usual. The mem
bers assembled in the white hall of
the palace, those not having the right

ing dress None of the socialist MEM

At the conclusion of the speech the

STOCKHOLM. Sweden. August 6.-The
labor conflict showed no material change
this morning. The workmen employed at
the power station which supplies the cleo
tricity for lighting the capital have joined
the strikers. and the service is now be-
ing maintained by officials of the lighting
department.


AS the strikers have been preventing
farmers from bringing provisions into the
city troops have been detailed to patrol
the country roads. The military author
tiles continue to dispense milk from the
railroad stations for the use of children.


The authorities have forbidden the sale
of methylated spirits, as it has been
found that the workmen. unable to OBJ
tain their usual drink, are resorting to
drinking this liquid.


Strikers Vote to Hold Out.


The strikers held their first general
at noon today and adopted resolution
to continue the strike until all the ques-
lions in dispute shall have been settled
to their satisfaction. They also issued a
demand that the railroad. postal. tele-
graph and telephone employees and the
printers join the movement. The meeting
was peaceful and neither soldiers nor
policemen. except a few detectives, were
present. The authorities. however. took
the precaution OF watching the assem-
bfaRe through telescopes from a captive
balloon that was in telephone commune
cation with military and police head
quarters. After singing the ''Marseil-
laise' the strikers dispersed to the woods
and had picnic lunch.


A dispatch from Gothenburg says the
street railroad employees Of that city have
Joined the movement.

noon one mile and a half from Napa

Engineman Paddy Ryan, Conductor
Moran and the train crew, who clam
bered on top of the freight cars and
applied the handbrakes.


Fifteen minutes after the freight
train, which was made up of %
heavily laden cars, left Cordelia
and was descending a steep grade.
one OF the driving rods of the loco
motive, broke. A piece Of the rod was
hurled through the cab window, and
striking the Westinghouse airbrake
appliance at the engineers side. rem
dered the pneumatic brakes useless.
In another instant the driving rod on
the other side of the locomotive broke
and the train darted down the incline,
gaining great momentum.


Engineer Ryan and his fireman
abandoned the cab after the whistle
had been blown calling the train crew
to the handbrakes on the tops of the
freight cars. When the crew reached
the brakes the train was speeding at
20 miles an hour


Another segment of one Of the broken
rods then crashed through the oil
tank on the tender and trail of
crude oil marked the frenzied flight of
the runaway engine. Another piece Of
a rod was hurled against the steam
chest and punctured it. releasing the
motive power. Although no steam was
left in the boiler the dead" engine
continued on its perilous journey until
the handbrakes were finally clamped
tightly upon the wheels of half the
freight cars. Smoke issued from every
axle box while the attempts were made
to check the runaway cars.


Various parts of the engine which
had been torn loose by the whirling
broken rods were strewn along the
path taken by the train. The track
in many places had been thrown out
of alignment where the rods had
smashed the ties.

Moroccan war. The strikers stoned the

One of the last things in the world

shire at an iron works within ten min

known as the Lord Nelson" and Skip
ping Sally" the officers using the former
name and the men the latter.

NEW YORK, January Trading in
stocks during the greater part of the
days business session was conducted upon
a smaller scale than yesterday. While
the dealings in the bond market exhibited
increased activity. The tone of both de-
partments was, on the whole, quite
steady.


The general market did not have to
contend with such sensational episodes
as these which occurred in consolidated
gas and New York Central early in the
week. and the professional traders whose
operations again furnished a large pro-
portion OF the total again ranged them
selves upon the bull side of the speculative
account on the theory that the decline
had run sufficiently far TO warrant some
degree of upward reaction.


At the same time nearly all of the more
extensive advances in prices were in the
so-calied railway specialtieS. Conspicuous
features In this respect were the Colorado
Southern shares, the 500 stocks, Chicago
and Alton and Wisconsin Central. The
further rise in Colorado Southern was at
tributed to the reports, as yet unconfirm-
ed, that these shares would be exchanged
some relative basis for the Burlington
and Quincy per cent bonds.


Among the standard railway issues the
strongest features were st. Paul. Union
and Southern Pacific, Reading and Chesa-
peake and Ohio. New York Central fluc-
tuated quite widely. but still ruled above
its final figures of yesterday.


Rock Island Exceptionally Strong.


The Rock Island company shares were
exceptionally strong and more definite
assertions were current that voting power
would soon be accorded the holders of the
common stock.


The local traction issues were less active
than of late, but were also fairly steady.


A fairly large volume of business was
transacted in the industrial and miscel-
laneous stocks. Consolidated Gas was the
center of interest in that department, but
the movements in that security today
were more in line with those in the re-
mainder of the market than has been the
case since Monday.


The first transaction that has taken
place in Brooklyn Union Gas for several
days was made this morning at decline
of eighteen points from the last sale The
United States Steel shares retained the
firm tone they have exhibited during the
past day or two Other leading stocks
in this quarter of the market were Col
orado Fuel and Iron, American Smelling
and Amalgamated Copper.


Foreign Houses Sellers.


American shares were decidedly strong
In the London stock market, but foreign
houses continued to sell here and dis
posed of upward of 5000 shares on bal
ance.


The Bank OF Englands rate of discount
was left unchanged at PA per cent and
the banks weekly statement showed
fairly satisfactory recovery from the low
ratio of reserves to liabilities usually re-
ported toward the end of the year.


Little alteration was noted in local
money market or foreign exchange con-
ditions. The banks have gained from
the subtreasury in their operations with
that institution since last Friday nearly
s5.6oo,00. a circumstance which lends
some interest to the figures of the bank
statement at the end of the week.

ESCANABA, Mich, August 27-Float-
ing for four days at the mercy OF the
wind and seas of Lake Michigan, with
nothing to eat and afraid to sleep lest
some ship might pass within hailing
distance unseen, DIR. G. A. Richie and
his nephew. Hal Richie. of SauIt Ste.
Marie were towed into this port today
by an ore carrier in an exhausted con-
dition.


Starting from Depere, Wis, Monday
with a new thirty foot cruising launch,
the two men struck boldly out into the
lake. When well out their engine,
which had been working badly for sew :
eral hours, stopped completely, and no
amount Of attention could bring an ex-
plosion in the gas chambers. That night
the two finished the small stock of food
and both kept watch.


All the next day they worked with
the engine. A heavy sea sprang up, and
a rude sea anchor was thrown out to
keep the little crafts bow to the wind
Even with this precaution it was often
half buried beneath the great rollers.
Another night and another day passed.
Growing weaker as each hour passed.
hoping each moment to sight a Iaks
boat. the two men fought off despair
subsisting on water alone. AS the days
passed and the expected boats did not
appear they grew more desperate, and
finally, when several large boats passed
them too far out to hail, they almost
abandoned hope. Finally they succeeded
in hailing the passing ore carrier.

ALAMEDA, Feb. 22.-When Carlton
Wall claimed Mrs. Violet Kesner as his
bride in New York city last week Dan
Cupid smiled triumphantly. for he knew
that one of his deadly darts had wrecked
prospective stage career and convert
ed an embryo actress into a devoted
matron Friends of Mrs. Wall admit
that when she started east prior to her
marriage it was with the intention of
preparing herself for a life behind the
footlights, and it is rumored that sew
eral enterprising theatrical managers
had made her fattering offers But
when the dashing and ardent Carlton
Wall followed her out of the west and
laid his heart at her feet she unhesi-
tatingly thrust aside all her other offers
to accept his.


Mrs. Kesner was accompanied on her
trip east by her sister. Mrs Carlin
Armstrong. According to a dispatch
sent from New York she was then
wearing diamond engagement ring,
but short time after her arrival in the
eastern metropolis some malicious busy
body sent her an anonymous letter con-
tanning the information that her fiance
was making himself unbecomingIy
merry with divers fair maids in Cali
fornia and was constantly seen in pub
lie with women. Impusively the beau
tiful Mrs Kesner posted back her en-
gagement ring to Wall, with brief
note explaining that she would not per-
nit the old adage of "out of sight out
of mind to apply in her case.


For a time Cupid was inconsolable
and it looked as though the stage would
surely cheat the hymeneal altar, but
Wallis appearance on the scene and his
assurances of the falsity of the letter
proved effective, and love triumphed in
the end.

ham Glass Company. Southside.

tunity to escape.

pened the car struck the ''bumpers' in
the little frame station at the bottom.
impact caused the station to collapse and

injured passengers.

Miller and K1enberger. the two dead.
badly mutilating them. It was some
time before the injured could be extri-

Romard, was steaming up the river when

learned by the police, was crushed to
death and then scalded by the steam. His
body lay on the deck, when Capt. Rom
ard attempted to steer his craft to shore.


Sunk Near Shore.

was thrown to her by the tug Director.


The Bee was drawn close to shore and
then the three unconscious men and the
body of the dead man were lifted to the
Director.

steam and made all speed to Bellevue
Hospital.

Cordell, a cook.

of the Chinese consul general here have
placarded the dead walls of the Chinese
quarter with notices giving alleged spe-
cific instances of misconduct of Hsu
Ping Chen, who is the representative of
China in this city. The opposition to the
consul has been at work for several
months, but the fight did not take def
mite form until placards. were posted.
Now the Chinese quarter has divided into
two hostile camps, irrespective of tong
and family affiliations.


1t is asserted Chen extorted money
from rich merchants who wished to
bring their families to this city by al
leging he needed the money to bribe the
immigration officials. Other placards as
serted that the consul made a regular
practice of importing slave girls.


The consurs friends tore the placards
from the walls and assert the charges
have been made against every man who
has ever held the position.

President Frank Hermann of the
State league is out with the statement
that the players which Bill Curtain
announced Sunday as having secured
from the State league is the bunk and
that neither of the trio of outlaws
will join the coasters.


According to Curtains story, Hap
Myers. the crack first baseman: Catcher
Tom Hackett and Pitcher Hester had
come into the fold of organized ball
and had agreed to play with the Sac
ramento team. With the desertion of
these men the future of the State
league looked dubious, as the players
were practically the backbone of the
Sacramento outlaws, and it would have
been difficult for the manager of the
team to fill their places at this time
The newly formed Sacramento club
looked stranded, and the fans could
not see anything but failure in sight
for the outlaw organization.


But Hermann's announcement gives
the situation different color. He says
that Myers, Hackett or Hester will
not desert, and that they will be with
the Sacramento State league when it
commences this weeks play. Hermann
says he has the word of the men,


Hermann says the State league will
finish the season as per schedule, and
that it has been experiencing more
prosperity since its reorganization than
before. He says that rowdyism will
be suppressed, and that players en-
ploying such tactics will be banished
from the league


1t remains to be seen who has an ace
in the hole-Curtain or Hermann. Cur
tain says the men will join his team,
while Hermann declares that the play
ers will not desert. The fans will wait
and see.

COTTAGE GROVE, Ore, June 5.--A
passenger train consisting of an engine,
tender and one car on the Oregon &
Southeastern railroad on its return trip
from Wildwood and the Bohemia mines
late today went through a bridge which
spans Roe river, about five miles east
of here.


About fifteen persons were injured
and W, H. Ostrander, the engineer, is
expected to die. His chest was crushed
and he was internally injured.
The bridge collapsed in the center
and the car and tender went down and
were partially submerged.
The promptness of Engineer Ostran-
der, who locked the brakes, saved the
engine from rolling back on top of the
wrecked cars.

tent by the husband and father, James

issued the warrants on Gibbons. ap-
plication yesterday. The neighbors
and friends of the women were as
founded.

hysterical after going to Justice
Rogers office to talk over the matter

for long time. She was removed to
her home without arraignment.

bond, which neighbors quickly fur
nished, asserting the girls character
was unstained.

cases on his own motion. Mrs. Glib
bons recently secured her husbands S
arrest on charges of failure to provide
and disturbing the peace. He is now
in the county jail. Justice Hart is
sued the warrants for his arrest. The
man then went to Justice Rogers and
asked. for warrants against his wife

Gibbons shrieked and wept piteously,

to provide herself with the necessities

AUBURN, y. Y, March 2s.-Murmur-
ing a prayer for her soul Mrs. Mary
Farmer was quietly led to the electric
chair in Auburn prison shortly after
6 O'Clock this morning and executed
for the murder of Mrs. Sarah Brennan
at Brownvilie last April


The execution of Mrs. Farmer-the
second inhiction of the death penalty
on a woman by electrocution in this
state-was effected without sensational
incidents Five women. two of whom
were prison attendants. were witnesses.
Father Hickey, spiritual adviser of the
condemned woman, following the exc
cution- gave out statement signed by
Mrs Farmer in which she declared that
her husband, James Farmer. was inno-
cent and knew nothing of the crime
until it had been committed.


Led by Father Hickey and with Mrs.
Dunnigan and Mrs. German. who have
attended her constantly since she was
brought to Auburn prison, Mrs. Farmer
walked unfalteringly to the death
chair, her eyes half closed and claspinS
crucihx in her hands. AS she was be-
ing strapped in the chair Father
Hickey stood at her side and offered
prayers for the dying.


KILLED BY FIRST SHOCK


DR.. John Germ, the prison physician.
said that the woman was dead after the
first shock but as there was still a
tremor of muscles reacting, two sue
ceeding contacts were given. State
Electrician Davis said that 1,S40 volts
and ~ amperes was the strength of
the current that passed through the
woman's body After Warden Benham
announced that the physician had pro-
nounced Mrs. Farmer dead DR.. Edward
Spitzka of Philadelphia and DIT. Charles
Lambert of the Pathological institute at
Wards island, New York. performed
the autopsy.


All night long the wretched woman
had prayed within her cell on the sec
ond tier of the woman's department in
the condemned row after she bade fare
well to her husband


FINAL HOUR WITH HUSBAND


Separated by steel bars and an in
tervening screen husband and wife
spent their final hour together I'm quiet
conversation. The final word was
spoken, last goodby. the weeping
husband returned to his cell and the
hGpless woman was led down the mar
row corridor Early this morning Father
Hickey joined the watchers at Mrs
Farmers cell door. In the pale ocher
light of the corridor the woman and
priest prayed together. the last sacra-
ment was administered and Mrs.
Farmer said she was not afraid to die.


Locked in his cell in a far away cor
ner OF the prison. Jim Farmer. the hus-
band, prayed during the hour OF his
wifes execution. Farmer will not be
taken back TO the death row. until
Wednesday morning.

SAN PEDRO, May 2.-Several hun

afternoon when the balloon which was
to carry Dick Eariston and his para
chute up for a spectacular drop was
burned at the last moment and nearly
destroyed.


The balloon, which was an old one,
was heavily inflated by hot air and
partially burst just as the aeronaut
was about to ascend. Part of the frail
cloth fell into the flames and in mo-
ment the whole bag assembled. Still
burning, the balloon went up but a
short distance when 1t collapsed and
fell to the ground practically con-
sumed. Many consider the accident a
godsend to Earlston, for should the rot
ten canvas have given way on some
other occasion when the daring aero
naut was ascending a fatal fall might
have been the result

i'm the harbOr

While playing with matches and a

Spalding, 31a years old, the son of Alex
ander Spalding, a plasterer living at

died several hours later at the Chill
dren's hospital. The little fellow was
conscious to the last; smiled and told

going to die. and kissed them all
good by.


Just how the accident occurred Is not
known. Mrs. Spalding had cleaned
some ribbons with a quantity of gaso-
line Saturday and had left the liquid
in a can on the rear porch. Yesterday
morning she and her husband arose
early and went downstairs in the parlor

lad awoke, slipped out of his little bed
and came downstairs in his flannel
nightgown. He passed through the
dining room, into the kitchen and went
out on the rear porch without the
parents being aware of it

Shortly afterward the child gave a
SCICdIl llldl Slttl tlth lllG
parents, and before they could investi-
gate the little fellow ran into the parlor
with his clothing ablaze.


Spalding seized the child and clasped
him to his breast and endeavored 10
beat out the fire. He was unsuccessful
and after burning his hands severely
took the lad into the bedroom and
clothes and succeeded In smothering out
the fire, but not before the child was
burned from head to foot.

physician, but was unsuccessful be-
cause of the latter not being at home.

ings were applied and retained con-
seriousness. He talked with his parents

realizing that he had but few min
utes to live, the little fellow threw his
arms about his mothers neck told her
how much he loved her and how sorry
he was to have to die and leave her.

his father and called TO his little play
mate and told him good by. Then, with
n smile on his disfgured little face, the
brave little fellow closed his eyes and

medical attention for her was neces-

The apples from Hood River valley are

NEW YORK. July 23.-Wild with rage
| because they were to be sent back to
Buenos Aires after travelling thousands
of miles and spending their money for
transportation. a band of gypsies fought
immigration deporting officers with feroc-
ity yesterday


They lay down upon the pier of the
Lamport & Holt line, near the old Rob-
erts stores, Brooklyn, and refused to
bulge. Then having been previously
stripped of all their weapons they grab
bed their little children using them as
bludgeons to attack the inspectors.
The band. consisting of twenty-four
persons. six men, eight women and ten
children. who had come here on the Ten
nyson on their way to Oakland Cal, had
been promptly ordered deported al
though they had twenty-five pieces of
baggage and S1,O0.


Commissioner Williams and the mem
bers of the board of inquiry decided that
the Romany tribe, even with their re-
sources, were not desirable aliens, ow-
ing to traditional fondness for other
peoples horses and chickens.
Told to Leave by Signs.
No interpreter on Ellis Island could
speak the Romany tongue and the pic





of their deportation only by signs They
were put board the tug John j. Tim
minis yesterday morning and taken to the
Verdi, which was to sail for Buenos
Aires at 10 o'clock


Their hands cleaned with rings. Fan
tastic necklaces and earrings relieved
the color of their dark skin. The men
were muscular, with white teath. The
big chief had long hair. with heavy black
mustache, broad trimmed ha; and gold
rings in his ears.


Their wicker basket and metal trunks
We're piled in the bow of the tug. When
the Verdi was reached and a plank run
out to a gate in the side of the steamer
the sypsies refused to move.
Inspector Tylson had the tug back
down upon the bulkhead AS the band
went ashore upon the bulkhead they
were rounded up by the four deporta-
ton officers. They were driven through
the door of the pier shed and down to
the gangway.


Women Shrieked and Bit.


TYSON grabbed the chief to run him
up the plank. when the women threw
themselves upon him, struck him with
their hands and flung themselves down
upon the pier. They shrieked and tried
to bite the chief inspector. AS he push
ed them back and struck out at them
the women rushed back to their children
and in a blind fury seized their offspring
by the legs swinging them about like
clubs. One woman with her main
strength dashed her baby against an
inspector struggling with her husband.


Working his way back from the ship
the chief seized a slim little girl and
used her for weapon. Her head struck
against a door, cutting her on the fore
head and the cheek When she was
wrested at last from the chiefs grip
the little girl was unconscious.


The passengers on the deck of the
Verdi were excited by so unusual and
violent a scene. Some women turned
away. The pier was in a riot, but the
crew was not allowed to interfere.


At last the husky longshoremen joined
in with the inspectors. They seized the
gypsies. kicked. showed and punched them
aboard the steamer. Two children, who
were being carried face down, with blood
streaming from their wounds, were taken
from their frenZied mothers.

OAKLAND, May 3.-An explosion
shattered the cartridge shell-filling
house at the Selby Smelling and Lead
company's plant at Vallejo Junction
today, causing the death of William
Aljets, a 16-year-old boy employed in
the plant and the serious injury of
Foreman Samuel Cunningham and
Miss Violet Cooper.


Half dozen others were slightly
injured. The shell-flling house is
stored with several different kinds of
explosives in small quantities, and
some fifteen persons are employed
there in placing the powder in car
fridge shells.


The supply of powder became ignited
in some unknown manner today and
the explosion which followed shattered
the walls of the building and burned
young Aljets so severely that he died
at the hospital two hours later.


Cunningham was severely burned
also and his condition is serious. Miss
Cooper was caught in the stampede of
employees for safety and thrown to the
ground with such violence that her leg
was broken.


The injured were put aboard spe-
cial train and hurried to this city for
treatment.


The officials of the plant are unable
to account for the accident.

Biddy now lays her egg where
thoroughbreds worth thousands of dol
lars once champed their oats. No
longer does the whinny of an impatient
race horse resound from the Enclosure;
instead fussy old white leghorns
scratch for worms and roost in stalls
once occupied by King James, Rose
ben, Jack Atkin or Montgomery. POM
pous white ROSTERS flap their wings
and crow from gates where once hung
the blue and white of Hildreth, the
white and yellow of the Saint James
stable or the Maltese cross of Lucky
Baldwin.


Every day the keeper goes forth pail
in hand. but the pail does not contain
rolled barley or bran mash; it Is for
the purpose Of gathering henfruit

Toward evening no silvery bugle is
heard summoning the ponies" for the
last race; instead is heard a chick
chick-chick, calling the hens for their
evening meal.


The stalls make excellent nests for
setting hens, while the track and in
closure are ideal foraging grounds. II
has even been proposed to turn the
judges stand into an incubator and
the paddock into a giant breeding
house. The betting ring has not as Yet
been put to any useful purpose. The
posts where formerly were hung the
numbers of the winning horses now
proclaim the price of eggs.


Mr.. and Mrs. H. Ryan, however, are
prospecting, for raising poultry is more
profitable than playing the ponies.

Both surf and yellowfin were running

quite an achievement for them. Skill
full handling of the boat by Captain
Hills and intelligent direction on his
part probably aided the San Jose men
in successfully handling their catch.


Catalina fishing was up to par but

PITTSBURG, June 29.-Greater Pitts
burg is happy today in the realization
that it does not have to walk down OF
around town. Street railway traffic
was resumed at an early hour this
morning and regular schedules caught
up before z o'clock


The street car strike was declared off
officially last night


For two whole days, between pouring
rain and a sun which made wet clothes
steam, the residents of the Smoky city
struggled the best way they could
against poor shuttle steam trains and
poorer dray carry-alls. The poor man
walked, the well-to-do walked and the
affluent walked.


There was no alternative. The seri-
Gus side of the two days traffic dis
turbance lies in the loss to the car COM
pany in fares, the loss of wages to the
men, the loss of department store trade,
salaries for extra police, and the gen
erai Generalization of business condi-
tions throughout the city. 1t has been
estimated that Monday alone brought
the total cost of the strike close to
$250,000


The agreement made and signed by
the Pittsburg Railway company and
the Street Car Mems union last night,
it is predicted, will forestall any traffic
strikes in Pittsburg for years to come.


The union men claim they have
gained their points, while the car COM
pany people are just as strong in the
assertion that they stood firm.


Mayor Magee. however. smilingly
states that he believed all trouble be-
tween the company and its men had for
once and all been done away with.


On every hand is heard commenda-
ton for the Efforts of Mayor William
A. Magee. Through his efforts the
strike was amicably settled.

BENDLETON, Ore, April 6.-Super'
stition--the belief of omens-has
been the impelling cause for the sac
rifice of every pair OF twins born into
the Cayuse Indian tribe for more than
century and half; and this same
dread OF displeasing spirits is the rea-
son why two little Cayuse twins, ToX-
e-lux and A-lompum are alive today
and are learning the white man :
ways at the Umatilla Indian school
near here.I instead of lying in Tiny
graves on the rolling prairie lands OF
eastern Oregon.


They are girls and are the only
twins who have not fallen victims 10
the customary death penalty meted
out 10 Cayuse babes unfortunate
enough TO come into the world at the
same time.


About the time when George Wash
ington was fighting Indians. Chief Aui-
a-mi-keen Cougar Shirt was chief OF
the Cayuses who then held sway Over
the lands from the Blue mountains to
the Columbia river. He was the IA
Their OF two girls, twins, and famed
beauties. They were budding into
womanhood when the young Bannock
braves paid friendly visit to the
Cayuse tribe, became enamored with
the duo and finally kidnapped them
and fed toward the Bannock territory
over the mountains to the Snake river.
Three hundred Cayuse warriors, head
ed by Cougar Shirt, went in pursuit..
but the Bannocks with their prizes es-
capped


The chieftain father swore vengeance.
Runners were dispatched TO the Wal
la Walla and Umatilla tribes. An al
lance was formed and war declared
on the Snake river redmen. But be-
fore the allies could get their warty
together, 1000 savage Bannocks cross
ed the mountains and swooped down
on the Cayuse braves who numbered
700 men. They met at the confluence
OF the Umatilla and Columbia rivers
and for three days bloody battle
ragged. The remnants OF the Cayuse
warriors were driven over the Cas-
cades, leaving their dead behind.
Since then twins have been looked
upon as a curse. a sign OF misfortune.
superstitious fear of them sprung
up and to guard against the recurrence
OF another visitation OF spiritual dis
pleasure, the head men decided that
all twins should be killed at birth.


The edict was always carried out
until Him-ye-an-hi-hi became the
mothermother of Tox-e-lux and Atom
pun. council was held and il was
decided 10 kill the babes. But the ia
Their was wise. He had a vision and
went before the council and told II he
was an actor. and succeed in making
the tribesmen believe that a spirit had
visited him in his sleep and told him
that he would be the father OF twins
and that they were to come as fav-
orable omen, the sign Of the Great
Spirits pleasure and guarantee or
good fortune to come. His intensity
and evident sincerity won. Today the
twins are growing into willowy maids
and give promise OF rivaling In beauty
the daughters of Cougar Shirt. the
first twins who brought death to 500

tribe

was badly wrecked. When Alexander
Williams. the wouldbe aviator. was
lifted from the twisted frame, he was
delirious. his left arm was broken and
his body bruised. His injuries, how
ever, are not serious.


The accident occurred on Hampstead
plain Mineola, where Curtiss has been
giving demonstrations for the New
York aeronautic society, to which he
recently sold his aeropIane for $1,000.
Williams, who is member of the So
eiety, is 40 years old.

SACRAMENTO, July 5.--By promptly
applying the brakes on his locomotive,
Engineer Mccoy of the Sacramento
Woodland local today saved the lives
of two boys. Everett Farley and Frank
Miscovisch. The lads were driving
grocery delivery wagon when the horse
ran away. throwing the two boys out
just as the wagon struck the railroad
track in Broderick, across the river
from Sacramento. The wagon was
overturned on the boys, pinning them
on the track. Those who witnessed the
accident heard the local train coming
and tagged it, Engineer Mccoy stop
ping his engine within 10 feet OF the
agon with the boys under it.

chauffeur, ]. F. WEIGH, was recovered

FITZGERALD, Ga, August Ell
Henry Taylor, d negro ex-convict,
charged with assaulting Mrs. Josh Wick
ers Tuesday and then numbering her
and her infant, was yesterday afternoon
taken from the sheriff Of Wilcox coun-
ty and lynched.


The crime for which the negro paid
the penalty at the hands of indignant
citizens was one of the most brutal ever
recorded in the criminal annals of Geor-
gia.


Brutal Crime Revealed.


Mrs. Vickers and her eight-month-old
baby were left at their home at Lump
kins Ferry Tuesday afternoon and that
night when the husband and father re-
turned from his work both his wife and
baby were missing. A search revealed
the fact that they were not at the
home of any neighbor. Soon their dis
appearance, with suspicion of foul play
was known throughout the neighbor-
hood, and search for them was imme-
diateiy commenced. Thursday after;
noon the bodies were found in small
pond not great ways from the Vickers
home. The woman had been assaulted
and then choked to DEATH while the
baby's skull had been crushed.


Henry Taylor had told of seeing Mrs
Vickers, with her baby. go in the di-
rection of the pond in which their bod
les were found. Suspicion was imme-
diately directed toward him upon the
finding of the bodies, but he had disap-
peared from the community.


Taylor Arrested on Suspicion.


Early yesterday Taylor was arrested
in Benhill county, near Lumpkins Ferry
He was taken in charge by the sheriff
Of Wilcox county, who Immediately
started for Fitzgerald. Finding that his
way was blocked by the presence of
large numbers of aroused people, a
circuitous route was taken. When the
citizens. however. learned of the change
of plans. and, continually augmented by
bloodthirsty men, the mob followed the
trail of the sheriff and finally came upon
him between Lumpkins Ferry and Nc
Rae, and quick work was made of the
negro. After being strung up a tree,
Taylor body was filled with bullets.


Taylor had only recently completed
serving a chain-gang sentence in this
county

And, stead of supper she would stare
Full hard against the moon.

God rest her aged bones somewhere;

Special Dispatch to The Star.


NEW YORK. January "a motor car
accident near Little Neck. L. l.. at
O'Clock this morning resulted in the in
stant death of wealthy young man and
more or less serious injuries to two other
men and three young women. Edward
Colt Gilman was the man killed. The ac-
cident followed swift dash over the Long
Island roads and was the Wind-up of an
amateur play given by the young people OF
Flushing in the Flushing Town Hall


Among those who took part in the play
was Miss Jeanette Mckimm, one of the
most beautiful young women in Flushing.
Her two most intimate friends, Miss Lucy
Bogert and Miss Dorothy Whittle, were
in the audience. Also in the audience was
Fred Lee, who is a man of means, and
who makes his home at Douglas Manor
Inn. With Lee was his chauffeur Bren-
nan, and Mr.. Gilman.


Lee was proud of new touring car he
had just acquired, and when the play
was over invited Gilman and the three
young women to take ride with him.


The machine had just struck steep
incline and was bounding along at a
mile-a-minute pace. Half way down the
hill one of the front wheels came off
and the machine literally leaped into
space and plunged head ong against d
fence before 1t turned completely over


Lee and Brennan We're thrown free
from the wreck and landed on the road
side with cut heads and other bruises Gil
man was dashed straight against the
fence and his head was split open. Miss
Mckimm fell alongside Lee and was rem
dered unconscious. Her two girl COM
panions were thrown free Of the over
turned car. but did not escape cuts and
bruises.


Lee and Brennan gained their feet and
called for help. DIR. Story of Bayside
came and pronounced Gilman dead The
physician then sent for automobiles and
the three girls We're taken to their homes
Glimans $ body was later taken to Flush
ing.


Gilman was a bachelor and thirty wears
old. Socially he was one of the most
popular men in Flushing.

His face was set and pale, for fierce struggle
against the unfairness and cruelty of life ragged
within him.


Outside the rocks were cawing in the distant
elms, and the clear note of robin came from
thicket. Through the trees-a network of golden
tracery-showed where the sun had set, and au-
tumn s mellow haze hung in the silent hollows.
Philip raised his head YEARLY. So this was his
last night in the old house. Henceforth that
peaceful country home would exist for him only
as a tender memory.


Would he ever return again9 Little did he care,
since Nep the comrade of his happest hours, had
deserted him. Small matter if friends seemed
cold and those he loved best understood him least.
Verify, fortune had dealt harshly with him.


From the WALL the portrait of his mother looked
tenderly down, in times gone by. Did she
understand and feel for him now2 he wondered


Phil IS thoughts travelled back to the days of his
childhood, and all unheeded the shadows length
ened and the clock licked on. How swiftly those
early wears had flown, yet how wildly could he
recall every event of his boyhoodl 1t seemed only
yesterday that he was shy lad of twelve, roam
ing the fields and lanes, and laughing with his
lighthearted little friend, Penelope Leighton.
Phil was the rector s only child He and the girl
were alike motherless, and this, perhaps, deepened
the bond of sympathy between them.


All! those were careless, sunny hours, but all
too feeting. Even at this early date cloud APP
peared on the fair horizon. Clearly the scene
rose before him hot sleepy afternoon in
July; the rectory garden; Nep hiding in the
shrubbery; the arrival of his father with tall,
dark stranger and handsome boy; an interrupt
ed game of robbers, and an invitation to the
hall.


1t all so unexpected and happened so
quickly. The stranger Sir Charles Newenham,
the squire, lately returned after long absence from
abroad and the boy his Frank.


''The two lads should make good companions, -
Sir Charles had said; but Phil had no desire for
a playmate; he had been happy enough with
Nep Vaguely he suspected this visit, and he felt
troubled and disinclined to continue the game as

PETALUMA, Jan. 12.-John Baker
Hinkle, who died at Palo Alto Saturday,
and was buried here today, was promi-
nently connected with the early history
of this section. He operated the first
mail and stage route to Cloverdale
and Ukiah, thence to Eureka


In the early sixties, when the serious
Indian troubles occurred, Hinkle was a
heavy loser when the Indians attacked
the Spruce Grove station, burning
barns and stables.


For three years Hinkle acted as land
agent for his brother in law. Charles
Mclaughlin, a railroad contractor of
the early days. Hinkle undertook sew
eral important contracts, including the
long tunnel of the Santa Fe and Union
Pacific near San Rafael.

Ten thousand persons filed Market
street at Third last night and
stretched far up the street, all
watching The Calls election bulletins.

gathered 70 watch the returns since the
fire and they were served with the
promptest and most accurate bulletins
that have been flashed upon canvas

festival in front of The Call Office, so
deeply packed were the people. From

men was stationed at the registrars

direct from the precinct booths, all
sending them into The Call by tele-
phone where experts compiled the to-

A network of wires at the same time,
brought direct news from all the large
cities in the country. Before the other
papers were ready to handle the re-
turns, The Call at $40 o'clock in the
evening had announced the election of
Gaynor as mayor of New York. A few
minutes later it began to receive local
returns and then for the rest of the
night in quick succession it displayed
the reports from all parts of San Fran
cisco and the big cities of the eastern
states.


The big throng without was kept in
constant touch with New York. Boston,
Cleveland and other centers of inter-
est. Before the other papers had made
any appreciable headway The Call had
compiled the local returns and before
the evening had grown two hours old

Special Dispatch to The Star.


NEW YORK. May 25.-One of those
unreasoning panics which seize East Side
mothers now and then happened this
morning in Stanton street.


There was a tenement fire. 1t was next
door to school, With great rapidity the
mothers of most of the $50 pupils got
the news and stormed the gates of the
school yard. The janitor had locked
them.


Outside hundreds of women collected
in struggling crowd and beat upon the
gates crying out for their children and
weeping. The frenzied women, the hum
ming engines, the thick black smoke and
the thousands of spectators combined to
make a striking picture.


The fire broke out in the uper part of
the six-story tenement at 30 Stanton
school No. 81, at Stanton and Forsythe
streets. Miss Mary Maclay is the princi-
pal. Miss Maclay kept cool through the
excitement and calmly surveying the fire
decided that there was no special cause
for alarm. She did not dismiss the chill
dren, who kept to their seats. Had she
let them go out among the frantic moth
ers they would have been in greater dan
ger than from the flames.


The upper stories of the double tenement
blazed fiercely. The tenants fled and
managed to get out without mishaps.
Somebody turned in an alarm and the
firemen were at work and had the fire
out in short time.

Galveston.-Fortified behind her sew
enteen-foot sea wall and elevated to
point above the danger line, Galveston
Wednesday passed safely through
hurricane which resembled in intens-
ity the disastrous storm of 1900.


Part of the island upon which the
city is situated was again inundated
the overflowing sea water reaching
height of seven or more feet. That
portion of the island which has been
protected suffered comparatively little
harm.


No lives were lost in the immediate
vicinity and the property damage will
not be large.


Sweeping westward the tropical
storm, which had been central over the
Gulf for twenty-four hours or more,
struck Galveston shortly after eleven
o'clock


The wind attained velocity of six
ty-eight miles an hour, heaved the wa
ters of Galveston Bay up against the
island and flooded that section which
had not been raised. The water backed
up into the main streets.


The principal damage was con-
fined to the beach front, where bath
houses and pleasure piers were swept
away, but shipping was undisturbed.


A hurricane for east Texas was fore
casted early in the day, and when the
storm broke Galveston was prepared.


The inhabitants of the few scattered
houses in the low section sought safe
t1r hn rid at
anchor in the bay.


The fury of the storm was soon
abated, and the anxiety of those who
entertained fears of another tidal
wave thus early relieved.


So short was it's duration that the
Mallory line steamer booked to sail
for New York shortly after noon left
on time.


A heavy dredge had been blown
against the single bridge which con-
meets Galveston Island with the main
land and the telegraph cables had
parted. AS a result all manner of ru-
mors were soon rife throughout the
country to the effect that Galveston
had again suffered such a storm as
that which practically destroyed the
city nine years ago. Men were put
at work at once repairing the bridge
and laying new cables.


Few buildings were blown down,
but 1t is believed many warehouses
were flooded and that goods on the
bottom floors of these buildings were
ruined. Consequently 1t will require
several days to ascertain the amount
of damage. The storm covered a wide
area along the Gulf coast.


One fishing pier seven miles from
the city was demolished by the wind
and waves. Thirty or forty people
were rescued by the pilot boat Texas
and brought to Galveston.


AS result of the damage to the
single bridge which connects Calves
ton with the mainland, and over
which all the trains entering or leav-
ing the city are forced to cross, COM
munication by rail with Galveston has
been cut off. Tugboats are carrying
passengers, mail and freight across
the bay to Galveston.


Ten people were drowned in the wa
ter that swept over portion of Tar
pom pier, seven miles from the city


They were washed from the rocky
promontories into the Gulf and the
bodies have not been recovered.


1t is reported that there has been
considerable loss of life at Palaces
and Blessing. 1t is also said Bay City
suffered greatly from the hurricane.

went badly. for the rover slew Frodi
and carried the hand mill and the
giantesses out to sea, where he ordered
them to grind salt. This for a whole
day they did; but when night came
they awoke their new master from his
sleep and asked if they had not ground
enough. But the sea rover sternly
bade them keep grinding till morning.
The maidens took him at his word and
worked with such vii that long be-

thronged from 8 o'clock in the morn

evening was delightfully."- cool.

registered 80 degrees in the shade, and
other thermometers were credited with
climbing to the 80 mark this afternoon.

pleasant that one of these rare, hot
days is productive Of much grumbling
and grunting on the part of the old
settlers and the tourist alike.

In the Golden Age, runs the old Morse
legend, the earth was ruled by a god
named Frodi, who, among other trifles,
possessed a beautiful hand mill that
ground out gold and happiness and
peace. and anything else that it was
asked for. The grinders were two
giantesses ruled over by Frodi, and all
went we'll until a sea rover appeared
on the scene. After this, however all
went badly, for the rover slew Frodi,
and carried the hand mill and the
giantesses out to sea, where he ordered
them to grind salt. This for a whole
day they did; but when night came they
awoke their new master from his sleep
and asked if they had not ground
enough. But the sea rover sternly bade
them keep grinding till morning. The
maidens took him at his word and
worked with such a will that long be-
fore daylight the great load of salt
they had made sank the ship.


And that, says the old Morse legend,
is why the sea is salt.-Answers.

couver.

ciety, the Prudential Insurance Company

pany.

Her Brothers declared this morning

in the east, where her history is not

quitta1


History of Case


Alma Bell was accused of shooting
.her lover, Joe Armes. The girl called
-Armes from the cabin where he was
sleeping with his brothers, and shortly
afterward pistol shot was heard from
the direction in which the couple had
gone Frank and Manuel Armes.
brothers of Joe, and Tony Grinko, who

mates that she had killed her lover.
She left. but returned later and said
that she knew he was not dead because
she could hear him crying She left
for the second time and was not seen
again until she was found the next
morning by Sheriff McAuley.


Visited Lovers Cabin


On the night of the shooting Alma.
Bell came to the chain occupied by Joe
Armes and his brother and demanded
admittance that she might explain some
stories which she asserted had been
told about her. After some parley she
was admitted and remained in the
cabin two hours. On leaving she per-
susded her lover to accompany her
and. according to the testimony of the
brothers. a shot was heard a moment
later. Immediately following the shot
the brothers asserted that Joe cried
."Oh. boys! oh. boysF' and that Alma
Bell exclaimed "Goodby joe" Accord
ing to the story of the sheriff. the girl
admitted the killing and asserted that
she fred the shot because her lover
had thrown her down" She admitted
to the sherif that she had been intimate
with Joe Armes. but denied that she
was in a delicate condition.


Betrayed by Armes

cumstances the girl had no sense OF

Williams was recently released from
jail for wife beating and found that
his wife had begun divorce proceed.
ings. He swore he would kill her.
Before daylight today Williams crept
into the yard His wife's guards were
all asleep. He got a heavy post and
battered down the door, rushed into
his wife's room and fired a shot into
her brain before she awoke, killing
her.


The battering at the door and shot
aroused Goodell who fired three times
at Williams as he ran toward the back
porch. At the door the murderer
stopped and fred twice into his own
brain. He died an hour later.

wheels were handled, the direction gained
with the shots and the small number of
tumbles. only three resulting. Following
the burlesque was the usual polo game
and tea at the Country Club, Mrs David

OAKLAND. April S.-Two tramps

washstands and every manner of ar

doomed before the engines had started

adjoining residences, as the wind was

the flames from spreading.

ANTIOCH, Jan. 23.-After with
standing the drenching rains and the
terrific pressure exerted by the flood
water of the past ten days the levee
on Upper Sherman island broke early
this morning near Perleys landing on
the Sacramento river.


The tide was at its lowest when the
embankment gave way and the weary
watchers who have been keeping a
day and night vigil believed the dan
ger point was passed.


Dozens of men hurried to the scene
and dredgerS are on their way to that
point with hope of closing the break,
but tonight the island is submerged


The western end of the island went
under several days ago, but it had
been thought the upper end could be
saved


The break when the levee first went
out was not serious, but men at the
point of danger were scarce and it was
impossible to get a dredger.


All day the fight for the levee was
kept up, but this evening when the
high tide came in the crevasse was 130
feet wide and the islanders gave up
hope.


Water Pours in Fast


At o'clock the water was pouring
through the broken levee in a broad
torrent, and tomorrow morning the
island will be full.


The people in the delta district think
that the submergence of Sherman may
relieve the pressure on the other
levees.


For two days the wind and sun have
hardened the crowns of the levees, and
tonight the islands are in better con-
dition than they have been since the
first day of the flood.


Other islands and reclamations in
Sacramento county are considered safe.


This island is one of the richest in
the river district, containing 10000
acres. The farmers are engaged in
dairying and raising alfalfa and veg
etables of all kinds. Unless the break
can be closed promptly the loss will
easily reach the half million mark.


This makes the fifth island to WELD
to the elements. Lower Sherman. Jer-
sey, Twitchell and Venice islands are
all under water, making a total of 28, 700
acres submerged.


Ten thousand acres which have with
stood the floods of years must now be
permitted to fill up. The loss will ex-
ceed $500. 900.

text:
LONG BRANCH, n. j.. June 4. 1909.


An unprecedented influx of cottagers
here has marked Memorial day week.
The numerous cottage colonies in the city.
notably those in the Elberon and West
End districts. have taken on summer
air. Practically all the summer residents
who own their own cottages are occupy
ing them. and those who lease cottages
are coming in rapidly. In two weeks
more probably not one Of the thousands
of cottages will be left on the market.


With the arrival OF the cottagers the
golf grounds. polo campuses and tennis
courts have been opened, and yachting,
boating fishing and other outdoor sports
have received an impetus. Surf bathing
is very popular for so very early In the
season, and early this week the beach
was thronged with bathers.


Preparations for the special attractions
of the season have also been stimulated.
The prize list of the Long Branch open
air horse show for Its sixteenth annual
exhibition. just issued; shows sixty
with nearly 5000 in cash prizes to be
distributed. The Bench Show Associa-
ton, which numbers among its members
the principal dog fanciers Of the country.
has added a number of special prizes.


Several innovations in the way of spe-
cal attractions are being planned by the
board OF trade. Among them are a day
of athletic contests and auto races on the
bluff drive and grand carnival and
masque fete on the bluff walk.


Washington Park. the new recreation
center in the western section of the city.
had brilliant opening Memorial day.
Thousands attended. and the streets in
the vicinity were blockaded with autos
and other vehicles during the concert and
special exercises.


The Festival Chorus Of 200, which will
render operas at the Ocean Park Casino
weekly this summer. is being drilled
regularly by Director Schmidt. The An
vii Chorus is being practiced this week.
and selections from Faust" will be taken
up next. Special singers are being en-
gagged also.


Since the new railroad schedule went
into effect a few days ago the resort has
ninety trains daily The full summer
schedule will give over 40. The Sandy
Hook steamers are already proving popu-
lar, and the Shrewsbury river boats have
been handling the largest traffic in their
history ever since Easter.


Pleasure Bay Park. on the Shrewsbury.
and the Ocean Park Theater both opened
for Memorial day.

Columbus, Miss. June 26-After a week
OF sunshine. inclement weather has re-
turned. and rain has fallen thirty-six
hours without cessation The farmers
took advantage OF the sunshine last week,
and got in some work in the fields. many
Of them having practically freed their
crops from grass.


They realize the fact that the time has
come when the crops must be either cul-
tivated or abandoned, and during the past
few days have been working regardless
Of the weather. It being no uncommon
sight TO see men chopping cotton and
hoeing corn with the rain pouring down
upon their heads.


The inclement weather has not only
retarded the cultivation Of crops, but
has practically prohibited all work OF
public roads Two years ago the
people Of Lowndes County voted a
special tax for the purpose OF keeping
up their public thoroughfares, and
competent men are employed to look
after the work.


Last year the roads throughout the
county were kept In good shape. but
there has been little opportunity for work
this spring on account OF the incessant
rains, and IN many places the roeds are
in a worse condition than usually pre-
walls during the fan and winter months.

NEW YORK, January 30.-An interesting
war that has been waging between the
few large and the many small maunfac-
turers of brass beds throughout the coun-
try for the past six month has just ended
in complete rout for the small manufac-
turers. The fight has proved most inter
esting throughout.


Owing to the considerable drop some
time ago in the price of copper, which
enters very largely into the construction
Of brass beds, these small manufacturers
found that they could undersell the pre-
yailing prices of the large manufacturers
and still maintain a substantial margin
of profit. The large manufacturers en-
deavored to hold the little factories in
line on the regular prices. but without
avail. Not only did the large manufac-
turers almost Immediately meet the cut
prices of their smaller competitors. but
made reductions SO great that small
manufacturers could not hope to compete
except at a loss.


For once the buying public has bene-
flied by a commercial war, but their
good fortune was short lived. Already
brass beds have Jumped back to prices
that often seem exorbitant.

had narrow escape from being crush
ed to death when his right leg
became entangled in the cogs of a car

noon. Fellow Worl1men rushed to his
assistance, but before the machinery
could be stopped Woodford's leg was
terribly mangled. He was taken to the
Crocker street hospital, where the
surgeons amputated the injured leg
above the knee. The surgeons says he
will recover.


WoOdford was operating the machine
and had leaned over to adjust loose
connection. In some manner his foot
got caught in the wheels and was
thrown between the cogs. He made a
desperate effort to extricate his foot,
but the sharp iron bit through his shoe
and held him and drew his leg into the
machinery. He called for help, but be-
fore assistance reached him and the
machine stopped his leg had been
ground to pieces.

Back TO 1832-perhaps to l494-the

The Creeks, strongest and proudest

Throughout all the Indian wars. the

always fighting against some white
races.


Andrew Jackson gained part OF his
reputation by his fights on the Creeks
when their undying hostility TO the
whites had aroused the new country
to frenzy. In succeeding years the
American executives bent their ener-
gies to getting this powerful and trou-
blesome nation, which would not be
placated nor remain peaceful, clear

This brought the treaty OF 1882, by
which the Indians were sent beyond

after several new wars. and after two
or three chiefs who were willing TO
treat with victorious white men, had

LONG BEACH, Aug. 2S.-The tug
Warrior was brought over from San
Pedro this afternoon and the dredger
was towed back out of the ocean
channel in preparation for the depart
ure shortly after o'clock tonight from
the Long Beach harbor of the tug
Vergil Bogue. built at the Craig ship
yard. The Bogue started from the har-
Dor under her own power. The War
rior was on hand to assist if any ac-
cident happened.


The Vergil Bogue is the first vessel
to leave the Long Beach harbor or to
pass through the ocean entrance. She
was built at a cost of $4,000 for the
Western Pacific Railway company's
use at San Francisco.


The channel through which the tug
left formerly was the scene of 1
stretch of yellow sand. The war de-
partment, having decided that the San
Gabriel river was navigable, ordered
the Salt Lake railroad to span the
clogged-up channel with a steel draw
bridge and the Western Marine dredg-
ing company under contract with the
Los Angeles Dock and Terminal COM
pany, builders of the harbor, dredged
the channel.


The officers of the Los Angeles Dock
and Terminal company announced to-
day with much enthusiasm that the
ocean entrance to the new Long Beach
harbor showed a depth of eleven feet,
and that next Monday afternoon the
big suction dredger would finish the
first cut through the entrance and
would return to the bridge to under
take the second cut. This cut will
make the channel eighteen feet deep.
The dredger's progress during the past
two days has been highly satisfactory.

leans and Kenner being under water

gulf coast of Mississippi meager re-
ports tell of much damage to shipping
and to buildings along the beach. AT
least one life was lost. Natchez, Miss,

wire.

has been reported, this section appar-
emily having escaped the force of the
storm In western Louisiana, at Crow
ley and Jennings, considerable prop
erty damage has resulted.


Two-thirds of the unharvested rice
crop is believed to have been destroyed.

Philadelphia, Oct. 23.-The University of
Pennsylvania and Pennsylvania State Col
lege football teams fought out a stirring
battle on Franklin Field here to-day that
ended in a tie score at To 3. During the
first half neither side was able to score
but in the second period each team scored
with drop kick from the field Thayer
sent the ball whirling between the posts
for Pennsylvania. and Captain Vorhis du-
plicated the performance a few minutes
later for State.


Pennsylvania played loosely throughout
the game, but the attack was more power
full than that of the visitors. In the first
half the Red and Blue had the ball within
scoring distance twice. but each time a
tumble by Sommer nullif1ed the previous
good work and gave the ball to the Wis
itors. who promptly punted it out of dan
ger. All through the game the State Col
lege players followed the ball more close
ly than Pennsylvania.


Pennsylvania scored early in the second
half. An exchange of punts put the ball
inside States 30-yard line. Here Pennsyl-
vania began rushing tactics but was tenn
porarily halted and moved back to the 80
yard line through penalties. AS a last re-
sort Thayer dropped back and kicked a
pretty goal from the 3J-yard line.


Pennsylvania State was able to dupli-
cate this score within five minutes After
an exchange of punts, Captain Miller of
the Pennsylvania team was disqualified for
what the officials declared to be too rough
a tackle. AS an additional penalty Penn
sylvania was set back half the distance TO
her goal line, and the ball given TO the Wis
! itors on the home teams 2O-yard line.


Pennsylvania State took full advantage
of this opportunity, and, after gaining only


five yards by two plunges into the line
! Captain Vorhis dropped back, and, stand
ing on the 25-yard line, dropped goal from

Mrs. Brown lives on the bank of the
Mokelumne river. She has one little
girl 3 years old.


One morning the butcher left the
gate open. That day when the little
girl came out to play the first thing she
saw was the open gate.


She was on the bank of the river
before her mother caught sight of her.


She gave scream just as she fell
in the river.


Don was lying asleep, but ,awoke
when he heard the cry, and dashlng
to the river plunged in and catching
the clothes of the child dragged her
out of the water.


By this time the mother reached
the shore and catching up Don hugged
and kissed him and wept joyful tears
to think he saved her dear baby.


That night when Mr.. Brown came
home she related the story of bravery
of faithful Don, and you can be sure
Don was treated with the best of care
until his death.

Col. Francis Ferari's Exposition Show,

and their fearless handling are eXcep-

some laughable, presented in the tented
circle. There are also good things to eat
and quite a number Of free acts given on
the outside. Harry Six. billed as the
worlds champion high diver" makes
twice daily plunge from the top of a
125-foot ladder into a tank below that
contains but three feet of water.


Then there is the tiny Russian Prince
Nichoii. but twenty-five inches high and

spends the most OF his time autogra PHI
ing his photograph for the ladies. with
whom he is a chief attraction. The "hu-

rlly over both troIting and running

az decision is complete victory for

Paris nutuel betting machines. Latonia
put in these machines. but claimed that

interfering with the races while book

for San Francisco.

completed this morning eight knots
were maintained with III revolutions
of the screw. On the cruise beginning
tomorrow nine knots will be attempt
ed. When the monitor completes its
special mission to San Francisco the
tests will be continued, three days for

I.AWRENCEBURG, Ind, September l..
Miss Alice White. the sixteen-year-old
sister OF Sheriff White, prevented a Jail
delivery here yesterday by arming her
self with revolver and holding three
desperate men at bay until help reached
her and the escaping prisoners were safe
ly locked in separate cells.


Sheriff White was temporarily absent
She descended and was soon convinced
where Tides Negley. George Griffin and
Edward Mitchell were confined.


She tiptoed into the jail corridor, and
saw the men at work with a file on the
bars of window overlooking the jail
yard.


Two OF the bars had been sawed in two
and the men were at work on third,
which would let them to liberty.


Miss White hurried back to her broth
er's room, obtained his revolver and. hur-
rying out into the yard, confronted the
prisoners just as they were getting out
Of the window. Leveiing the pistol at
them she ordered them back and said
that she would shoot the first one who
moved another inch toward her.


The girl called for help, but was un-
heard. She kept the revolver on the Win
dow for fully ten minutes. when Sheriff
White returned, and running to her, ask
ed her what was the matter.


After she had explained he went into
the jail. while she remained on guard
on the outside, and removed the three
men to other cells.


Miss White did not appear to think she
had performed brave act, and when
the story got out and her friends began
to congratulate her she seemed rather
bored over the incident.

SAN FRANCISCO, Cal, May 15.-Hugo
Kelly of Chicago was knocked out in
the first round by Billy Papke, the Illinois
Thunderbolt, at Calmo today in a bout
scheduled to go forty-five rounds. for
the middleweight championship. which
Stanley ketcheli surrendered some time
ago to become heavyweight. A large
crowd gathered at the ringside, expecting
to see long drawn-out battle, as both
men. were trained to the minute, and
the betting was even money. Ed Smith was
the referee, and both fighters made the
weight at the appointed time.


A preliminary bout. was over when
Kelly and Papke entered the ring and
received big. greeting. They looked
in splendid physical condition and evenly
matched. Both wore adhesive bandages
over their knuckles, which each examined
before the gloves were drawn on. 1t
was then 2:30 o'clock, and no time was
wasted in ringing the gong.


Kelly had won the toss and occupied
the southwest corner, with the sun at
his back, but before the fight began there
was howl from Papke, who wanted the
same corner, rather than have the sun
blaze directly into his eyes. The referee
finally settled the matter. and the struggle
began.


Papke opened with wild rush and
forced Kelly to the ropes, where the
Chicago man, blocking several terrific
swings for the head, came back with a
couple of hard body blows. Papke stuck
close. however. ripping in tremendous
punches, which had great power behind
them. Kelly retreated before this merci-
less onslaught. jabbing Papke in the
face with short hooks and jolts. Papke
finally got his man into corner and
put right and left hard to the jaw. These
blows were overpowering. and Kelly
dropped to the boards, while the referee
counted nine seconds.


when Kelly got up he was helplessly
groggy. He staggered blindly along one
side of the ring. clutching at the ropes.
Papke rushed in close, took deliberate
aim and then banked the Chicago man
that. nearly did the trick. This was
quickly followed by a left hook, which
landed squarely on the point of the jaw,
and Kelly fell like log, the back of his
head hitting the floor with a crash. 1t
was a clean knockout, for after ten sec
onds had been counted, Kelly was still
unconscious. He soon revived. however,
and asked what had happened. Papke
was declared the winner, of course, and
lenge ketchell, who stopped him in eleven
rounds last November, for the middle
weight title. Papke said that IL Ketchel
had really left the middIeweight class,
he would defend the title against ali
comerS.


1t was not chance blow that beat
Kelly. He was simply punched into SUBJ
mission by better man in every respect.
The shortness of the mill. however, did
did not last more than a minute and a
half

after name.

DUBLIN. February S.--A policeman
was shot dead and two others wounded
in an affray which occurred last Thurs
day night at Craughwel village five
miles from County Galway, where there
has been long-standinS trouble over a
farm from which an eviction had taken
place.


About twenty years ago John Gilligan
was evicted from a holding on the estate
Of Lord Clanricarde. near Craughwel.
Three years ago Mrs. Ryan took the
farm and since then has been under po-
lice protection.


Thursday night, when ii was known
that Mrs. Ryan's cowherd was on the
premises, an attack was made on the
house. Several shots were fired through
the windows, and the contents OF one
charge struck the man, causing him seri-
Gus injury.


The police barrack is directly opposite
the house, and on hearing the shots the
constables armed themselves and made a
rush toward the spot. They observed
several men moving off and gave chase.
In short time they came close UP to the
fugitives. who turned and fired a volley,
killing Constable McGoldrick on the spot
and slightly wounding two other men who
were with him. The attackers made
good their escape. but three men have
since been arrested.

CAMBRIDGE, Mass, April 17.-With a
powerful and finished stroke the Harvard
varsity crew defeated weaker and less
expert crew from Columbia on the
Charles river today by six full lengths
in a race of a mile and seven-eighths.
After the first few dashing strokes which
followed the referees pistol shot there
was never any question regarding the
outcome. AS IL impelled by a powerful
motor. the Harvard shell swept proudly
down the Charles river basin before 10000
people on the river bank and shot like
an arrow across the finish line. Behind
them trailed the Columbia she'll, with the
oarsmen plunging their blue and white
blades into the water in a vain effort
even to keep up with the flying Crimson
shell. Despite the almost perfect river
conditions, the Columbia boat rolled like
a knock-about in heavy sea, and 1t
was with difficulty that Coxswain Rock
wood kept the nose of his boat heading
down the course. Harvard's veteran crew
showed all the dash and force which
were out Yale at New London last year,
while the exhibition of Columbia, even to
Coach Rice. was disappointing.


The Start.


It was a few minutes before o'clock
when the two crews backed to their
punts underneath the Cottage Farm
bridge. The start came almost exactly
ut p. m. With the firing OF the pistol
the Crimson shell was the first to get
away. Both crews hit up the stroke
above forty, and for hundred yards
more rowed side by side. Then Harvard
began to draw away. Columbia continued
the high stroke for a couple OF minutes
longer. but presently Capt. Cerussi
dropped back to thirty-six. At the quar-
ter mile Harvard was half a length to
the good. and at the half-mile flag there
was open water between the boats. The
Harvard boat gained steadily. the Grim
son stroke decreasing to thirtytwo. and
a one time to as low as twenty-eight.
In the Columbia boat Coxswain Rockwell
was continually shouting encourag cement
TO his men, but with only partial sue
cess.


Under Harvard bridge dashed the Grim
son crew. with 5000 people watching.
Ten seconds later the Columbia shell
swept underneath and the two crews
started down the last mile Of the course.
Ths water was now rougher than in the
upper reaches of the river. The motion
Rad no effect whatever on the Harvard
shell, but the unsteadiness of the Blue
and White boat was the feature Of the
race from this point on.


Columbia's Spurt Futile.


Stroke Sergeant Of the Harvard crew
again dropped the stroke below thirty
but when the mile and a half flags were
passed there were five lengths Of water
between the boats. Coming down to the
finish. Columbia was the first to spurt,
but there was no gain on Harvard.


AS the finish line was neared Sar-
geant called upon his men for the last
effort. Up went the Harvard stroke
while astern the Columbia shell wobbled
uncertainty.


Then the red flag fell and Harvard

the city to teach her what they have
learned of religion, science, music, art.

classrooms of the city school Of life.

10 the rock. The policeman impressed

homes.

Crossing the bay yesterday was either
good fun or a perilous and distressing
experience, according to the point OF
view and stability of the stomach. Even
the big Southern Pacific ferry steamers
rolled and pitched with drunken aban-
don, and the little yellow steamers of
the Key route fairly danced up hill and
down dale on their way from one shore
to the other There were strong men
who stayed on this side of the bay all
night rather than risk their lives again
on the angry waters, and there We're
girls who had commutation tickets on
the Southern Pacific who paid fare on
the Key route for the sheer JOY OF the
extra pitching and tossing that a voy-
age on one of the smaller boats insured


A heavy ground swell has been run
ming in the harbor for a week, and yes
terdays southeaster churned the heav-
ing waters into a sea such as seldom
runs inside the heads. Several of the
ferry boats shipped considerable water
and In several cases windows on the
lower deck were broken. Seasickness
was a popular complaint during the
forenoon. when the boats did the most
rolling, but those who enjoyed the
rough sea and those who didn't were
frankly scared. but on the other hand.
many of the sufferers from NAL de mer
took comfort in the popular supposition
that seasickness was good for the liver.
None of the latter. however. made a
return trip right away in search of
more topsy turvey treatment.


Along the water front the south
easter was responsible for some dam
age. A pile driver belonging to the
Thompson bridge company lying at
Folsom street wharf, became water
logged during the night and about 9
o'clock turned turtle. 1t will be raised
when the weather moderates.


Barge No. of the Associated oil
company's fleet broke adrift from an
anchorage off Black point during the
afternoon and went wallowing away
before the wind, in the direction of
Sausalito. The tug Restless gave chase,
captured the runaway and towed 1t to
the seawall, where it was made fast.
