Brushing and sweeping and busting,
little Swedish girl was busily clean
ing a big schoolroom in Stockholm.
She warbled and sang as she worked,
like bird in springtime. A lady
riding past in her carriage heard the
song, and stopped to listen to the
sweet voice then entered the build
ing and hunted about till she found
the little singer. The child was shy,
and not at all pretty; but her manner
was so courteous that the lady was
charmed.


II must take your daughter to
Cralius, the famous music master, :"
she said to the mother, who was the
janitressof the school building. "She
has voice that will make her for
tune"


So the lady took the little girl
away with her to see the music mas
ter. The great man was delighted
with her voice. IT must take her
to Count Puche," he said che is a
great judge of music"


But Count Puche looked coldly at
the young singer, and gruf1y asked
the music master what he expected
him to do with such child.


"Only to hear her sing" answered
Crelius.


This the Count consented to do,
and when she had finished, he cried
out in delight: "She shall have the
advantages of the Stockholm acad-
emy."


At the academy the child sang and
studied, and studied and sang. She
was not yet twelve, and with all the
praise and attention showered upon
her she was almost in danger of being
spoiled.


One evening at an entertainment
she was to sing higher part than
she had ever tried before. The house
was filled and everybody was looking
for the little favorite. She took her
place before the audience, but when
she tried to sing there was no sound.
She tried again, but all her silvery
notes were gone. The master was
very angry. Her friends were sur
prised and grieved, and the poor little
songstress dropped with sorrow.


Her voice did not come back next
day, nor the next. Slowly the beau-
tiful dream of fame and fortune faded
away yet she bore her disappoint-
ment bravely, and said: 81 will
study"


Four years passed, and the people
had quite forgotten the little singer,
till one day someone was wanted for
an unimportant partin chorus which
none of the regular singers was will
ing to take, and the master thought
again of his poor little pupil. Would
she take it? Pleased to be useful
and oblige her kind master, she con-
sented to sing.


While practicing her part, to the
surprise and Joy of both pupil and
teacher, the long-lost voice suddenly y
returned with all its beauty and rich
ness. All who remembered the lit
tie nightingale received her back
with a hearty welcome, and she af-
terward became one of the most won
derful singers the world has ever
known.


Have you guessed the little Swed-
ish girls name? 1t was Jenny Lind.
--DeaconeSs Ady0cate.

fessed, but refused to give any reason.

Vienna Feb 5-The session OF the Austrian par
lament ended this morning after scene OF turbu-
lence extraordinary even for assembly where
violent outbreaks are comparatively common.


The trouble which arose from the old racial feel
ing between the Germans and the Czechs broke
out during the debate government bin the OBJ
ject which reconcile these differences.
The radical Czechs who have been hindering the
debate this measure for several days with a
continuous din from drums and tin whistles so
exasperated the Germans this morning that the op-
posing Deputies came TO close quarters and fight
ensued. One Of the radical Czechs named Speczek
captured and whipped until he howled for
mercy. Another Czech bitten by German on
the cheek, and black eyes and sore heads were
numerous. The Premier. Baron Won Bienerth, sus-
pended the session.


The departure Of the ministers was followed hy
another free fight. in which the opposing factions
rushed each other the strains of revolutionary
songs. and confusion Teigned for half an hour.
The Deputies finally became exhausted, and the
battlefield gradually Geyerted.


The sudden closing OF the session and the politl
cal import the disorder have had adverse
effect upon the Bourse.


It is expected that Parliament Will reopen at the
March in another effort TO reconcile the con-
fictng parties and pursue legislative programme
II this succeeds. coalition Cabinet viii be
formed; but if It fails the present officials Will
remain in office and carry urgent business by
administrative order.

Viennese operetta, which has delighted
eastern audiences for the past two
years, is at last making it's way to Los
Angeles. Early in the season, the ia
nous Lehar operetta "The Merry
Widow" was sung for the first time
on a local stage, and last night an
equally musical and delightful COM
position by another Vienna musician
pleased a large audience at the Audi
torium.


In Mile. Mischief, Corinne has found
a vehicle which allows ample oppor-
tunity for the display of her own
winsome personality, at the same
time giving chance for brilliant
chorus work, and much amusing
comedy of the more polite sort. The
music and orchestration is beautiful
and the songs are catchy without de-
scending to the commonplace.


Many of the melodies have that per-
sistent haunting quality which makes
for success and yet they are well
above the grade of the average pop
ular music. Two of the songs, Sweet
heart" and Lonesome" made a pro-
nounced success with the audience last
night and bid fair to achieve decided
furore during the engagement of the
Mile. Mischief company here.


Corinne, accustomed all her life to
stardom, took the center of the stage
as the mischievious girl disguised as
a boy and Venturing to the barracks.
She cajoled the old colonel and be-
fooled the young "leftenant" to the
huge delight of the spectators. Despite
some most ungainly costumes, she held
the attention and admiration of her
audience which she charmed with her
nonsense and with her sprightly and
graceful dancing. Her voice is pleas
ant and the songs she sings well
adapted to its range and quality, and
her gayety throughout the piece is
most infectious


Other principals of the cast who
proved decidedly meritorious vocally
or dramatically were Harry Linkey,
whose excellent voice showed to ad-
vantage in the song with chorus, THE
Army Corps" and Bonnie Farley and
Louise Brunelle, who sang and danced
with a pleasurable chic and wore delec-
table .frocks. Albert Howson and
Charles w. Meyer were adequate in
their parts and Edward w. Cutler
played the part of the rich mans son
with quite the necessary stiffness
which the lines demanded.


The chorus includes large number
of young men and women VINO sing
well, dance gracefully and work with
a snap and verve which brings the en-
tire performance up to an excellent
and inspiring finale. The costumes are
all in excellent taste and unusually
beautiful without the bizarre effect
which has been the goal OF costumars
for the last few seasons Small details
of the toilette as boots, hats and
hosiery are points in which the general
carefulness of the company manage
ment is we'll demonstrated Each oil
the three scenes presents an unusual
and beautiful stage picture, and the
audience last night displayed genuine
pleasure in the performance and high
appreciation Of the artistry Of cast
and chorus.

Strange as ii sounds history has two
authentic accounts of the employment
of bees as missiles of defense in war
fare.


The first instance occurred at the
siege of Themiscyra, in Pontus by Lu-
cullus, in his war against Mithridates.
The Romans made huge mounds out
side the city walls, inside which they
gathered their machinery for mining.
etc. But the Themiscyrans had
happy thought. They dug open these
mounds from the top and cast down
upon the soldiers inside bears and
other wild animals, and huge hives and
swarms Of bees


The second time that bees were put
to this extraordinary use was when the
Danes and Norwegians attacked Ches-
ter, which was gallantly defended by
the Saxons. All sorts of stratagems
were used on both sides, but the hon
ors remained fairly even until the Sax
ons, after collecting all the liquid in
the town, boiling it, and pouring 1t
over their besiegers, followed this up
by unexpectedly throwing down all
their beehives.


Very soon after this the Danes and
Norwegians desisted and marched
away from Chester.

The government of the United States
has recently paid unusual honor to the
memory of Maj. LEnfant, the engineer
who made the plan for the Federal capi-
tai on the Potomac. We can all admire
now the artistic judgment which fore
saw the beautiful city that Washington
has since become. To his own genera
tfon LEnfant was an extravagant
dreamer and his magnificent dis
tances' were long the subject Of popular
derision. Yet as the city has grown up
to 1t the plan has commanded increasing
regard, not only for it's picturesque effect,
but for it's plain common sense. 1t super
imposed upon the simple rectangular ar
rangement of streets. then already famil-
lar in Philadelphia, the supreme advan-
tage of great diagonal avenues. giving di-
rect passage and opening broad vistas in
every direction. magnifying the dignity Of
the principal buildings and leaving fire.
quent open spaces both for use and for
adornment.


This essential feature of L'Enfant's
plan nearly every city. old and new. has
learned to envy and many have sought
to initiate. The same leading idea con-
trolled the epoch-making reconstruction
of old Paris and the later improvements
in London, where vast sums have been
profitably expended to open wide high
ways through congested districts, as well
as to create within the city such ele-
ments of beauty as those which have
been developed upon the suggestions Of
LEnfant's plan at Washington.

PITTSBURG, Oct S.-Billy Papke,
the Illinois Thunderbolt, easily defeated
Willie Lewis, the New York fighter, to-
night at Duquesna gardens before the
National Sporting club of Pittsburg.
Both men were standing at the end of
the sixth round, with Lewis all but out.


Papke easily was given the public's s
verdict. Lewis, holding on, and half
unrecognizable after his fifteen minute
beating, weakly signified his intention
to ask for a return match with Papke,
who, unmarked and smiling, said he
believed he had proved his supremacy
over Lewis and would not agree to
a return match at any date.


Both Papke and Lewis entered the
ring shortly after 10 o'clock, smiling
and confident. AS the gong sounded
for the opening round, Lewis rushed IN
with a rapid succession of rights and
lefts to Papke's body. None OF the
blows, however, having steam behind
them. After careful sparring, Papke
led with a vicious right jolt to the
stomach.


In the clinches Papke was warned
three times to break clean, the crowd
hooting his slowness in getting away
from Lewis.


AS they came up for the secont
round, Papke turned loose a right
swing to the jaw. Lewis, off his guard,
took the blow fair and fell to the floor
resting until the count Of nine. The
third round was a repetition Of the
second, with Lewis taking blows on
the body, which forced him to rest
twice for the full time allowance
Papke came out of the round without
a mark, while Lewis had a badly split
lip and his right eye was closed.


Lewis came back after minute s
rest in the fifth round, seemingly great
ly rested and before Papke could
cover, had sprung series of left and
right swings that plainly staggered
his opponent. Papke caught himself
and before the fight period had ended
Lewis was hanging on and waiting for
the bell.


In the sixth round, Papke easily led
the New Yorker. Lewis was helpless
BY hanging on and refusing to break
Lewis finally stayed until the gong
saved him.


The fight was fast throughout.

TOMBSTONE, Ariz, May 12.-The
first day in the trial of Magon, Villa
real and Rivera, the three alleged revo-
lutionists charged with conspiring to
invade Mexico with an armed force
who are on trial here for violating the
neutrality laws, was taken up in secur-
ing a jury. Seven men out of the neces-
sary twenty-four were accepted today.


The jurors are subjected to searching
inquiries for qualification, and several
tilts were exchanged between the at
torneys during the course of the exam
ination.


In court today Attorney Cleary, for
the prisoners, openly charged United
States Attorney Alexander with order
ing the United States marshal to open
all mail of the alleged revolutionists,
and declared his intention of bringing
same to the attention of the grand
jury The United States attorney, in a
heated retort, admitted the course
which he declared within his rights
and in the interest of preventing fur
ther conspiracy and violation of United
States laws.


The grand jury returned four more
counts against the prisoners this week
on conspiracy charges The prisoners
appeared in court neatly dressed and
have been the recipients of bouquets
daily from sympathizers and friends.
Many United States officials, line
riders, detectives, secret service men
and Mexican officials are here as wit
nesses and some sensational evidence
is anticipated.

CARSON CITY, New. March 3.-Judge
Harrington Of the United States circuit
court this afternoon rendered his deci-
sion in the maximum freight rate suit.


The Southern Pacific company and
other railroads of the state attacked
the constitutionality of the railroad
commission of Nevada on various
grounds. but the court upnolds the com
mission.


On the subject of maximum rates the
court holds that in the case of the
Central Pacific the rates are not con-
fiscatory. The Nevada and California
railroad rates We're held insufficient,
but that the company was denied an
injunction because the commission had
taken no action to enforce the maxi
mum rates.


In the case of the San Pedro and
Los Angeles railroad the evidence does
not show the rate TO be confiscatory.
The court holds that the Eureka and
Palisade railroad, the Tonopah and
Goldfield and the Virginia and Truckee
railroad failed to prove a case, if they
had one


The bills are all dismissed and the
restraining orders vacated, but the dis
missal of the bill of the Nevada and
California is without prejudice.

SEOUL, Oct 10.-Cholera threatenL
to become seriously epidemic here.


The authorities are taking every pre-
caution but Seoul is not a sanitary
city and the disease has spread rapid
ly.


The palace Of the ex-emperor has
been invaded and the home of the resi-
dent-general has not been immune. The
schools are closed regularly for fumi-
cation.


For year the sanitary authorities
appointed by the Japanese resident
general have been cleaning up the city,
but only those who have gone into
the alleys and byways of Seoul into
know of it's uncleanliness.


Two years ago cholera would have
swept Seoul like a hurricane as the
city then was without drainage or
sanitation of any kind. The rain was
the only scavenger.


Now there is a reasonably good wa
ter supply and some kind of open
drains have been made.


With the use of disinfectants there
is reason to hope that the plague may
be checked.


Physicians of the Dai-Han hospital,
which Prince Ito recently opened, are
doing tremendous work in disinfection
and are ably seconded by medical mis-
sionaries.

worse. All four grabbed buckets

gained. In a short time they were up

FORT WILLIAMS. Ont, Aug. 12.-
Fort Williams for the first time in its
history is under martial law. This
resulted from a fight waged on special
Canadian Pacific police today by 1000
striking dock laborers.


Twenty-four men were injured, three
fatally. including Chief Ball of the
railway company's local force, and
two strikers.


A regiment of militia was called out
after Mayor Pelletier had read the
riot act.


The strikers had twenty-five railway
constables penned up in the Canadian
Pacific railroad bunkhouse. They
fired through the windows and were
preparing to storm the house when
the police persuaded them to desist.
The strikers threatened tonight to
burn the Canadian Pacific grain ele-
vators.

SEOUL, Korea. October 11.-Cholera
threatens to become seriously epidemic
here. The authorities are taking every
precaution. but Seoul is not a sanitary
city and the disease has spread rapidly.
The palace Of the ex-emperor has been in
vaded and the home Of the resident gen.
eral has not been immune. The schools
are closed regularly for fumigation.


For year the sanitary authorities ap-
pointed by the Japanese resident general
have been cleaning up the city. but only
those who have gone into the alleys and
byways Of Seoul can know the uncleanli-
ness Of the place. Two years ago cholera
would have swept Seoul. as the city then
was without drainage Of any kind. The
rain was the only scavenger. Now there
is a reasonably good water supply and
some kind of operating drains have been
made.


With the use of disinfectants there is
reason to hope that the plague may be
checked. Physicians Of the Dai-Han Hos
pital, which Prince Ito recently opened.
are doing tremendous work in disinfecting
and are ably seconded by medical mission
aries

Los. ANGELES, Sept. 15.-Heroic
service of volunteer and government
fire lighters have checked three of the
five great forest fires sweeping south
ern California mountains, but the two
that still burn threaten to do untold
damage unless controlled Immediately.
The areas now ablaze are in San Diego
county, where heavy forests are suffer-
ing together with several large hay
ranches and much stock grazing
ground, and in Ventura county, where
bee culturists, ranchers and bean grow
ers are overwhelmed, many fruitful lit
tie valleys are threatened.


The most serious fire is that about
Somis and Moor Park. near Oxnard.
Hundreds of acres of hay and beans
have been wiped out and today the fire
is threatening Moor Park. On the
north side of the range the sweep has
been clean from Wileys on the east to
Santa Paula and almost to Saticoy.
Many ranch houses have been destroyed
with their surrounding fields and oil
wells near Bardsdale are reported
burned. Telephone communication has
been cut off and most of the news is
brought ein by fire fighters exhausted
by 80 and 20 hours conflict.


In the mountains east of San Diego,
near 'Palomar and Valley Center, ex-
tensive fires are raging in the heavily
wooded canyons and at a late hour
tonight it was reported that control
seemed improbable for days Reports
as to the exact extent of these flames
are meager


The water supply of the town of Es-
condido has been partially cut off by
destruction of fumes. The total dam
age by all these fires will probably
run into the hundreds of thousands of
dollars. Every government ranger is
on the scene of the flames and volun-
teers and ranchers, fighting for their
homes and property, are assisting.

Entering the front door in Indian file

coin they could find and walked out
of the saloon, while the others covered
his retreat.


None of those lined up were molested.
Deputy sheriffs are working on the
case, but have no clew.

COWES, Aug. 2.-The Russian I'M
perial yacht STANDARD. bringing the em-
peror and empress from Cherbourg TO
Cowes on a visit to King Edward,
anchored in the roadstead shortly be-

The two rulers were given an official
welcome even more imposing than
usually attends such important occa-

Queen Alexandra, the prince and
princess of Wales and a large gathering
of other members of the royal family
present to greet their guests, but fifteen
of the pick of the British war fleet,
dressed in flags from stem to stern and

anchorage allotted to the STANDARD.

secretary, Sir Edward Grey; M. Iswol-
sky, the Russian minister of foreign af-

Russian ambassador to Great Britain,
further emphasized the significance at
tached in the diplomatic world to this
visit of the Russian emperor to Eng
| land.


The unusual welcome of this morning
was arranged designedly for the double
purpose of helping to strengthen the
| links in the chain binding Great Britain,
France and Russia in triple entente
and to dissipate continual Ill feeling
engendered by the harsh denunciation
of Emperor Nicholas and his methods
so frequently vented by the members
of the labor party both in and out Of
parliament since the coming of the en-
peror first was announced.

and Albert and met the STANDARD out

SAN PEDRO, Sept. 1.-Capt. w.
ziegenmeyer of the German steamer
Erna was arrested here this morning
on a warrant issued out of the United
States district court, charging him with
smuggling. United States Marshal Leo
Youngworth took Capt. ziegenmeyer to
Los Angeles, where he appeared before
the United States commissioners.


The warrant called for the arrest of
Capt Ziegenmeyer and ]. F. Solorzano,
a Mexican, who is charged with bring
ing $40 Panama hats into the country
without paying duty on them.


The Erna, which makes regular trips
between Puget sound and Mexican and
Central American ports, called here
July northbound. The hats were
dropped from the steamers side into
sl1iff and sold in Los Angeles. The
local custom house heard of the trans
action and the officers in the north
We're notified. After the steamer had
stopped at San Francisco, Victoria and
Seattle and again started on the return
trip it was decided to make the arrest
here.


Captain Protests Innocence


Deputy Marshal Hart came here last
evening and was on hand with the war
rant when the steamer dropped anchor
in the outer harbor at o'clock this
morning.


The captain, however, was not taken
from the vessel until it reached its
dock at the Crescent wharf on the high
tide at II o'clock. Marshal Youngworth
then took personal charge of Capt.
Ziegenmeyer, who protested he had alb
solutely nothing to do with the snug
Cling.


Purser Morgan explained Solorozano
alone was responsible for bringing in
the hats and the captain had nothing
to do with it. From Morgan also came
the information the Mexican had left
the vessel at Seattle and gone back to
Panama via New Orleans.


The steamer brought in seventeen
passengers from the north and will
take out ten passengers from here and
fifty tons of apricots consigned to
Havre, France, via Salina Cruz.


Capt. Ziegenmeyer was arraigned be-
fore United States Marshal Leo Young
worth yesterday and was released under
bonds of $5OOO

OCEAN PARK, Sept. 15.-Several
hundred persons lolling on the beach
at 11:15 o'clock this morning received
rude and damp shocks when three inn
mense waves dashed clear to the ce.
ment walk Men sprawled out on the
sand, dreaming of distant shores,
aWoke suddenly to find themselves
surrounded by foaming water. Women,
reclining in the shade of huge parasols,
scrambled hastily to their feet, their
skirts dripping with brine.


The miniature tidal waves resulted
from the heavy sea that was running
all day, indicative of a severe storm
at sea. Heavy ground swells and inn
mense pillows tossed about the bay
The waves repeatedly exceeded the
lines indicated by the government
tide charts for this season. The tidal
waves were observed at all the Cres-
cent bay beaches.


Anglers on the new concrete pier at
Santa Monica say that when the i'm
mense waves struck that wharf the
vibration was considerable, the rollers
dashing over the deck and drenching
many fishermen.


Heavy seas were running today at
Long Beach and all other beaches in
the vicinity of Los Angeles, but no.
where did waves approaching the di-
mensions of tidal waves occur except
at the Crescent bay.


The story of the morning tidal waves
spread and the usual number of per-
sons sprawled out on the sand was
lacking this afternoon. Although a
repetition of the tidal waves did not
occur, amateur seafaring men kept a
weather eye out for further trouble.

NORFOLK, Va. February 21.-Norfok
enjoyed the distinction today of being the
first American city to entertain the blue
jackets of the American battleshp fleet
after their long cruise around the world.


Two thousand sturdy. trim-looking
young men. who make up the greater
part of the enlisted personnel of the
fleet, paraded through the principal
streets of the city during the forenoon,
and afterward were Toasted and feted at
the new Naval Y. NJ c. a. building. COM
pleted since the fleet set sail on its
voyage.


Nearly 200 officers from the feet were
entertained at an elaborate luncheon at
the Monticello Hotel by the citizens
committee.


Night Procession.


Tonight. although the salormen are
once more safely slowed away in their
hammocks aboard the various ships of the
fleet Norfolk is continuing the celebration
of the homecoming. The downtown sec
ton of the city is brilliantly Illuminated
with festoons of incandescent lights.


There was an Illuminated parade during
the evening. Uniquely designed floats and
equipages were in line.


The splendid appearance and the SOL
dierly bearing of the tidy bluejackets as
they marched through the streets today
could not fail to elicit the warmest ad-
miration.- The people of Norfolk, to
whom naval displays are old. old stories.
and who are Enthusiastically undemon-
strative, were impressed and paid trib-
ute of silent admiration and pride, which
had d deeper meaning than the cheers
which broke now and then from the
thousands who thronged the streets and
sidewalks along the line of march.


Cheers for Tars.

out to witness the review of the blue
jackets. There was spontaneous cheer
when the sailors first came into view be-
hind an escort of coast artillery from Fort
Monroe.


There We're more cheers for the men of
the battleship Virginia. for the Vermont
companies proudly exhibiting their red

climbed out on the narrow window ledges

up scaling ladders soon as they arriv-
ed and also spread the fire nets.

jumped before the firemen could reach
them. One of these was caught in fire
net and escaped with a fractured leg.

held for moment and then gave way.
dropping her into the arms of a police
man who was standing on the sidewalks.

From the New York World.


The congress Of Swiss Women's Socie-
ties. which has just been meeting in
Berne. passed a resolution urging con-
scription for women.


The Swiss women not only seek equal
privileges with men. but are willing Ia
assume the burden of equal responsible
ties and equa. duties. Yet they have
common sense enough to realize that the
duties Of men and women are not the
same; SO, while the CONSUMPTION for men
requires their service in the army, the
CONSUMPTION the women ask for them
selves will require their service to learn
and practice nursing. first aid to the in
jured. the administration of civic or ma
tional relief to the poor and the general
work of phianthropic institutions. They
ask that all women between eighteen and
twenty years of age be subject to it for
two years.


These Swiss women also petitioned the
national congress to distribute copies OF
the civil code free to every member OF
their societies. The legislature promptly
acceded to this request. and now all the
women of Switzerland are busy studying
law.


What practical nation is the Swiss!
And what lessons in wisdom and COM
mon sense might not our professional
women and the more radical suffragettes
of England learn from their Swiss Sis
ters!

MARYSVILLE. Aug. 26.-The assault
and serious injury of Brakeman Capito
by four tramps at Chico Tuesday night
is being investigated by the sheriffs OF
Tehama and Butte counties.


The prisoners accused of attacking
the brakeman say that one of their
number was knocked from the train
near Tehama by Capito. who used an
iron bar in attacking their comrade.
They say, moreover, that the train crew
attempted to throw the whole party
from the train.


During the last six months many
tramps have been thrown from trains
and there has been considerable indig-
nation over this inhuman method. Sew
eral times tramps have been found on
the track severely injured.


On one or two occasions dead men
have been found on the right of way,
indicating that the crews have been
throwing men from trains while in mo-
tion.

VANCOUVER. B. c., May 27.-One
man is dead and four others SO badly
burned that they may die as the result
of a fire which occurred early this
morning on board the coasting freight
steamer Coquitlam on her way through
the Gulf of Georgia from this port.


The fire started just after daylight,
when Second Engineer Black and
fireman, name unknown, were alone in
the engine room. How the blaze orig
mated no one knows, but suddenly the
engine room was ablaze and the wood
work and flooring, saturated with oil
and very dry, burned fiercely. One fire.
man was roasted alive. Second En-
gineer Black nearly lost his life trying
to rescue the fireman. Second Mate
Watts was badly injured, and the burns
sustained by two Japanese firemen may
prove fatal.


The crew after a hard fight extin.
guished the fire and turned the steamer
back to Vancouver where the injured
were taken to hospitals. The financial
loss is several thousand dollars.

Mrs. e. c. Ransom, SO years old,
nurse in the Civil War, after whom the
Ransom home for friendless women in
Los Angeles was named, died early
yesterday morning at the Angelus hos
pital. She had been i'll since March Z,
when she accidentally fell and injured
her hip.


Mrs. Ransom, who was lovingly
friends as Mother" and "Aunty" Ran
som, had long been famous for her
charitable work, both i'll the east and
in Los Angeles.


She was one of the first recognized
regular women army nurses employed
in the Civil War, and during those
stormy times visited the army hospitals
and fields of battle, tending the wound
ed, sick and dying. For her valiant
services she was pensioned.


Mrs Ransom was greatly interested
in several homes for friendlesS women
in Richmond, Ind, and on coming to
Los Angeles, about twenty-siX years
ago, continued her interest in local
works She started the First Methodist
mission among the Chinese of Los An
geles about twenty-five years ago. This
mission, however, was broken up
through the anti-Chinese riots, which
occurred soon after its establishment.
Since coming 10 LOS Angeles MIS-

in the First Methodist church, of which
she was a member at the time of her
death. During the early struggles of
the home for friendless girls and wo-


men in Los Angeles, Mrs. Ransom gave
| her experience, interest and many of
| her worldly possessions to its support.
She always maintained a deep inter-


est in its welfare, and in that of the
girls and women who entered it. The
Home Missionary society was another

much of her attention.

There were 100 persons on board.


The escapes from the blazing vessel
were marvellous. A wild panic reigned.


The gang plank was thrown down to
allow the passengers to board a num-
ber of row boats that had been hur-
ried to the rescue, but it burned,
throwing fifteen people into the water
These were rescued with difficulty.

plank seized two little children and
swan to shore with them.


Captain Swain ordered the boat
beached. Life preservers were dis
tributed and the crew helped the
frightened passengers into the row
boats by which they were taken ashore
safely.

LONG BEACH, Oct. 21.-Commander
Eva c. Booth, commander-in-chi Of
the Salvation Army in the United States,
lectured at the First Methodist church
tonight to a huge and interested
throng, her subject being Bridging the
Gulf" About 5000 people crowded into
the church and many were turned
away, despite the fact that this church
has the largest auditorium of any
church on the coast. The lecture dealt
with many Of the interesting features
of the busy young woman's life. Her
audience was swayed from laughter to
tears many times, and the general eff
feet of the address was inspiring.


Miss Booth told of her work among
the poor and the degraded and of the
great need for the enlisting Of others
in the work. She gave many surpris-
ing facts regarding the people among
whom her work has been.


A regular street meeting under the
auspices of the local branch preceded
the lecture. A Salvation Army band
from Los Angeles played in the streets
here earlier in the evening and led the
way to the church at Fifth street and
Pacific avenue after the street service.
Miss Booth was the guest of the man
agement Of Hotel Virginia and mem
bers of her staff were guests at the
Hotel Kennebec.

RHYOLITE, New. Sept. 13.-The
bodies of Emory Bodge and Tom Flanz.
two miners who perished of thirst
while attempting to cross Death val
ley. were found Saturday four miles
west of Skidoo. Cal. by members of
the searching party securing the des-
.ert for a brother of President Eldridge
of the National sewing machine COM
pany, who has been lost for three
weeks.


The men whose bodies were found,
left Rhyolite late in August and started
across the floor of Death valley, where
the Thermometers reaches 130 degrees in
the shade during the summer months
They carried two canteens of water
each, but this supply was exhausted
before they had gone half way. Crazed
by thirst they wandered about until
they were overcome by the heat and
lay down to die.


I Young Eldridge was attempting to
reach this place from his mining claims
in the Panamint range. He left his
companions three weeks ago and never
arrived in Rhyolite. Men from all the
desert camps have searched the desert
and the burro which he took with him
when he started across the valley was
found few days ago, but there was
no trace of the man.

which the latter was victor, took place
yesterday in the barn of Manuel Comes,
a rancher. The reptile and the rodent
were turned loose together, with no es-
cape allowed for either, and while
Comes and his brother, Joseph, watched
them, they fought a battle that resulted
in the death of the rattler.


Twelve times the snake coiled and
shot out for the rat. Every time the
latter lodged. When the snake threw
itself forward for the thirteenth time
the rat got the hold it had failed to
get on the IL former attempts, and
strangled the reptile. When the fight
was over the rat was so exhausted
that it made no attempt to move when
the men approached it. They spared
the animal after its brave fight.


Joseph Comes caught the snake,
which was an enormous one. with 13
his brothers. barn, where the fight was
arranged. Manuel Comes had caught
an immense rat just previously. All
the cracks in the barn were carefully
closed The rat tried for long time to
find way out, but not succeeding, gave
fight to the rattlesnake. The rodent
circled about watching for chance
to sink its teeth into the snakes neck.
The snake struck out whenever a
chance to hit seemed likely. Every
time the snake jumped the rat got on
the snakes neck, but failed to get a
good hold until the thirteenth round.

NILES, Dec 21-The safe of the

packages whose value is unknown.


Mail sacks were piled about the safe

postoffice within the last four years.
Two years ago the same safe was blown

repaired and used again. but was old
and could offer little resistance to ex-
perienced dynamite burglars.

registered letters and packages can

contained many Christmas presents

An investigation this morning showed
that both front and rear doors of the
postoff1ce had been pried open to OBJ
tain admission to the building. The
Niles postoffice is isolated and affords
a good opportunity for thieves to work
unobserved. The entire place had been
ransacked, all the drawers and chests

NOGALES, A. T., May Yesterday
three prominent families of Nogales
on the Sonora, Mexico, side, narrowly
escaped being poisoned fatally by eat
ing dry mushrooms bought of a Chi
nese merchant.


Three Frenchmen, one the proprietor
of a hotel, one the manager of mer
camille house and one a druggist,
bought the mushrooms. The cook in
one family suspected they were the
poisonous species while she was cooking
them and threw them away.


The cook in the merchants family
prepared his, and the family partook
of some of the dish, but owing to the
peculiar taste the members of the fam
lily ate but little. Later all the mem
bers of the family were thrown into
convulsions, but soon recovered.


The druggist tested his dish while
cooking, detected the poisonous quality
and notified his friends and the health
officials. The matter will be 'rigidly in
vestigated. The mushrooms were inn
ported from China.

SAN BERNARDINO, July 24-The
thrilling tale of the narrow escape

by reliable railroad men from Hes
peria For two days the members Of
the party. which included George Nor
ton, Paul Dennison and Pedro Garcia.
were lost on the desert and wandered
miles from their original course with
out a drop of water one member OF
the party becoming demented through
the lack of drink and the intense heat


The lives of the entire party were
saved by the thunderstorm which Fri
day broke over the mountains and des-
ert The men left Sheep Hole noun
tain. where they have valuable claims,
Thursday morning, intending to make
their way to Rose mine and then into
San Bernardno by the way Of Bear
valley In some manner they lost
their way and wandered for two days
and nights on the parched desert with
out water.


Finally Garcia, who was the most
familiar with the desert, recognized
Copper Peak in the distance, but in
the exhausted condition of their bur
Tos they We're unable to proceed. Nor
ton was suffering from delirium ana
was on the verge of insanity and the
other two members of the party gave
up hope of reaching water alive.


Suddenly the thunderstorm broke
in the mountains and for twenty min
utes the rain poured down on them.
Dennison threw Morton on his back
and himself lay down facing the drip
ping heavens with wide open mouth
to catch a few drops of rain.


Garcia had the presence of mind to
rush to the wagon and spread out the
cooking utensils and also a large cam
vas in which sufficient water was
caught to save their lives.


The party made its way to Box
Springs and then into Hesperia, where
the train for Los Angeles was taken.

pIiSl SpdCc, anu STc WAS asked Wndt

SAUSALITO, Sept. 13.-Test maneu-
versA We're made by the United states
submarines Pike and Grampus in the
bay off California City today, and ac-
cording to the officers in command We're
most satisfactory. The Pike, in COM
mand of Lieutenant K. B. Crittenden,
left her moorings here at $3.50 this
morning and, accompanied by the United
States tug Fortune, proceeded to the
place chosen for the experiments.


The little submarine was trimmed and
everything made snug, with Lieutenant
Crittenden and 10 men aboard. Gradu-
ally the cigar shaped hull sank beneath
the surface, until only the tube through
which reflections of tie horizon are seen
remained in view. Fourteen feet under
the water the crew crouched at their
various stations, breathing air supplied
from tanks, which contain 10000 pounds
under pressure.


For almost an hour the men remained
submerged, while the Pike dove and
rose at various levels and covered sew
eral miles in her maneuyers. The eight
tons of water which had been used to
sink the boat were forced from the
tanks by means of compressed air when
the signal was given for the rise, and
the little craft shot into the daylight
like spouting whale.


Other experiments. such as turning
out the electric lights when the craft
was submerged and forcing the men to
work the machinery in the dark, were
tried and proved very successful


The conditions and possible accidents
of warfare will all be taken into con-
sidera ton during the tests, which will
continue for several months.

LIVERPOOL, Aug. 15-The Cunard
line steamer Lucania lies submerged
tonight at the Husklsson dock, serious
ly damaged from fire that broke out
on board Saturday evening. The flames
are supposed to have originated in the
saloon kitchen.


The flames gradually worked forward
until they reached the steerage, con-
suming every particle of the woodwork,
and then played havoc with the fore
hold The heat was tremendous and
the flames, shooting high from the ves-
sci, attracted thousands of persons to
the river, where they remained
throughout the night.


At 3 o'clock this morning II was de-
cided to flood the vessel by admitting
water from the deck. Soon she heeled
over and her tunnels came i'm contact
with the Cranes dock and were badly
damaged. A half dozen firemen who
were on the gangway at this time
were thrown into the water, but all
were rescued. A fleet of tugs pulled
the liner upright and held her until
she settled finally on the mud bottom.
1t was 10 o'clock this morning before
the fire was under control.


The second class quarters and the
whole after part of the boat, including
the engine room, escaped injury, and
comparatively little damage was done
to the exterior of the vessel.


Her upper part is considerably above
water. The first saloon skylghts were
destroyed and the decks forward badly
buckled. Some of the hull plates were
warped by the heat.


Late tonight the Lucania was re-
f1oated with the aid of salvage tugs and.
powerful pumps. She will be dry
docked and towed to Glasgow for re-
pairs.

ish lines declares that Spanish prison
ers, after being horribly tortured and

ruga.

whelming thirst, they have drunk from
stagnant pools. Many cases of poison

men have died from this cause.

SAN BERNARDINO, Oct. 23.-Ship-

wandering for two days without food
on the rugged desert regions bordering
the river, Capt. e. Nelson and his mate,
Max Bley, have just reached the min
ing camp at Eldorado with the tale of
their terrible experience.


With a cargo on their small river
boat, the two men left Riverside ranch
for Homestake mine, and while battling
against a terrific north wind and a
swift current the ship was dashed
against a half submerged rock and cap
sized. Nelson and Bley managed to
reach the shore after a hard fight in
the current which swept them for a
long distance down stream before they
We're able to pull themselves exhausted
on to the rugged bank.


AS is the custom of the river
mariners, neither men was wearing
shoes at the time the boat sank, and,
stranded on the bleak shore without
food and little clothing, they nearly
perished Aefore reaching the mining
camp. They used their underclothing to
protect their feet in the long walk over
the rugged desert country.


The cold winds sweeping off the river
and the lack of food made the men
physical wrecks, and it will be days
before they recover from their hard
ships in their search for help.

text:
James Donnelly, half breed Indian
1 OF the Hoopa valley reservation in
Humboldt county has been arrested by
| the United states authorities and is
| confined in the Alameda county Jail to
answer to the charge of numbering
Chickasaw, an Indian, more than six
/ years ago. The murder was the eli


max of a feud. far reaching and as


fierce as any that Kentucky or Ten


nessee ever knew.


Murder was followed by murder un-
til at length all those who had ranged


themselves as partisans of one side or
| the other were killed except only the


Indian, Chickasaw, and his never sleep
| Ing enemy, the halfbreed, Donnelly,
| who, combining with his native cruelty
the cunning of the white man. nursed


the blood feud and kept alive the fame


Of hate.


LIFE AGAINST LIFE


| For years the hills and remote, al


most unexplored valleys that hide away
among the mountains of Humboldt
county formed hunting ground where


Indian against halfbreed played the
game of life and death-a game that


meant fnality for one of them. The
game was played alone, the other In
dians knowing that to take sides meant
but to furnish fresh fuel to the fury
of the feud And halfbreed skill and
cunning, the lore OF woods from In
dian ancestry and the cold calcula-
ton Of the Anglo-Saxon mind, deter


mined who should win the game.
From far niountainside, where shell
tering trees made a close ambush, a


rifle bullet sped one day. and then
an Indian lay below the plying skies.
the Indian Chickasaw, marking the
last play of the game, mute evidence
that the blood feud had been wiped


away with blood.


For years the murderer kept in hid
ing. but finally his caution lost it's
edge and he returned to the Hoopa
valley reservation, where the Indians
sheltered him, through fear, perhaps
perhaps not caring to fan the feud
again into an active flame. But in the
end the law of blood for blood called
for accounting and demanded life for
life.


MANY SUBSEQUENT MURDERS
The federal officers whose duty de-
mands that they keep peace on Indian
reservations were called to Humboldt
county by what seemed almost an cpl
demic of crime. Oscar Porter, a store
keeper on the reservation, had been
murdered In cold blood and shortly fol-
lowing Bert Porter, a white man. and
Joe Vierra. a Portuguese, had yielded up
their lives to some assassin. This was
in December of last year.


Slowly but surely the government
cast and drew its net and when the
meshes filtered all the suspects the


murder of six long slow passing years
arose to call for blood atonement. A
mere hint here, a mere breath there
and threads gathered into q rope that
bound the halfbreed to the corpse that
lay below the California skies so long
ago. Slowly but immutably the law
built up its case and now, before the
halfbreed whose stealth and cunning
carried him through all the dangers of
the feud there lifts the shadow of the
gallows. the stern and unforgetting
justice OF the white mans law.


That Donnelly had any hand in the
murders which were responsible for
his capture is not believed. Since com
ing down from where the mountains
gave him sanctuary he has been free
from trouble of any kind. The feud
that burned so brightly was ended. the
game that he had played had ended to
rifle bullet flying forth from ambush
and the faction that he fought was
dead and gone. But back of it. still
unforgetting, justice with blinded ewes
slept not and in the end it trapped him
and confronts him with the rope

The origin of dominos has been attribut-
ed variously to the Greeks. the Chinese
and Jews. but a Paris contemporary has
discovered that the ever-popnlar game
owes its invention to the Benedictines OF
Mont Cassin. Two Of the order were sent
into lengthy retreat, and they hit upon a
method OF Willing away the spare time
without infringing the rules OF silence by
playing with square stones, upon which
various dots were marked. While per-
fecting themselves. they perfected,
rather evolved. the game. and were ac-
customed to frequently repeat when play
ing in the evening psalms from vespers,
especially the first. that is. Psalm CIN.
which begins .'Dixit Dominus Domino
meo" When the retreat was over the
game was soon known in the convent
Then its fame spread 10 the village and
beyond The verse was reduced to one
word Domino hence the name as we
have received it.

Seeing burglar attempting to enter
her residence through rear window
shortly, after midnight yesterday Mrs.
Amelia Fest. wife of William Fest, a
shoe dealer, 13S Devisadero street.
grabbed revolver and sent two shots
above his head. The man dropped to
the ground and, doubling like hare
scurried over a fence and was lost to
sight.


Mrs. Fest was alone in the house
with her children, her husband having
been detained down town on business.
She had retired for the night, but was
awakened by servant maid, who told
her that she thought there was a burg
lar walking about the back yard.


Without moments hesitation Mrs.
Fest reached for the revolver that was
kept in the house for just such emer-
gencies. Walking to a room off the
kitchen she switched on the lights
bringing to full view the form of 8
man in the act of entering through the
window.


What do you want?" she asked.


The burglar hesitated and then made
a movement as if to enter the room at
all costs. The next instant the plucky
woman swung around with her re-
volver and fired twice, both shots pass
ing over the mans head. The burglar
hesitated no longer. He dropped to the
ground and sought the darkness like
iackrabbit. The matter was reported
TO the police yesterday.

Two hundred and fifty soldiers at
Angel island fought big brush fire
last night that swept over the hillside,
laid nearly half the acreage bare. and
threatened to destroy the buildings of
the quarantine station. The men
battled against the flames from 5
o'clock in the evening until II o'clock
termined efforts that the federal prop
erty was saved


The fire broke out in the dry grass
on the northeastern slope of the island
at point opposite California City.
The brush at this point is thick and,
parched by the heat of the last few
days, made easy fuel for the blaze An
alarm was sounded and the entire force
stationed at the post. was called out.
The men were quickly organized into
three brigades. one hurrying TO the
front with wet sacks, another carry
ing buckets OF water to the scene.
apparatus to good advantage to save
the quarantine buildings and the new
immigration station.


The flames ran rapidly through the
brush, swept down to the waters edge
and then, covering a broad area, con-
tinued across the island. The smoke
was so dense that it made the work
unusually difficult. Several men were
forced to stop from exhaustion. Others
were overcome by the smoke.


At o'clock at night the fire was
turned away from the buildings and
the entire force attacked the blazing
brush. A trench was run ahead of
the fire, but it leaped the gap and
broke out afresh. 1t was II o'clock at
night before the flames were finally
checked. Almost half the area of the
island was laid waste.

CINCINNATI. March 26.--After trav-
cling for four months through the body
Of Mrs. Oakla Bay Jennings, piercing
the walls of the stomach and penetrat-
ing the lungs, a glass-headed steel pin,
accidentally swallowed by Mrs. Jen-
nings, again made its appearance in her
mouth and has been extracted.


Mrs. Jennings was walking along the
street one day about four months ago,
when she swallowed the pin. Within
a few days her lungs became affected
and she was attacked with severe
coughing spells.


Her condition grew worse and with
in the past several weeks she almost
lost her voice. Wednesday night she
was seized with a severe choking at
tack, threw up her hands and called
to her husband for assistance.


She put her hand to her mouth and
extracted the pin from the soft palate,
from which one end of it projected.


The pin had made a complete circuit
in the woman's body. 1t had become
very rusty and a hard substance had
accumulated on it, making it almost
twice as large as it originally had been.


Mrs. Jennings experienced instant re-
lief upon its extraction and is hopefully
looking forward to complete recovery.

She should have had larger audience
though she could hardly have had a
more enthusiastic one. After every

applause that silenced for the time

siasm.

ber the Chopin waltz in d fat and
after many recalls gave Schumann's s
..Nachstuck" In everything she played

clan and the touch of the artist


After the presentation of Liszt's sec

program. Miss Goodson was given an
ovation She had shown herself equal
to the task of presenting the master
pieces of piano compositions from
Beethoven to Strauss and the last
number was the final evidence of her
technical and emotional possibilities
The audience, though small, would not
let her go, and individually proved that
the praise which has been given the
player elsewhere was not more than a
due and proper recognition of her
worth


In her Schumann numbers she showed
romance: in her Beethoven sonata-the
one in sharp minor-she displayed
strength and virility; in the Brahms
and Strauss pieces she discovered to
her hearers wrists of steel and a
fine musical intelligence, and finally in
the Tschaikowsky "Humoresuue" she
showed herself poet. The only pity
was that the rain pattered down on the
streets and kept music lovers away.

Z GALVESTON, Tex. October 0.-The oil
steamship Winifred. Capt Jenkins, came
across the waterlogged schooner Kate
Feore, early this week, in the gulf, 500
miles from land.


The schooner had been adrift for twenty
days. For sixteen days the crew had
been without food and for several days
without water.


The schooner was bound from Mobile
to Matanzas. Cuba. A day before the oil
steamship picked up the wreck. $50 miles
out of its course. one of the crew, Carl
Rudolf. died. Another sailor. Will Behr-
man, was washed overheard.


The schooner sailed from Mobile
September 49, was struck by hurricane
In the gulf September 10. disabled and
waterlogged after four-day fight with
the storm.


A few cans of tomatoes and corn were
fished from the water filled cabin. The
water supply was ruined.


September o. six days without water
the crew caught about eight quarts of
rain water In cans and managed to make
this do about four days. Three Of the
crew had to be tied to the deckhouse to
keep them from consuming all the water.


From September % the men were with
out food or water. Five of them, 1t Is
feared. may never fully recover from the
experience.


For several days before rescue they
had been eating barnacles scraped from
the sides of the schooner by three of their
associates. the others being too weak to
do this


To add to their sufferings the men saw
four steamers pass within hailing dis
tance.

the signal to the engineer to hoist.


He was carried to the surface and
escaped with his life, although not
before he received severe scalp wounds
by flying rock.


His companions got the full force of

Several tons of rock fell over them,

pathies were also clearly with the young

injured.

the left leg below and above the knee

laying bare the knee joint and the
femur its entire length.

of the accident to his home, where Drs.
Garrett and Dewitt attended him, the
police surgeon making the run from
the city jail to the boys home in less
than three minutes in an automobile.
